Putin believes that if he inflicts enough terror on Ukrainian civilians, he can compel a new, massive wave of migrants to flee the country for Europe ahead of regional elections in Germany and a presidential election in France, bolstering anti-Ukraine, far-right parties in both places and pushing the continent away from Kyiv. Should this bombing campaign alone not be enough to turn the tide and force Kyiv to accept Putin’s demands, the Kremlin can increase the pressure by mobilizing more men. Putin has mobilized the country once, in late 2022, when he conscripted people from across the country’s provinces. This succeeded at generating hundreds of thousands of new troops, but it led to a temporary drop in Putin’s approval rating and an exodus of hundreds of thousands of military-age men. In response, he switched to using cash incentives. But now that this system is reaching its limits, the regime is preparing to switch back to conscription—this time relying on electronic draft notices that are quieter and can be sent out year-round to thousands of potential conscripts. These conscripts, unlike the ones of 2022, would be blocked at the border if they tried to leave Russia. The country’s law enforcement agencies could also use digital surveillance cameras and facial recognition tools to search for draft dodgers and threaten them with a (newly introduced) two-year prison sentence. The mobilization will almost certainly cause some renewed discontent, but the process will be far less flashy than in 2022, when Putin went on national TV and announced a mobilization, and will thus attract less attention. The Kremlin is also likely to make sure that the mobilization effort largely skips over the capital and other large cities, and instead focuses on poorer areas. Moscow can also further increase the pressure on Europe. It could carry out more hybrid attacks, or deniable military operations that fall short of outright warfare but still damage or threaten a target. Throughout the previous four years, Russia has, for example, sent drones and clandestine operatives to disrupt European defense production facilities, military bases, and transport infrastructure. (It denies responsibility for all these attacks.) But it could expand its list of targets in hopes of further disrupting life for ordinary Europeans, including by damaging commercial warehouses with cheap drones. BITTER END Not everyone in the Russian establishment wants to continue the war, let alone escalate it. Among the country’s elite, one can now find voices calling for genuine negotiations. ln May, for example, Russia’s flagship foreign affairs journal published an article by Vasily Kashin, a prominent, pragmatic but nationalistic military analyst, that made the case for freezing the conflict. Russia, Kashin argued, could not achieve more on the battlefield in the short to medium term, and the costs of prolonged war were starting to outstrip strategic benefits. Given the journal’s prominence, Kashin’s article was almost certainly previewed and green-lighted by officials in the Kremlin, likely as a way of giving voice to the pragmatists in the Russian security establishment. Likewise, on June 30, the CEO of Russia’s largest bank (and a longtime Putin lieutenant) suggested that it was time to wrap up the conflict. “I don’t think there is a single person in the country who has any concerns other than the swiftest conclusion of the hostilities,” he said. But this option is currently of no interest to Putin. Although he tolerates cautious calls for peace and sometimes sends signals that he is interested in a settlement, too, Putin’s actions suggest that he is not ready to crawl out of the hole he is now in. In fact, he seems to want to keep digging. As long as Putin is convinced that he has an advantage over Ukraine with the destructiveness of his ballistic missiles and that Ukraine is vulnerable because of its lack of interceptors, he is likely to keep trying to wear Ukraine down—no matter the damage to his country. He views uncoordinated calls from Americans and Europeans for talks or for a cease-fire as a ploy to buy Ukraine more time. “We know that the West continues to pursue Russia’s strategic defeat,” he said in the June 28 interview. “Why are they calling for a cease-fire and peace negotiations? . . . If Ukraine is, as they claim, capturing more and more territory . . . then Western leaders simply need to wait. Russia’s strategic defeat would, it would seem, come about of its own accord.” Ukraine and its allies need to prepare for a long and bumpy road. Kyiv may be in the best position in the war since late 2022, but the Kremlin believes it will crush the will of Ukraine and its friends this winter. Russia may be struggling, but Putin has not exhausted his options. He still wants to fight for as long as possible. You are reading a free article Subscribe to Foreign Affairs to get unlimited access. - Paywall-free reading of new articles and over a century of archives - Six issues a year in print and online, plus audio articles - Unlock access to the Foreign Affairs app for reading on the go

item.title: Your Apple Watch Is Quietly Gaining a New Feature to Help Extend Its Battery Life
item.description:
Source: Gear Patrol Score: 5.27
The weakest aspect of the Apple Watch has always been its battery life. Its so-called “all day” battery life pales in comparison to other smartwatches on the market, which, depending on the model, can last for multiple days, weeks or even longer. In recent years, Apple has rolled out numerous new features to help extend the battery life of its smartwatch. This includes a Low Power mode, minimizing notifications and turning off the always-on display (which every one of its current models now has). With watchOS 27, the upcoming new operating system set to launch in September, Apple is quietly giving the Apple Watch another feature that aims to get more out of its battery life. It’s called Proactive Battery Extension Notifications. Smart (battery) savings As initially reported by 9to5Mac, Proactive Battery Extension Notifications is a new feature coming with watchOS 27 that effectively works in the background, observes your habits and which battery-draining features you aren’t using, and then disables them on your Apple Watch.

item.title: G-Shock’s Ultra-Rugged Mudmaster Gets a Beautiful Gold-Toned Makeover
item.description:
Source: Gear Patrol Score: 4.93
In 2015, G-Shock expanded its Master of G line with an “extreme land” model, the Mudmaster. It wasn’t just shock-resistant and durable but was engineered to keep fine dirt, sand and mud from getting inside the watch. Since then, the Mudmaster has evolved considerably, becoming the watchmaker’s flagship. The GG-B1000 became the first to introduce Carbon Core Guard construction and Bluetooth connectivity. And it even added step tracking, a fourth sensor to go along with the altimeter/barometer, compass and thermometer. Needless to say, the Mudmaster is arguably G-Shock’s most rugged option. However, with its latest version, you’d never guess it. Into the sunset Launched as part of its Master of Horizon Gold series, this new Mudmaster variant (GG-B100XMH-5A) features a beautiful stainless steel bezel finished in a yellow-gold ion plating. According to the brand, it’s “inspired by the golden horizon where earth meets sky.” Locked down with a brown cage, the bezel foregrounds a black carbon case and a dark brown resin strap. Other components, such as the metal pins in the bezel receive brown ion plating.

item.title: Nike’s New ACG Hiker Quietly Doubles as an All-Black, All-Conditions Tactical Boot
item.description:
Source: Gear Patrol Score: 4.88
Nike’s ACG Zegama Hike already headlines the relaunch of the company’s cult-favorite outdoor division, All Conditions Gear. But the capable boot is only now beginning to show its true colors. The ACG Zegama Hike “Anthracite” drops the earthy, trail-coded palette of earlier releases in favor of a blacked-out finish that wouldn’t look out of place in a special-ops field kit. All black gear On the technical side, little has changed under the hood. Nike built the Zegama Hike around a breathable upper, Vibram Megagrip outsole and a dual-compound midsole made with ZoomX foam, grounding the boot in technology that established Nike’s reputation on the roads.

item.title: New Balance’s Latest 2010 Variant Proves Carbon Fiber Works Just as Well on Sneakers
item.description:
Source: Gear Patrol Score: 4.72
Ever since Nike dropped the Vaporfly 4% in 2017 and invented the modern super shoe category, pretty much every running brand has been implementing carbon fiber in their own footwear. However, the strong, lightweight material is typically only used on the interior of the midsole; you know it’s there but you don’t see it (with the occasional exception, of course). New Balance has also used carbon fiber plenty, from the very first 5280 to the current flagship FuelCell SuperComp Elite racing shoe. But with the latest version of its 2010 lifestyle sneaker, the brand has yet to really employ exposed carbon as an aesthetic element. From cars to sneakers Much like we’ve seen in the automotive and watch industries, where carbon fiber might get showcased front and center, New Balance has now done the same for its new silhouette. This time, it transitions from its running catalog to one of its most popular streetwear shoes in recent years: the 99X-inspired 2010. Luckily, the footwear icon doesn’t go overkill with the material. Exposed carbon can really only be seen embedded in the upper, right below the top of the laces and around the heel area, as well as at the side of the tongue.

item.title: Porter Yoshida Uses Genuine Japanese Space Fabric in Its Utilitarian ‘Bounce’ EDC Bags
item.description:
Source: Gear Patrol Score: 4.71
For the past 14 months, Porter Yoshida & Co, the beloved Japanese EDC and travel bag purveyor, has been oddly quiet. Now we’ve found out at least one of the reasons why: the outfit has been working on an impressive new collection. Called Porter Yoshida Bounce, this set of five bags was built on literal space-age technology. And soon, it can be yours. Spacefaring fabric The brand’s first new launch in over a year is certainly one worth waiting for, and that’s largely thanks to the material the collection is built upon. Called “Triaxial Woven Fabric,” this material comes directly from Japan’s space program. In fact, this very fabric was used in the Hayabusa space probe, developed by the Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency to travel to a near-Earth asteroid, collect material samples and return to our home planet.

item.title: Yeti Evolves Its Ranchero EDC Bag Into a Smaller, Speedier Pack with a Unique Magnetic Closure
item.description:
Source: Gear Patrol Score: 4.69
In 2024, Yeti acquired cult-favorite travel and outdoor bag brand Mystery Ranch for a whopping $36.2 million. Together, the brands’ first project was a limited-edition backpack called the Bozeman. By 2025, the EDC and travel bag had evolved into a permanent part of Yeti’s catalog, renamed the Ranchero. Now, that same bag has gone through another evolution, getting smaller and speedier without losing its stellar construction and feature set in the Yeti Ranchero Crossbody. Rancherito The original Yeti Ranchero is a full-sized backpack. At the moment, there are four sizes, ranging from 12 liters to 27 liters, but they all share the same overall format and construction, including a signature three-zipper opening (a fan-favorite holdover from Mystery Ranch). The Ranchero Crossbody, perhaps unsurprisingly, takes the same overall construction, design and feature set ethos and pares it down to a far more compact, entirely new silhouette: a crossbody bag (or sling or fanny pack, depending on who you ask). While they share functional, material and stylistic elements, they also vary greatly.

item.title: Mitsubishi’s Latest Teaser Just Proved Its Pajero Revival’s Rugged Ambitions
item.description:
Source: Gear Patrol Score: 4.53
Mitsubishi hasn’t been shy in its efforts to drum up excitement for the relaunch of the Pajero. Between shadowy rollers, headlight signatures and triptych gauge clusters, there have been plenty of sneak peeks. For good reason. As part of its comeback effort, Mitsubishi is setting its sights on rugged off-roaders like the Toyota Land Cruiser and the Nissan Patrol. It means a truly rugged SUV, not just a revival in name. Just take the latest teaser, for example. As a show of good faith, Mitsubishi has offered a first look at the upcoming Pajero’s undercarriage and confirmed some key details. Climbing the ladder It’s just what you’d hope for in an authentically off-road-capable SUV. Along with a ladder frame construction, Mitsubishi has also stated that the forthcoming Pajero will tout the brand’s Super-All Wheel Control (S-AWC) tech. In the case of the former, the benefits are obvious. Body-on-frame SUVs make for far superior off-roaders compared to their unibody counterparts, as they’re generally tougher and more capable.

item.title: Seiko’s $750 Speedtimer Chronograph Gets a New “Edo Purple” Dial
item.description:
Source: Gear Patrol Score: 4.50
Seiko continues its yearlong celebration of 145 years in business with a new quintet of limited-edition watches. This time, the connecting theme is color, with all five dials decorated in “Edo purple.” The color has a rich cultural significance and deep ties to Seiko’s hometown of Tokyo, originally known as Edo, but it also just looks really good on a watch dial. The Prospex Speedtimer stands out for its stark departure from the muted black, white and steel or flashy warm colors typically found on racing chronographs. The Prospex Speedtimer 145th Anniversary Limited Edition “Edo purple” follows the collection’s standard blueprint, featuring a 42mm stainless steel case topped with a fixed aluminum tachymeter bezel operated with dual button pushers flanking a fluted crown. The eye-catching violet dial is enhanced with a sunburst finish and encircled by a metallic rehaut with a black rule-style seconds track. The beveled hour and minute hands and applied hour markers have gold-tone plating and white LumiBrite inserts. A need for speed This is a solar quartz version of the Prospex Speedtimer, powered by a Seiko Caliber V192 movement. It has a stated accuracy of ±15 seconds per month and will run for six months on a full charge. The Panda-style black subdials consist of a synched 24-hour time at 3:00, a 60-minute totalizer at 6:00 and a small seconds at 9:00. A date window is tucked away at 4:30 with a white track on a black disc.

item.title: Huckberry’s Best-Selling In-House Jeans Get a Japanese Shuttle Loom Upgrade
item.description:
Source: Gear Patrol Score: 4.49
Huckberry maintains one of the best-curated selections of wholesale accessories and apparel on the internet. While the Austin-based company is a go-to source for cool products and respected brands, it has quietly built a substantial in-house roster that covers the full spectrum of wardrobe needs. Most of the brands, like Proof, Wills and Luca, are small and specialized, but Flint & Tinder is the flagship and could easily stand on its own as a full-service apparel brand. One category it does really well is jeans, and its selection just got even better with the addition of a Japanese stretch selvedge denim. Flint and Tinder’s new Japanese Stretch Selvedge Denim was a pet project for the brand’s Design Director, and noted denim head, Nick Kemp. His goal was to create something that retained the look and feel of well-loved vintage denim with just enough stretch baked in to negate a break-in period. To execute his vision, Kemp went to Kaihara Mills, one of Japan’s oldest textile manufacturers. Its vertically integrated facilities produce close to half of all Japanese denim annually and supply premium lines for big brands like Levi’s Blue Label, Lee 101 and J.Crew. The result is a 12.5-ounce selvedge denim made from 98-percent cotton and 2-percent elastane, woven on vintage shuttle looms.

item.title: Hoka’s New Clifton Is Trail-Inspired, Forecast-Proof and Long Overdue
item.description:
Source: Gear Patrol Score: 4.39
It’s been a few years since the Hoka Clifton really lived up to its reputation as a “do-it-all” workhorse. Though previous iterations of the longstanding franchise have prioritized versatility with lightweight midsoles and tried-and-true materials, Hoka made a perplexing call with the Clifton 10. In short, it chose not to release a winterized version of the shoe, leaving fans between a rock and hard place: either suck it up or opt for a previous generation. The just-released Clifton 11 has already remedied the issue. Set to drop September 1, the upcoming Clifton 11 GTX is the first Gore-Tex-equipped Clifton since 2023. The model shares some of the specs found in the baseline Clifton model, including the same stack height (42mm), drop (8mm) and midsole material (compression-molded EVA foam).

item.title: Marantz’s New Receivers Are Built for Serious Home Theater Setups
item.description:
Source: Gear Patrol Score: 4.37
Marantz has just introduced its first new batch of AV receivers in several years. The all-new Cinema Series 2 is the second generation of its 2022 Cinema range. And, like before, it consists of three options: the Cinema 50 Series 2, the Cinema 60 Series 2 and the Cinema 70s Series 2. According to the American-Japanese hi-fi manufacturer, the new Series 2 models “introduce meaningful advancements in sound quality, connectivity, gaming compatibility, and installation flexibility.” Marantz Cinema Series 2 All three AV receivers in the Cinema Series 2 feature numerous improvements. Each now packs a new 32-bit, eight-channel DAC that promises to help deliver higher-resolution audio across all channels. They’ve been integrated with the latest HEOS platform for superior multi-room functionality. And they pack numerous HDMI 2.1 inputs, supporting more advanced gaming technologies (like 144p video pass-through and AMD FreeSync).

item.title: Ford’s New Small Electric Pickup Finally Gets a Name (and Price)
item.description:
Source: Gear Patrol Score: 4.36
Last fall, Ford announced it would be shaking up the industry with a concept known as the universal electric vehicle (UEV). With a modular design and assembly-tree manufacturing, it promised to disrupt the BEV segment in price and range. As if that wasn’t enough, the brand also stated that the first vehicle to bring the platform to market would be a compact pickup. Designed for affordability down to the inch, the truck sounded like a refreshing break from the usual industry bloat. The Blue Oval still isn’t quite ready to reveal the upcoming truck in full, but it has at least decided on what to call it and how much it plans to charge. Meet (well, at least in name) the Fathom, Ford’s $28,350 challenge to the status quo. Accessible modern potential If you can’t fathom (sorry, just one) why Ford decided to name the truck what it did over something, say, a little more grounded in history, know that you’re not alone. I too had my hopes up for a Ranchero.

item.title: Ram’s 1500 Pickups Are Returning to the V8 Option Truck Fans Really Want
item.description:
Source: Gear Patrol Score: 4.35
When Ram reintroduced the 5.7-liter Hemi to the 1500 pickup, the brand was so proud of the moment that it even designed a “symbol of protest” badge in celebration. It’s a little ironic, honestly. Because although the move did mark the return of a V8 once dropped in the name of emissions, its revival was accompanied by eTorque tech. Yep, a mild hybrid. But now it seems the brand is ready to prove its commitment once again. If the latest reports are to be believed, Ram will soon drop eTorque from its 1500 pickups in favor of the simpler, gas-only setup. Down with Hemi eTorque The confirmation comes courtesy of Mopar Insiders, as the outlet received word from a spokesperson stating that “Starting early in the 2027 model year, Ram will phase out the 5.7-liter HEMI V8 eTorque, replacing it with the non-hybridized version of the 5.7-liter HEMI V8.”

item.title: Creative’s New Affordable Desktop Speakers Promise a True Hi-Fi Experience in a Compact Package
item.description:
Source: Gear Patrol Score: 4.35
Creative’s New Affordable Desktop Speakers Promise a True Hi-Fi Experience in a Compact Package Creative continues showing how computer speakers are properly done. Plus, Mercedes-AMG reveals its first production-ready AMG GT EV, a new nostalgic portable MP3 player startup and more. The Creative XF1 is a set of powered computer speakers designed to deliver impressive sound from a small package. Each speaker has a bi-amp configuration, meaning a dedicated amp powers the tweeter and the woofer, and the system delivers 72 watts and has a frequency range of 55Hz to 40kHz. The system features USB-C and aux inputs, so they can easily be used as speakers for your computer or turntable. They have built-in Bluetooth with LDAC support, so you can stream high-resolution audio to them. And they are compatible with the Creative Nexus app, which allow you to further fine-tune audio settings. Mercedes-AMG just revealed its first production-ready entrant to its radical new performance EV, the radically new AMG GT 53 Four-Door Coupe. Heralded as the Three-Point Star’s biggest new vehicles of the decade, the AMG GT 53 represents the first of many rollouts based on the shocking AMG GT XX Concept from last year. The AMG GT 53 Four-Door Coupe kicks off the production lineup with 536 horsepower an 590 pound-feet of torque, resulting in a 0-60 mph in just 3.4 seconds. But because the new AMG GT represents Mercedes-Benz and AMG’s most innovative electric powertrains and the summation of all its related efforts, the AMG GT 53 sports the company’s latest Formula One-derived 800-volt electric propulsion system. The result is a projected range of 540 miles, 311 of which can be recharged in under 10 minutes. There’s also an emulator, which will simulate the experience of the company’s gasoline inline six. The AMG GT 53 Four-Door Coupe is scheduled to hit US dealers in early 2027. If the Game Boy and the iPod had a baby, this would be it. The AP30 Music Boy is a miniature music player with tactile controls for selecting and streaming your music with hi-res audio. You can connect via Bluetooth or USB to your phone, or you can insert a microUSB up to 256GB. Designed to be handheld and portable, the Music Boy can either hang around your neck or attach to the back of your phone with a removable magnetic clip. Funding on Kickstarter ends August 17. Even before they appeared in The Sandlot, P.F. Flyers were iconic American sneakers. But this new collaboration with Story Mfg, a London-based sustainable fashion label, kicks the craftsmanship into high gear, courtesy of a new handwoven, naturally dyed upper. This classic sneaker is available in two versions (one solid indigo blue and another indigo-and-sepia checkered), and each example is unique, courtesy of the imperfections of its hand-crafted elements. Both shoes are limited-edition and come with their own dust bags to keep them in good shape between wears. Daniel Craig’s first on-screen outfit as James Bond is back. The “Madagascar Outfit” from Casino Royale has been recreated by Anthony Sinclair, 007’s original on-screen tailor, and Academy Costumes, the outfitter that made the original clothing seen in the film 20 years ago. The outfit consists of the Madagascar Shirt and Trousers, both of which were made using the original patterns from the film and reproduce all original details. The short-sleeve patterned shirt is made from the same Liberty printed cotton fabric as the original, while the gray drawstring trousers are made from 100 percent Irish linen. Both items are priced at $395 each.

item.title: Bose Just Upgraded Its Entry-Level QuietComfort Headphones with Flagship Features and Wired Hi-Fi
item.description:
Source: Gear Patrol Score: 4.35
Bose’s line of QuietComfort headphones has been synonymous with best-in-class active noise-cancellation for decades. After some odd naming conventions, the iconic American audio brand returned to form and revamped the line in late 2023 with two new models: the QuietComfort Headphones and the flagship QuietComfort Ultra Headphones. Obviously, advancements in tech and acoustics happen fast. So, just two years later, Bose introduced second-generation versions of its QuietComfort Ultra Headphones. Compared to the previous flagships, they delivered improved sound, better active noise cancellation, longer battery life and some new features … chief among them, support for lossless audio via a USB-C wired connection. Bose’s revamped QuietComforts However, at the time, Bose did not update the QuietComfort Headphones, which are the more affordable siblings to the QuietComfort Ultra Headphones. That’s now finally changing. Bose has finally introduced the QuietComfort Headphones (2nd-Gen). They’re still positioned as more affordable versions of Bose’s flagship noise-canceling cans, the QuietComfort Ultra Headphones (2nd-Gen), but they have been upgraded in some key areas and have gained some of the Ultra’s flagship features.

item.title: Triangle Just Gave Its Beloved Hi-Fi Speakers a Beautiful and Timeless Upgrade
item.description:
Source: Gear Patrol Score: 4.25
In January of this year, Triangle introduced the Capella 2, a second-generation version of its 2024-released wireless speaker system. It features a pair of active bookshelf speakers and a separate streaming hub (which houses all its wireless and wired connections). The system costs $3,500. If that’s too rich for your blood, the French loudspeaker specialist offers a more affordable active wireless speaker system: the AIO Twin. Introduced in 2021, it’s almost as versatile and just as easy to set up, and it brings the company’s signature sound to a sub-$1,000 price point. As of today, Triangle has announced that it’s releasing its AIO Twin speaker system in a new finish: Macassar. An ever-changing wood veneer The new Macassar finish is inspired by Macassar ebony, an Indonesian hardwood known for its dark brown color and striking golden-yellow stripes. Additionally, the finish is unique because its appearance changes with the room’s lighting or your viewing angle. Triangle claims “its interpretation on the AIO Twin reveals a vertical grain in which fine lines with golden highlights run through a rich, dark brown base, creating a natural contrast of great elegance.”

item.title: Timex’s Military-Inspired MK1 Chrono Field Watch Gets an Elevated Dial Upgrade
item.description:
Source: Gear Patrol Score: 4.19
Launched in 2018, Timex’s Mk1 Chronograph field watch has quickly become a fan favorite. That is largely thanks to its connection to military history and understated styling. However, that watch just got a big upgrade courtesy of a seemingly simple change. Two new Timex Mk1 Chronographs have come out for 2026, and they’re even more stunning than before. Out of left field There are two new options for the Mk1 Chronograph, and while they share a similar tweak, they’re also distinct. So, let’s start with what’s similar. Both get a new dial finish. Instead of a flat matte color, they’ve been equipped with a sunray finish, an ultra-fine brushing that radiates out from the center toward the edge. In effect, this allows the watch to catch the light and reflect it in a shimmering, color-changing manner. It’s both elegant and elevated, adding some character to the watch without taking any away.

item.title: Orient’s Affordable Automatic Sports Watch Is Back with Some Gorgeous Dials
item.description:
Source: Gear Patrol Score: 4.12
Orient debuted the current Stretto Semi Skeleton collection in 2024, featuring a larger case and a more complicated dial than the standard Stretto. The eye-catching iteration on one of Orient’s most versatile all-purpose watches just got a limited-edition restock, and according to the brand, this is the last chance to pick one up. Better still, it is selling for the discounted price of $420. The Stretto Semi Skeleton dial deviates significantly from the Stretto’s three-hand, time-and-date format. However, it retains much of the design language that makes the watch so attractive. Encircling the dial is the same hour track of faceted wedge indices running along a sunken ring, each punctuated with a lume dot on the outer rim. The remainder of the rim is filled with a black dash minutes track. At the center are the same beveled obelisk hour and minute hands fitted with lume inserts. Orient’s logo is printed below 12:00 with an applied coat of arms.

item.title: BSA’s Super-Approachable Retro-Styled Bantam 350 Roadster Gets a Heritage-Honoring New Hue
item.description:
Source: Gear Patrol Score: 4.12
Last July, the legendary, recently revived BSA brought back a familiar nameplate in the form of the Bantam 350, a small-displacement, rider-friendly roadster. Now comes news that the brand is leaning harder into its history with a new colorway that pays tribute to the first-ever Bantam moto, which dates back to 1948. Dubbed Mist Green, it adds a new dimension to the bike without any increase in its wallet-friendly cost of £3,499, which roughly converts to $4,700 USD. The bike retains the features that have made it so compelling to begin with, including the liquid-cooled 344cc single-cylinder engine making 29 horsepower and 22 Ib-ft of torque at 6,000 rpm. Also returning are a 320mm floating caliper up front and a 240mm caliper at the rear, complete with ABS.

item.title: Civivi’s Revered Elementum EDC Knife Gets a Bronze Age Retool Fit for ‘The Odyssey’
item.description:
Source: Gear Patrol Score: 4.08
The Civivi Elementum is the brand’s most popular and best-selling knife. And there are some pretty straightforward reasons why: it’s relatively inexpensive (usually), incredibly versatile and has more variants than you can shake a stick at. The latter just became even more the case, as the brand has announced another pair of new editions. But these Civivi Elementum Flippers (the C18062AM-1 and C18062AM-2) aren’t just any old material or color tweaks. Both of these knives have elements that appear to harken to the Bronze Age and, more specifically, Greek mythology. Labyrinthian edge For the most part, these two Elementums are built exactly the same. Their only actual difference is in their handle scales. One boasts Ultem scales (which are naturally yellow) and the other has clear Lexan scales. While there is a slight price difference, they’ll ultimately function the same, so it’s really a choice of which appearance you like best.

item.title: Yeti Just Brought Back Its Discontinued Dog Bed and Made It Cheaper
item.description:
Source: Gear Patrol Score: 4.07
Roy and Ryan Seiders founded Yeti to service anglers in need of serious ice retention on the open water. But their audience has since grown to include hunters, cooks and even “canine customers,” as Derek Sullivan puts it. Sullivan, who’s been with the company for over a decade, leads industrial design at Yeti, and he oversaw the creation of brand’s limited-edition dog toys late last year. As it turns out, they weren’t a one-off. Ruff and ready Though the toys themselves remain MIA, Yeti dug its dog bed out of the archive, giving the coveted piece of gear a new name and lower price. Now called the Boomer Dog Bed, matching the brand’s longstanding dog bowl, the release picks up where the Trailhead Dog Bed left off back in 2022.

item.title: Monos Thoughtfully Revamps Its Beloved Aluminum Carry-On for International Travel
item.description:
Source: Gear Patrol Score: 4.07
Monos Thoughtfully Revamps Its Beloved Aluminum Carry-On for International Travel This tough-as-nails, sleek rolling suitcase downsizes without sacrificing functionality. Plus, a pair of suave, overbuilt sunglasses, a celebratory bourbon and more. Monos’ Aluminum Carry-On is one of the brand’s best luggage offerings, combining stunning design with a highly functional, durable construction. However, it had previously been designed for domestic travel, making it a bit too large for international flights and smaller, regional aircraft. Now, the brand has redesigned it to meet more stringent requirements, bringing the capacity down to 34 liters (from just under 40) without losing any of the things that made it such a great bag in the first place. Jacques Marie Mage, the uber-luxury sunglasses brand known for its wildly expensive acetate frames, expands further into metal territory with its Ti Series of titanium frames. The limited series takes three of JMM’s most iconic acetate frames: Dealan, Torino and Zephirin, and reimagines them in 6mm-thick Grade 6 titanium. All three feature mixed cellulose acetate temples and ornate hairline-engraved decoration on the bridges, temples and hinges. Each reference is limited to 200 pieces, and all are priced at $1,315. Celebrating America’s 250th birthday, Wyoming Whiskey debuts its State of the Union. This is a 6-year-old straight bourbon that comes from locally-sourced grain in Wyoming. Bottled at 98 proof, it exhibits notes of raspberries, white chocolate, brown sugar and sweet tea. As of right now, it can only be purchased in the state of Wyoming at select retailers but the brand says its working on online availability. Ram 1500 Rumble Bee Direct Connection Supercharger Kit and Upgrades Hot off the debut of the Ram 1500 Rumble Bee street pickup trucks, Stellantis’ Mopar division just unveiled its comprehensive lineup of OEM, factory-backed performance upgrades, parts and accessories, compliments of Direct Connection. The biggest standout however, is the company’s own supercharger kit, which transforms the Rumble Bee into one serious straight-line beast. For the same cost of a decent used car, the supercharger kit consists of a 3.0-liter twin-screw supercharger. Available on both the 5.7-liter and 6.2-liter “392” HEMI V8s, power can jump from 395 horsepower to 600-plus on the 5.7 and over 700 for the 6.2. Should you be feeling really ambitious, the kit also works on the Rumble Bee SRT, which swaps out the original 2.4-liter supercharger on the Hellcat 6.2-liter HEMI, and bumps power from 777 to 900 horses. Other upgrades include exterior and interior enhancements and even custom exhaust systems from Magnaflow, to suspension upgrades from Ridetech. Rogue Territory transforms its signature Dry Wax Supply Jacket into a vest by, well, just cutting off the arms. The pointed collar is also replaced by a more vest-appropriate curved collar. It is otherwise identical, featuring a welted exterior chest pocket, interior patch pocket, D-panel hand pockets and custom steel donut rivet buttons. It is made from 10-ounce pure cotton dry wax canvas, available in brown and charcoal gray. Sony released its current flagship noise-canceling headphones, the WH-1000XM6, in May 2026. And they feature some key upgrades of their predecessors, the 2022-released XM5, including improved sound, call quality and active noise-cancellation, as well as a more foldable design. Since the release, Sony has rolled out a few new colorways of the XM6. And the latest one is Olive Gray.

item.title: Birkenstock Reunites with Korean Brand Ader Error to Revise the Beloved Boston Clog
item.description:
Source: Gear Patrol Score: 4.00
When it comes to clogs and slip-on casual footwear, Birkenstock is second to none. But that hasn’t kept the long-standing brand from iterating on and innovating its most iconic staples. Such is the case with the Birkenstock 1774 x Ader Error Boston Clogs, which sees one of the German brand’s most beloved silhouettes reinterpreted by its South Korean collaborator in two distinct ways, unified by a shared theme. Different vibe, same clog Lovers of the classic Boston Clog will be happy to know that most of the shoe’s elements remain intact in this reinterpretation. Think of it less as a reimagining and more as adding to its already spectacular base. For instance, the upper remains a stunning, textured suede that looks as soft as it feels. The shoe also retains its signature closed-toe design and iconic buckle-fastening strap, so you can be sure this mule remains a snug fit.

item.title: Onkyo Is Running a Rare Sale on Its Retro-Inspired CD Player
item.description:
Source: Gear Patrol Score: 3.96
The Onkyo DX-390 is one of two CD players that the Japanese hi-fi company still makes. It’s not the brand’s latest and greatest model. That’s the Onkyo Icon C-30, which was just announced last year and costs $400. Instead, the Onkyo DX-390 is better suited to audiophiles with extensive CD collections who want long, uninterrupted listening sessions. That’s because it has a 6-disc carousel, so you can load six CDs and they can each play right after the previous one. On the flip side, the company’s Icon C-30 only holds one CD at a time. Dust off your old CDs Another cool feature of this CD carousel is that you can swap CDs without interrupting what’s playing. So you can technically keep swapping out CDs, playing new albums, without the music ever stopping. But just because it’s not as elite as the Icon C-30, Onkyo’s DX-390 is very much a high-quality CD player. According to the brand, it’s “incorporated decades of acoustic technology into the player to provide audiophile-grade sound for a new generation.”

item.title: America Just Might Get the Euro Wagon Influx Fans Have Been Clamoring For
item.description:
Source: Gear Patrol Score: 3.94
Wagon fans in America, especially German wagon fans, may get their wishes granted. Multiple reports suggest several Deutschland-based carmakers are considering expanding their long-roof offerings here in the States. Word on the street is that automakers like Audi and BMW are canvassing ways to offer more wagons for American buyers after noticing a recent explosion in demand. The renewed interest comes after BMW demonstrated profound success with its M5 Touring. It also received an overwhelmingly positive reaction to the recent M3 Touring. It made BMW and other German carmakers realize there’s real desire for wagons. In fact, so much so that there’s a convincing business case brewing. BMW may actually send us an M3 Touring and 3 Series Sport Wagon According to enthusiast site BMW Blog, Munich is at the forefront of the renewed movement. The Bavarian automaker reportedly is serious about sending us the new M3 Touring when it arrives in the coming years, according to a leaked product guide on community site, Bimmerpost. The supposed decision comes hot off the M5 Touring’s recent sales success here in America. Shortly afterwards, BMW revealed the M3 Touring for Europe and it too was met with positive reception, particularly on this side of the pond.

item.title: Luminox Refines Its Tactical Navy SEAL Dive Watch, Maintaining Its Strength and Capability
item.description:
Source: Gear Patrol Score: 3.90
Luminox is known for crafting incredibly tough watches, especially those with a tactical edge. Much of that reputation can be attributed to its ongoing partnership with the U.S. Navy SEALs, which has produced a long-running roster of incredibly formidable tactical divers. That legacy just got even deeper with the launch of the brand-new Luminox Navy SEAL 3550 Series, which sees the fan-favorite lineup get a refined redesign without losing any of its formidability. A 32-year legacy This watch series dates all the way back to 1994, when Luminox released its first-ever Navy SEAL collaborative dive watches. It’s also a direct follow-up to the most recent lineup, the Navy SEAL 3500 Series. In terms of construction and functionality, these watches remain largely unchanged from the previous series. And that’s a great thing, as they were already a near-ideal blend of strength, capability and affordability.

item.title: Timex’s New Retroware Digital Looks Like a Futuristic Watch from the ’80s
item.description:
Source: Gear Patrol Score: 3.82
Unlike Casio’s repertoire of throwback timepieces, Timex’s catalog often bucks familiarity in favor of raising eyebrows. This is never more evident than reissues like the uber-simple SSQ, the futuristic LCA or the obscure 1972 Time Machine. But with its latest effort, the watchmaker creates a brand-new reference that looks like it could’ve been hanging in a department store case in the early ‘80s. Homage horology As opposed to Timex’s slew of Q Timex revivals, the Retroware Digital is an original model that pastiches old-school digital sports watches. The parking meter shape is reminiscent of the brand’s original Triathlon and Ironman references from the mid-’80s.

item.title: Ford Sets Its Ambitions to Become the Performance King of the Off-Roading World
item.description:
Source: Gear Patrol Score: 3.79
Ford is apparently setting some lofty ambitions for its new vehicle strategy. As part of some new developments, Dearborn is looking to amp up its reputation in the off-roading space with the ultimate goal of becoming the end-all, be-all. According to reports citing interviews with some executives, including CEO Jim Farley, the carmaker is looking to re-inject some big-time excitement into its near-future product range. Farley wants to transform Ford into the ultimate performance off-roading brand. However, that does come at a considerable expense. Seeking to become the “Porsche of off-roading” Ford has been in a bit of a pickle after dialing back its aggressive electrification strategy. The rollback cost the company huge sums of investment capital. It’s also cast a major shadow over the brand’s financial future and sustainability. Since then, the product planners at Dearborn have been trying to figure out their best path forward.

item.title: Seiko & Honda Team Up for a Very Japanese Affordable Field Watch
item.description:
Source: Gear Patrol Score: 3.78
If I ask you to name two Japanese brands, it probably won’t be long before Seiko and Honda are both named. Two of the world’s largest and most influential brands in their respective categories of watches and motoring, these Japanese giants represent quality and value at a level most other companies can only dream of. So it makes perfect sense that Seiko and Honda would team up to produce a watch based on one of the latter’s most decidedly Japanese creations. Know when to fold ’em Seiko’s new watch is based on the Honda Motocompo, a legendary folding motorized scooter that was produced from 1981 to 1983 as a JDM add-on to the Honda City car. The Motocompo was innovative in that it folded into a compact rectangular shape to fit into the City’s trunk. Its quirky design and rarity have led to the scooter’s current cult status as a collector’s item. The new watch, a heavily customized Seiko 5 Sports Field, was created in honor of the iconic scooter’s 45th anniversary this year.

item.title: Yamaha’s Retro-Styled XSR900 GP, Arguably Its Coolest Bike, Is Finally Headed to US Shores
item.description:
Source: Gear Patrol Score: 3.69
Last fall, my moto-loving colleague Gray Van Dyke waxed ecstatic about Yamaha’s XSR900 GP donning a stunning new hue, ‘Legend Yellow.’ The paint scheme paid tribute to ‘King’ Kenny Roberts, the first American rider to capture a World Championship in the 500cc era, ultimately three-peating from 1978 to 1980. This nod to a superstar, who also counts an AMA Grand Slam and multiple Daytona 200 wins among many accolades, was achingly ironic considering the bike was not available in the US. Thankfully, this injustice is soon to be remedied, as motorcycle.com reports that the California Air Resources Board has issued an executive order certifying the XSR900 GP as a 2027 model. National certification from the EPA should be forthcoming, followed by an announcement by Yamaha Motor USA in a matter of weeks.

item.title: Stetson Embarks on New Territory with the Debut of Its First-Ever Bourbon
item.description:
Source: Gear Patrol Score: 3.65
From Coors to Aston Martin to Metallica, everyone seems to be getting into whiskey-making these days. And now you can add Stetson to the list. That’s right, the brand known for creating the blueprint for the modern cowboy hat over 160 years ago has now launched its first-ever bourbon brand. In case you missed it Stetson didn’t literally invent the cowboy hat (wide-brimmed hats had been used for centuries around the world) but it quickly became synonymous with the style after the introduction of the Boss of the Plains hat in 1865. This specific design featured a high, rounded crown, a 4-inch brim and a leather band around the outside. Not initially a fashion accessory, this inaugural Stetson was created to be an all-purpose hat for workers in the American West. But as ranchers and cowboys began curling the brim to keep out the rain and pinching the crown to make it easier to remove, Stetson started releasing pre-shaped hats straight from the factory. That kind of connection between brand and consumer has never gone away at Stetson. And now it applies that ethos to the world of whiskey.

item.title: Nike’s Air Max 95 Goes Denim Once Again, and This Time, They’ll Be Easier to Get
item.description:
Source: Gear Patrol Score: 3.57
Last year, Nike dropped a highly-coveted collaboration with Levi’s that included a trio of denim-covered Air Max 95s: all-black, white/ecru and the classic blue Obsidian. To say these sneakers were hot would be an understatement. While the black and white options were available via a drawing on Nike’s SNKRS app, the coveted Obsidian was a Levi’s exclusive. Those eyeing the sneakers for weeks ahead of launch were champing at the bit to get a pair. Nevertheless, all three colorways sold out very quickly and, unfortunately, more people were left empty handed than not. Now, Nike may have a fairly adequate consolation prize for those who missed out on the Obsidian AM95s. Jeans to an end The new colorway features several shades of blue, unlike last year’s mostly-indigo scheme. This time around, there’s no connection to Levi’s, which might downplay the hype, but that’s also a good thing for those with slow fingers or even-slower internet connections.

item.title: TVS’s New $1,100 Doctor Doom Raider Rewrites the Script for Small-Displacement Motos
item.description:
Source: Gear Patrol Score: 3.39
Considering all the motorcycles I write about, including loads of Hondas and Harleys, Yamahas and Triumphs, it’s kind of crazy to consider how little I’ve covered TVS. The Indian brand really isn’t on the radar of most American moto enthusiasts, but it is making huge waves behind the scenes. After all, it’s the force behind Norton’s stunning re-emergence (in the premium space, no less), and it has helped BMW bring the approachable F 450 GS adventure bike to life. That’s to say nothing of its own branded bikes, which prove the power of small-displacement, as its latest Raider, the devilish Doomsday edition, reminds us. Green machine With its graphics and paint scheme, the latest Super Squad Edition bike joins the brand’s stable of Marvel-themed rides, following the Deadpool, Wolverine, Black Panther and Iron Man treatments. Beyond the shimmering Spectral Green paint and Victor Von Doom’s metal-clad visage gazing out from the gas tank, however, this bike is another small-displacement, high-volume dart flung toward the entry-level moto market’s bullseye.

item.title: In Case You Miss This Severely Underappreciated Toyota, It’s Still Alive and Kicking Elsewhere
item.description:
Source: Gear Patrol Score: 3.36
If you were a fan of the Toyota Venza and wondered what happened to it here in America, the model isn’t actually dead. Toyota pulled the crossover SUV from the Stateside market after shockingly slow sales. Over in Japan, it lives on as the Harrier. In fact, Toyota just rolled out some updates for the JDM model. While this means we can no longer appreciate the Venza stateside, Toyota’s revisions remind us just how much we’re missing. America lost its chance to appreciate one of the brand’s more compelling crossovers. The Venza lives on, but only in Japan In 2020, Toyota introduced the second-generation Venza after a brief hiatus. The Japanese automaker then pulled the model from the US market in 2024, replacing it with the Crown and Crown Signia. The original Venza debuted in 2008 and remained in production up until 2017. It was basically Toyota’s attempt at a slightly more upscale, not-quite-a-Lexus crossover.

item.title: This 25-Year-Old, 100k-Mile Toyota Land Cruiser Just Shockingly Sold for Nearly as Much as a New One
item.description:
Source: Gear Patrol Score: 3.34
For $50,000, would you rather have a brand-new Toyota J250 Land Cruiser or opt for an incredibly clean, well-maintained one-owner J100 with just over 100,000 miles on it? That’s the question that’s top of mind here at GP. It’s a dilemma that arose after what is arguably one of the cleanest J100 Land Cruisers we’ve ever seen crossed the Bring a Trailer auction block. In addition to selling for almost the same price as a new one, it also really challenges the notion that “newer is better” when it comes to legends like old Land Cruisers. A legendary SUV with a legendary price tag Most Land Cruiser fans are aware that it’s pretty typical for the SUV to be worth a good chunk of change, especially for a used car. Old Land Cruisers are known to hold their value. That’s because old Land Cruisers are highly regarded for their robust reliability, brick-house-like build quality and worldly dependability. Especially ones from the ’90s and ’00s.

item.title: Converse Retools the Classic All Star Sneaker with Heritage Military Style
item.description:
Source: Gear Patrol Score: 3.33
The Converse All Star needs no introduction, but it could probably use a quick history lesson. That’s because before it won over pioneering basketball players, ’90s punk rockers and even modern weightlifters, it outfit US troops during both World Wars. Converse claims it completed more than 50 military contracts throughout the 20th century, with some Navy SEALs reportedly still choosing the company’s iconic canvas sneaker over high-tech combat boots. While the company has dabbled in camo colorways over the years, the Japan-exclusive All Star MA Nylon OX arrives as an unofficial tribute to Converse’s rich military past. The new design trades the All Star’s signature canvas upper for one fashioned out of nylon, referencing MA-1 bomber jackets issued to pilots starting in the ’60s.

item.title: Honda’s CR-V Stokes an Ongoing Toyota Upset with Its Best July Ever
item.description:
Source: Gear Patrol Score: 3.31
The Toyota RAV4 has been the best-selling SUV in the United States for nearly a decade at this point, as it’s managed to hold onto the top spot since 2017. However, this year is shaping up to be different. Following a shift in the winds at the end of 2025, the Honda CR-V has carried its momentum towards an upset that has it well ahead of its Toyota rival. Now the SUV has just driven another nail into the RAV4’s proverbial coffin with its best July ever. The CR-V has a breakout month Yep, you read that correctly. According to the latest sales report, the Honda CR-V just posted some all-time record-breaking figures for the month of July. In practice, this means that the Japanese SUV showed a 18.8 percent bump over the same time in 2025, improving from some 32,268 units moved up to 38,335. That puts it at 264,449 on the year, an 8 percent jump.

item.title: Casio’s New Retro Timepiece Takes Heavy Cues from Seiko’s ’70s-Era Icon
item.description:
Source: Gear Patrol Score: 3.18
Seiko isn’t known as an unorthodox watch brand. But every now and then, it surely pushes the needle. That’s what happened in 1976 when it debuted the Time Sonar, one of the most unusual mechanical watches it’s ever produced. It combined a transparent dial, one of the world’s earliest display casebacks and a futuristic design. The timepiece’s unique look is reminiscent of a submarine sonar screen, hence the name. Now, Casio takes a perhaps-inadvertent stab at the aesthetic … to a degree. I’m looking through you Admittedly, the new MTP-E740 isn’t a faithful dupe of the Time Sonar. However, it’ll get you the same overall vibe at one-fourth of the cost. For the task, Casio goes with a transparent dial just like Seiko’s, and in five colorways: black, orange, blue, navy blue and teal. The minute track on the outside isn’t as sophisticated and ditches numerals entirely. However, the end result is something decidedly cleaner overall.

item.title: One of America’s Youngest Watch Brands Just Made Its Most Important Move
item.description:
Source: Gear Patrol Score: 3.15
Trafford Watch Co. is an up-and-comer to look out for in the indie watch world. After three years of releasing small-batch, one-off collections, the Austin-based brand debuts its first regular production line. Dubbed the Core Collection, it anoints the brand’s two most popular designs as the foundation going forward. Both watches should be available for purchase at any point for the foreseeable future. Ask anyone familiar with the brand, and they will likely point to the time-only Daytripper as Trafford’s flagship watch. But to me, the Touring GMT stands out as a more unique design and has much more to offer. As advertised, it features a GMT complication, executed as an arrow-tipped hand indicating a two-tone, raised 24-hour track encircling the dial. The hand’s arrow tip and the track follow the tonal navy-and-sky-blue color scheme decorating the dial. Local time is handled by navy-coated syringe-style hour and minute hands, along with an orange needle-style seconds hand. Applied hour markers consist of even numerals and a combination of dash and arrow indices. Both debut Core Collection models use the same 39mm stainless steel case, featuring twisted lugs, a signed crown and a polished finish with a hardened coating. Each one is topped with an AR-coated domed sapphire crystal.

item.title: Kawasaki’s Coolest Ninja Moto Scores Its Sweetest Update Yet
item.description:
Source: Gear Patrol Score: 3.11
Fans of Kawasaki’s long-running Ninja nameplate will be stoked to hear it’s back for the 2027 model year, with four versions just announced. The Ninja ZX-6R “636” is the headliner, joined by the ZX-4R, ZX-4RR and Ninja 500, which also gets a Special Edition variant. Thankfully, the ZX-6R retains all the performance and tech features that make it such an appealing mid-size super sport. It also scores arguably the best-looking paint schemes in years. Go Ninja go The beating heart of the bike is its 636cc liquid-cooled in-line four-cylinder engine, whose six speeds are easy to cycle through thanks to the Assist & Slipper Clutch.

item.title: The Best New Honda Motorcycles of 2026 (So Far)
item.description:
Source: Gear Patrol Score: 3.06
“You meet the nicest people on a Honda.” It’s a tagline the brand ran back in the 1960s, but it continues to echo even in 2026 through the diversity of its motorcycle lineup. After all, Honda introduced the slogan as a tactic to change perception around bikes. At the time, most of the public associated motorcycles with dangerous outlaws and big Harley V-twins, and the brand wanted to cut through the stereotypes. To that end, Honda has been rolling out everything from an updated Monkey to a dramatically overhauled CRF and even a first-ever electric production bike. It’s a range that caters to a wide variety of riders. Now that we’re halfway through the year, we’ve rounded up the most notable Honda releases we’ve covered so far in 2026. We’ll continue updating this running report card as more motos and gear arrive, but these are the launches that have defined the Honda brand year to date.

item.title: Visiting the UAE as an Independent Traveler: The Visa Guide
item.description:
Source: GoBackpacking Score: 6.15
The United Arab Emirates (UAE) is one of those places that rewards going it alone. Skip the packaged tour, and you can watch the sun come up over the Hajar Mountains, sleep out in the Liwa dunes, haggle your way through a Deira souk, and still make it back to a hostel bunk in the city by midnight. The country makes independent travel easy in almost every way but one: the visa. Sort that before you fly, and everything else falls into place. Here is what a solo, self-organized traveler needs to know. First, Do You Even Need a Visa? Maybe not. It comes down entirely to your passport, and travelers split into three groups. Some nationalities get visa-free entry and walk through immigration. Others get a visa on arrival, stamped at the airport for a fee. Everyone else has to arrange an e-visa before they fly. That third group is bigger than most expect, and this is where independent travelers get caught. You cannot always sort it at the airport. The only way to be certain is to check whether your nationality needs a visa before booking any flight. Do it early. It changes how you plan the whole trip. Which Visa Fits an Independent Trip? If you need to apply, the choices are simple: Tourist visit visas come in 14-, 30-, and 60-day versions, each single- or multiple-entry. There is also a 96-hour transit visa for long layovers. For a proper trip, the 30-day is the workhorse. Going for longer, or planning to base yourself in Dubai and explore slowly? The 60-day earns its keep. Only choose multiple entry if you plan to duck out and back, like a side trip into Oman and return over the border. Most people overbuy here. Match the visa to the trip you are actually taking, not the one you are daydreaming about. What To Sort Before You Apply The paperwork is light, but border officers do check it. Have these ready for yourself and anyone traveling with you, since everything is per person: - A passport valid for at least six months from your arrival date. - A clear passport-style photo on a plain background. - A confirmed onward or return ticket. - Proof of where you are staying, even if it is just the first hostel booking. - Enough funds to cover your stay, and valid travel insurance. That last one is no longer optional. More on why in a second. The 2026 Rules That Catch Travelers Off-Guard The UAE tightened its entry rules in 2026, and a few of the changes bite independent travelers specifically, because we are the ones improvising as we go. First, travel insurance covering your whole stay is now expected, not optional. Buy it before you land, not after. Second, and this is the big one: the overstay grace period is gone. Overstay your visa now, and you are fined AED 50 a day ($13.60) from day one, with no warning or buffer. For anyone used to extending a trip on a whim, that is a genuine mindset shift. Set a reminder for your exit date and treat it as fixed. The friendlier change: most visit visas can now be extended online through the ICP portal twice, adding 30 days each time, without leaving the country. Thus flexibility still exists. You have to arrange it properly instead of winging it. How To Apply When Nobody Is Sponsoring You Here is the part that confuses first-timers. You do not need a UAE resident to sponsor you, and you do not need a travel agency. A tourist visa is something you arrange yourself, directly. The process is quick. Pick your duration, upload your passport page and photo, pay, and wait for the e-visa to arrive in your inbox, usually within one to three working days. You can do it through your airline, an official portal, or a licensed visa platform such as GOVR, where you apply for a UAE tourist visa online and track the approval. Whichever route you pick, apply a week or two in advance. Leaving it until the night before is the habit that turns a smooth trip into a stressful one. Once You Are Through the Gate Arrival is painless. Many travelers clear passport control at a smart gate in under a minute, but keep your onward ticket and first accommodation address handy in case an officer asks. Then the real trip starts. This is where going independent pays off. The skyline gets the headlines, but the UAE is small, and the good stuff is close. You can be among the red dunes of the desert within an hour of the city or scrambling through wadis in the Hajar Mountains by lunch. Sort the visa, respect your exit date, and the rest of the country opens up on your terms. Getting around solo is easy on the wallet if you skip taxis. Grab a Nol card at any metro station; it covers trains and most buses across Dubai. Intercity coaches link the emirates for a few dirhams, and for the mountains or desert you can usually split a car with other travelers from your hostel. For inexpensive meals, try the casual restaurants in Karama and Deira. A full plate costs less than a coffee back home. None of it needs a guide or fixed plan. That freedom is the whole reason to come independent in the first place. Frequently Asked Questions Do I need a visa to visit the UAE? It depends on your nationality. Some passport holders enter visa-free, some get a visa on arrival, and the rest must arrange an e-visa before flying. Check your own status before booking, because you cannot always fix it at the airport. Can I get a UAE visa on arrival? Some nationalities can, others cannot. If you are in the visa-on-arrival group, you pay and get stamped in. If you are not, you must apply online in advance. There is no universal rule, so confirm for your passport specifically. Do I really need travel insurance now? Yes. As of 2026, valid insurance covering your full stay is expected for UAE visits. Buy it before you arrive, not after, and make sure the coverage dates span your whole trip, including any extension you might add later.? Can I apply for a UAE visa without a sponsor? Yes. A tourist visit visa needs no local sponsor and no travel agency. You apply yourself directly, through an airline, an official portal, or a licensed platform, then receive the e-visa by email, usually within one to three working days. What happens if I overstay? You pay. Since 2026, the grace period is gone, and overstaying triggers a fine of AED 50 per day from the first day. If you want longer, extend your visit visa online before it expires rather than letting it lapse. How long can I stay, and can I extend? Tourist visas run 14, 30, or 60 days depending on what you buy. Most can be extended twice, 30 days at a time, through the ICP portal without leaving the country, so a 60-day visa can stretch a good deal further if you plan. This story is provided in partnership with GOVR.

item.title: How To Choose the Right Dive Center in Koh Tao
item.description:
Source: GoBackpacking Score: 5.87
What's the difference between the dive centers in Koh Tao, Thailand? They all seem the same. With over 80 dive centers on one small island, Koh Tao is one of the most competitive and confusing places in the world to get certified. In fact, every dive center in Koh Tao offers similar-looking courses, making it hard to tell what actually separates one from another. A cheaper course might seem like a great deal, but you may end up in a larger group with less personal attention. Two dive centers can offer the same certification, but the quality of instruction, safety standards, and overall experience can differ greatly. It can be difficult to choose a quality dive center absent prior experience. Here are the eight factors that actually separate one dive center from another. 8 Things to Consider When Choosing a Dive Center in Koh Tao 1. Start With the Course That Fits Your Goals Koh Tao offers diving courses for every type of traveler. Before you choose a dive center, think about what you want to achieve underwater. Here are the types of courses that most dive centers offer. Try Dive Try Dive offers a beginner-friendly scuba experience. It does not require certification. This course is ideal if you are curious about scuba diving but aren't ready to commit to a certification course. Open Water Course (4 days, No Experience Needed) The RAID Open Water Course is an entry-level scuba certification that qualifies you to descend up to 18 meters. This course includes theory lessons, one pool session, and four ocean dives. Advanced Explorer 30 Course This course expands your diving skills and certifies you to 30 meters. It includes four day dives and one night dive with a focus on buoyancy, navigation, and deeper diving techniques. Master Rescue Course (4 days) Master Rescue Course requires you to have an Explorer or Advanced certification plus valid First Aid and Oxygen Administration certifications. This course develops rescue techniques, oxygen administration, and diver safety awareness. Divemaster Course (Approximately 2 Months) Divemaster course requires you to have First Aid, Oxygen Administration, and Rescue certifications. This course develops leadership skills through theory lessons, pool sessions, unlimited ocean diving, and real-life training assisting instructors. Deep 40 and Nitrox specialty certifications are also required before completing the course if you do not already have them. 2. Don't Choose Based on Price Alone A common story in Koh Tao is a diver books the cheapest course and ends up in a group of 8-10 with one instructor. The diver spends more time waiting than learning. By the time they realize the mistake, they have already paid. Here is why you should not choose a dive center based on price alone: - Some budget centers reduce the price of the course by taking more students per instructor. - Scuba diving calls for patience and confidence. The right course includes proper guidance, explanations, and an instructor who supports you. - Some low-cost options focus on completing the course quickly. A quality dive center makes sure you understand the skills before moving on. 3. Choose a Great Instructor First When choosing a quality dive center, consider the instructor's experience. A great instructor can impact your experience more than the certification agency or course price. Here is how to choose a great instructor. Read Reviews About the Specific Instructors When checking reviews, look out for: - Patience and teaching style. - Clear explanations. - Making beginners feel comfortable. - Professionalism and safety awareness. Look for Experience and Qualifications Consider: - How long they have been teaching. - Their diving experience. - Their ability to teach beginners. - Whether they are active and knowledgeable about local dive sites. Choose Someone Who Makes You Comfortable Many first-time divers feel nervous before going underwater. Look for instructors who: - Listen to your concerns. - Answer your questions. - Avoid rushing you. - Help you build confidence step by step. Ask Who Will Teach Your Course Some dive centers advertise qualified instructors but assign you to someone else. Before booking, ask: - Who will be my instructor? - How many students will they teach? - Can I meet or speak with them before starting? 4. Ask About Student-to-Instructor Ratios Group size affects your training more than most beginners realize. This is why: - With fewer students, the instructor has more time to observe your skills, answer questions, and provide individual feedback. - Smaller groups make it easier for instructors to slow down when needed and correct concerns before they become big problems. Before booking, consider asking a few questions such as: - How many students will be in my group? - How many instructors will be teaching? - Are groups smaller for beginners? - Will the same instructor teach me throughout the course? 5. Check the Quality of the Equipment A reputable dive center should routinely inspect, service, and replace equipment. Here are things to consider: Ask About How Often Equipment Is Serviced Before booking, ask how frequently they inspect and service important gear like: - Regulators - BCDs (Buoyancy Control Devices) - Dive computers - Tanks These pieces of gear reduce most problems underwater. Check the Condition of Rental Gear Before starting your course, take a look at: - Masks that fit properly and do not show cracks. - Regulators that are clean and well maintained. - BCDs that inflate and deflate smoothly. - Wetsuits that are free of excessive damage. - Fins and straps that are in good condition. Look for Clean and Organized Equipment Areas A well-managed dive center keeps its gear storage clean and organized. Proper storage, drying, and maintenance show it takes care of its equipment. 6. Look for Strong Safety Standards Safety should not be an afterthought. Here is what to look for: They Explain Safety Procedures Clearly Check things such as: - How to use your equipment. - Underwater communication signals. - Emergency procedures. - What to do if you feel uncomfortable during a dive. Ask About Instructor Supervision Your instructor should actively monitor students throughout the course and dives. Look for: - Instructors who stay close to beginners underwater. - Clear demonstrations of skills prior to diving. - Regular checks to confirm everyone feels comfortable. Check if They Follow Proper Training Procedures Quality training usually includes: - Classroom theory - Confined water practice - Skill demonstrations - Open water training dives - Final skill assessments 7. Choose a Center That Answers Your Questions A good dive center should make you feel knowledgeable and comfortable before booking. Here are things to consider. Pay Attention to How Quickly They Respond Look for: - Helpful answers. - Clear information about the courses and schedules. - Staff who take time to understand your needs. Ask About Course Details For example, you can ask: - How long does the course take? - What's included in the price? - How many dives are included? - What does the daily schedule look like? - How does the certification process work? Visit or Message More Than One Dive Center Compare a few options before deciding based on these factors: - Response quality - Friendliness - Transparency - Attention to detail 8. Choose a Center That Teaches in Your Language The final tip is to choose a dive center that teaches in a language that you are comfortable with. Many dive centers in Koh Tao offer instruction in several languages, such as: - English - Spanish - French - German Before booking, check if the course is taught in a language you are comfortable with. Also check if the course materials are available in that language. Frequently Asked Questions (FAQs) 1. Are all dive centers in Koh Tao certified? Reputable dive centers generally operate through recognized training agencies such as RAID, PADI, or SSI. Before booking, confirm the center's agency affiliation and review its instructor qualifications, safety procedures, equipment standards, and recent customer feedback. 2. What questions should I ask before booking a dive course? You can ask questions related to certification, costs, schedule, logistics, gear, and health. 3. How do I know if a dive center is safe? Look for affiliation with a recognized training agency such as RAID, PADI, or SSI. Ask about instructor qualifications, group sizes, emergency procedures, equipment maintenance, and medical screening. They should verify any certification you possess when your selected course or dive requires prior certification. 4. Are online reviews reliable when choosing a dive center? Yes, reviews can be helpful in choosing a dive center. Here is what you need to focus on: - Look for recurring safety complaints, broken equipment, or overcrowded groups. - See how the shop replies to negative feedback to judge their professionalism and accountability. - Look at candid photos. 5. What is the difference between a dive shop and a dive center? A dive shop focuses on retail sales and gear servicing, while a dive center provides professional training courses. If you're planning a longer island stay, explore these other things to do in Koh Tao between your diving sessions. Conclusion You can choose a quality dive center in Koh Tao by considering these tips: - Your goals for the course. - The instructor's experience and teaching style. - Student-to-instructor ratio. - Equipment quality and maintenance. - Safety standards and training procedures. - How responsive and transparent the center is. - Whether they teach in your language. Take time to message a couple of centers and ask questions directly. This article was published in partnership with La Bombona Diving.

item.title: Why Ordering Dinner Abroad Feels So Different Now - A Traveler's Look at Restaurant Tech
item.description:
Source: GoBackpacking Score: 4.96
The first time I ate in Bangkok, back in 2011, the waiter scribbled my order on a carbon-copy pad, tore off the pink sheet, and clipped it on a wire above the kitchen window. Last spring, in the same neighborhood, I scanned a QR code, ordered pad kra pao in English, paid from my phone, and watched a runner bring it out eight minutes later. Nobody wrote anything down. Nobody even asked what I wanted. If you've traveled anywhere in the past few years, you've noticed this shift. It's not just the shiny rooftop places in Singapore or Dubai. It's the family-run taverna on a Greek island, the soup stall in Hanoi, the cellar restaurant in Bucharest where the grandmother still makes the sarmale but the granddaughter runs orders through a tablet. Eating out abroad has quietly changed, and the change has followed us to every corner of the map. What's behind it is less mysterious than it looks. Most of these places now run some version of an ePOS system for restaurants, software that handles the menu, orders, kitchen tickets, and payments in one place. A café owner I met in Porto told me she compared platforms for weeks before opening, and she mentioned the Tableview.com solution when searching for an ePOS system for your restaurant as a natural starting point for small independent places like hers, since it bundles ordering, payments, and daily reporting without requiring a technician to set it up. She runs the whole café from a tablet by the espresso machine. Ten years ago, that would have meant a bulky terminal, a service contract, and a bank loan. The QR Code Menu Followed You Around the World Love them or hate them, QR menus are now part of the travel experience. I've scanned codes taped to bamboo tables in Laos and printed on linen cards in Lyon. For travelers, they solve real problems: - Menus translate instantly, so you're no longer pointing at a stranger's plate and hoping. - Prices are current, which matters in countries where inflation moves fast. - Photos help when the dish name means nothing to you. - You can order a second beer without flagging anyone down. What's actually happening when you scan That code isn't magic. It connects to the same restaurant ePOS system that the staff use, so your order lands directly on a kitchen screen. No handwriting to misread, no server juggling six tables in their head. That's why your food in a packed Hanoi café sometimes arrives faster than it would at a half-full restaurant back home. The order never had a chance to get lost. Why the Tiny Family Place Takes Cards Now One of the biggest quiet changes for budget travelers: the near-death of "cash only." I still carry local currency everywhere, old habits and all, but I use it less every year. Even remote spots have caught up, and there's a practical reason. Modern cloud-based POS systems for restaurants run on ordinary tablets and phones over a normal internet connection. The restaurant doesn't buy expensive hardware or host anything on site. The software lives online, updates itself, and works the same whether the business is a beach shack in the Philippines or a bistro in Berlin. A card reader the size of a deck of cards plugs into the same setup. For a small owner, the cost of accepting your Visa dropped from painful to trivial. For travelers, that means: - Fewer desperate ATM hunts in towns with one broken machine. - Itemized digital receipts, which anyone who has filed a travel expense report will appreciate. - Less risk carrying wads of cash through crowded markets. - Tipping and currency conversion are handled on screen, not in mental math. Splitting the Bill Without the Uncomfortable Napkin Math If you've traveled with a group, you know the scene. Eight backpackers, one bill, three currencies of cash on the table, and somebody who "only had the salad." Hostel friendships have ended over less. The same hospitality ePOS systems that power the kitchen also changed this ritual. Many now let the staff split a bill by seat, by item, or equally with a couple of taps. In Seoul, our table of six paid six separate ways: two phones, three cards, one handful of won, and the server didn't blink. In 2012, that request would have earned us a sigh you could hear from the kitchen. The human side hasn't disappeared. A fair worry: does all this screen-tapping kill the charm of eating abroad? Mostly, no. The best meals I've had recently still involved a conversation, a recommendation, a dish I didn't order but got anyway. What the technology removed was the friction around the meal, not the meal itself. The grandmother in Bucharest still tells you what to eat. The tablet makes sure the kitchen hears her. What This Means for How You Eat on the Road None of this requires you to do anything differently, which is the point. But a few habits help you get the best of it: - Keep cash as a backup; rural connectivity still fails, and some cultures prefer it. - Check the digital receipt before paying, since tourist-area "adjustments" haven't gone extinct. - Don't assume a modest storefront means cash only anymore; ask first. - If a QR menu confuses you, ask for a paper one; nearly every place keeps a few on hand. The romance of travel dining was never really about the carbon-copy pad or the drawer of crumpled bills. It was the food, the people, and the modest victory of ordering well in a language you don't speak. The systems humming behind the counter, from a one-tablet café in Porto to a three-floor restaurant in Bangkok, have gotten better at staying out of the way. Frankly, after fifteen years of watching my orders get lost in translation, I don't miss the pink carbon copy at all. This story is provided in partnership with Tableview.

item.title: 4 Days in Charleston: The Perfect First-Time Itinerary
item.description:
Source: GoBackpacking Score: 4.62
Charleston lingered on my travel wish list for years. The city's historic architecture, tempting restaurants, and that breezy waterfront always called to me. Add in the convenience of a direct flight from Austin, and it seemed like the ideal place for a long weekend. When I finally made it to Charleston, thanks to a collaboration with Explore Charleston and Wentworth Mansion, Kel and I set out to see as much as we could in four days and nights. Over 4 days in Charleston, we wandered the historic district on foot, visited attractions ranging from Fort Sumter to the South Carolina Aquarium, and ate our fair share of Southern food. Charleston's main sights are close enough that you can walk between them, but I soon realized the value of retreating to our hotel for an afternoon breather. That pause in the cool, quiet room made the difference between feeling refreshed for dinner and dragging my feet through the evening heat. What follows is the four-day route Kel and I took, refined with a few adjustments I'd make if planning the trip again. Consider it a firsthand blueprint for your own first visit. Disclosure: My first trip to Charleston was produced in collaboration with Explore Charleston and Wentworth Mansion.
