item.title: Mortgage Rates Flatten, but They’re Already Higher Than July’s Average
item.description:
Source: NerdWallet Score: 5.74
In the first week of August, the average 30-year mortgage rate stayed mostly flat at 6.63% APR. This is three basis points lower than a week ago. A basis point is one one-hundredth of a percentage point, and we calculate our weekly average using daily APRs provided by Zillow over the past five business days. This is also 13 basis points higher than July’s monthly average of 6.5%. Mortgage rates gradually increased throughout the month, beginning at 6.28% on July 1 and ending at 6.7% on July 31. Over the past five days, the lowest average APR was 6.47% on Thursday, Aug. 6, according to Zillow data. This was a 12-basis-point drop from the previous day’s average. Rates fell after national payroll processor ADP released its July data, which showed that real private sector job growth (44,000 additions) was weaker than forecasted (75,000 additions, as reported by Dow Jones). Mortgage lenders are thinking about how July’s job data will be interpreted by central bankers. Futures traders have been expecting that the Federal Reserve might rein in inflation by raising borrowing rates in September. However, doing so can put more pressure on the labor market and drive up unemployment. If Friday’s jobs report from the Bureau of Labor Statistics upholds the downward trend seen in ADP’s release, the odds of a rate hike could fall further for September — and mortgage rates with them. According to Zillow data, the highest average APR reported over the past five days was 6.7% on Tuesday, Aug. 4. This was on par with where rates ended the last week of July. Throughout last month, mortgage rates trended higher when fighting and tensions escalated in Iran. The highest average daily rate reading for the whole month was 6.75% on July 27, the day after the U.S. completed 13 consecutive nights of strikes on Iranian targets. Rates then began to fall once the attacks were paused. Won't affect your credit score Next week we’ll get the Consumer Price Index, a key indicator of inflation. Current federal inflation data is from June, before the ceasefire in Iran crumbled. July’s data will give us our first real look at the economic effects of the resumed attacks. Analysts will be looking at this data in relation to Friday’s jobs report. Odds of a rate hike in September will likely drop if unemployment is rising, but inflation isn’t as bad as some fear. The odds could also fall if both inflation and unemployment are relatively flat. Either scenario would likely bring lower mortgage rates next week. On the other hand, odds of a rate hike in September will likely increase if unemployment is manageable, but inflation is rising faster than expected. Rising odds of a September rate hike would push mortgage rates up. If unemployment and inflation are both rising, it will be harder to gauge central bankers’ potential rate decision just yet. One thing to keep in mind here: July’s data is backwards-looking, and mortgage lenders are always looking to the future. Any news from Iran will also sway rates day-to-day — potentially running counter to how we’d expect rates to react to the economic data alone. While it’s impossible to time the market to get the lowest rate, there are certain predictable patterns that can guide your strategy. For example, news from Iran that points to a possible peace agreement tends to lead to lower mortgage rates the next day. If you’re hearing positive rumblings, it could be a good time to apply. Timing is only part of the equation, though. You should also shop around with multiple lenders to compare term options and find the lowest rate. We recommend getting quotes from at least three lenders. And if the rates you’re seeing are just not in your budget right now, you can make the most of this time by focusing on tightening up your financial profile. By paying down existing debts and working on your credit health, you’ll be in a better position to score a good deal once rates come down. Related articles

item.title: Mortgage Rates Today, Wednesday, August 5: Noticeably Lower
item.description:
Source: NerdWallet Score: 4.95
If you've been waiting for lower mortgage rates, today just might be your day. The average interest rate on a 30-year, fixed-rate mortgage dropped to 6.59% APR, according to rates provided to NerdWallet by Zillow. This is 11 basis points lower than yesterday and two basis points lower than a week ago. (See our chart below for more specifics.) A basis point is one one-hundredth of a percentage point. Rates fell after the payroll processor ADP released private employment data for July, which showed that job growth fell short of expectations last month. The Federal Reserve only considers federal data when setting monetary policy, but ADP’s report gives us a glimpse of what we might expect when the Bureau of Labor Statistics drops the next jobs report on Friday. “With the overall private sector growth coming in lower than expected, job seekers outside of education and health services are likely feeling squeezed,” said Elizabeth Renter, NerdWallet senior economist. Mortgage lenders had previously expected the Federal Reserve to hike the federal funds rate in September. Since ADP released their July data, odds of a rate hike have dropped to almost 50-50, according to CME FedWatch. When the likelihood of a federal rate hike falls, so can mortgage rates. Average mortgage rates, last 30 days 📈 What influences mortgage rates? Mortgage rates are constantly changing, since a major part of how rates are set depends on reactions to new inflation reports, job numbers, Fed meetings, global news ... you name it. For example, even tiny changes in the bond market can shift mortgage pricing. This week, the Nerds are looking forward to Friday's jobs report. This will be one of the most consequential pieces of federal data in a while, since it will capture employers' initial reactions to the war restarting last month (and with it, a renewed possibility of rising inflation on the horizon). If the data shows that hiring slowed last month or fell short of expectations (like ADP's private sector data), the Fed might continue to hold rates steady in September. On the other hand, if employment seems manageable, higher rates may still be coming in late summer. Next week we'll be watching the Consumer Price Index, a key measure of inflation. Again, since it reflects data collected through July, it will give analysts an early look at the effects of rising oil prices on the economy. If both inflation and unemployment are on the rise, central bankers will be in the unenviable position of balancing opposing priorities. Refinancing might make sense if today’s rates are at least 0.5 to 0.75 of a percentage point lower than your current rate (and if you plan to stay in your home long enough to break even on closing costs). With rates where they are right now, you may want to start considering a refi if your current rate is around 7.09% or higher. Also consider your goals: Are you trying to lower your monthly payment, shorten your loan term or turn home equity into cash? For example, you might be more comfortable with paying a higher rate for a cash-out refinance than you would for a rate-and-term refinance, so long as the overall costs are lower than if you kept your original mortgage and added a HELOC or home equity loan. If you're looking for a lower rate, use NerdWallet's refinance calculator to estimate savings and understand how long it would take to break even on the costs of refinancing. 🏡 Should I start shopping for a home? There is no universal “right” time to start shopping — what matters is whether you can comfortably afford a mortgage now at today’s rates. If the answer is yes, don’t get too hung up on whether you could be missing out on lower rates later; you can refinance down the road. Focus on getting preapproved, comparing lender offers, and understanding what monthly payment works for your budget. NerdWallet’s affordability calculator can help you estimate your potential monthly payment. If a new home isn’t in the cards right now, there are still things you can do to strengthen your buyer profile. Take this time to pay down existing debts and build your down payment savings. Not only will this free up more cash flow for a future mortgage payment, it can also get you a better interest rate when you’re ready to buy. If you already have a quote you’re happy with, you should consider locking your mortgage rate, especially if your lender offers a float-down option. A float-down lets you take advantage of a better rate if the market drops during your lock period. Rate locks protect you from increases while your loan is processed, and with the market forever bouncing around, that peace of mind can be worth it. 🤓 Nerdy Reminder: Rates can change daily, and even hourly. If you’re happy with the deal you have, it’s okay to commit. 🧐 Why is the rate I saw online different from the quote I got? The rate you see advertised is a sample rate — usually for a borrower with perfect credit, making a big down payment, and paying for mortgage points. That won't match every buyer's circumstances. In addition to market factors outside of your control, your customized quote depends on your: Even two people with similar credit scores might get different rates, depending on their overall financial profiles. 👀 If I apply now, can I get the rate I saw today? Maybe — but even personalized rate quotes can change until you lock. That’s because lenders adjust pricing multiple times a day in response to market changes.

item.title: What You Can Learn From the Nerds’ Home Improvement Projects
item.description:
Source: NerdWallet Score: 4.24
Do you have a home improvement project on your to-do list? You might have a deck to build or a leaky toilet to fix. If so, you’re in good company. Searches for “home renovation” and “home improvement” reached their highest levels so far this year in June, according to Google Trends data. Renovations and repairs don’t exactly come cheap. On average, home improvement projects cost about $6,200 each, according to NerdWallet’s analysis of the most recent American Housing Survey from the U.S. Census Bureau. If you plan to work on your home, knowing what to expect can help you avoid costly mistakes. We asked members of NerdWallet’s editorial team to share their experiences and money-saving ideas from this summer’s projects. 🤓 Nerd: Sara Rathner, senior writer/spokesperson 📍 Location: Richmond, Virginia. 🏡 The project: We're finishing our basement. It's something we always thought about doing, especially after visiting friends with finished basements. They were such useful spaces for kids, entertaining and hanging out. I'm looking forward to my basement looking like a cozy family room instead of a raw, industrial space haunted by a vengeful ghost. 💰 Money saving strategy: Hahahaha. It's so expensive. Like laughably expensive. But we're only doing this once, so we want to do it right. Money has no meaning anymore. It's like scooping up a handful of sand and letting it filter out through your fingers. 😮 Something surprising: We interviewed contractors for months. I didn't realize how many would promise to draw up an estimate, only to disappear. Or how many would send us estimates that were missing major parts of the project. If you get an estimate that seems low, go through it line by line. 💡 Tip: Take whatever you thought it was going to cost and add another $10,000. 🤓 Nerd: Jeanette Margle, head of content 📍 Location: The suburbs of Houston, Texas. 🏡 The project: We renovated an unfinished attic and patio space into a bonus room/bedroom to add square footage to our home. 💰 Money saving strategy: We compared multiple quotes for all contractors to get competitive bids, and decided to DIY some things like painting. We used a zero-interest credit card offer (instead of a loan) to help finance piecemeal items, like A/C upgrades that were out-of-scope for the contractor. 😮 Something surprising: I didn't anticipate how much even a small home renovation affects the normal working patterns of your household. Managing various parties coming and going at all hours for weeks was harder than I expected! 💡 Tip: Make sure to compare bids apples-to-apples. If you get one bid that includes additional details, don't assume your lower-priced bid also includes work at the same scope — ask to get clarity. 🤓 Nerd: Julie Myhre-Nunes, managing editor 📍 Location: San Jose, California. 🏡 The project: We replaced our front door and added an electric insert to our fireplace. We redid the windows three years ago, but didn't have the budget to do our front doors — they're double doors and a custom size, so they're more expensive. We knew this upgrade would make our house more energy efficient and better help regulate the temperature in our house. We opted to do the fireplace because we knew ours was not safe to use, and burning wood in my area isn't very common because of “Spare the Air” days. We have lived in our house for six years and finally wanted to have a cozy fireplace for the holidays. 💰 Money saving strategy: We saved up for the doors, but realized our "ideal budget" didn't really reflect reality. We have a HELOC, so we did have to dip into that a bit for the doors. We are in our forever home, and didn't want to settle for doors we didn't love, so we splurged a bit and got the exact door we wanted. Our house had the original doors (from 1966), so this was a major upgrade. We were able to pay cash for the fireplace. We joke that the theme with our house is nothing is a "standard size," which was also true of our fireplace. We had to get a custom insert, which wasn't as expensive as we thought. 😮 Something surprising: Our fireplace was cleaned and repaired before the insert was added. We've never had it cleaned before, and we didn't realize it could be cleaned without getting the dust/soot in the house. That was cool to learn. The doors didn't come with many surprises because we rebuilt all of the windows in our house years before. That project came with unlimited surprises (dry rot, termite damage, sagging windows and more). We expected some with the front doors, but it was a really smooth process. 💡 Tip: Understand your skills and be practical with yourself about what you can and can't handle. We've done a handful of DIY, and I originally intended on doing the fireplace upgrade myself. Once I got started, it was overwhelming and confusing, so we opted to hire a professional. Really get a feel for the salesperson/contractor and ask all the questions to get an idea of whether you can work with them. They may need to communicate something or collaborate with you during the project, and you don't want to be stuck with someone you can't work alongside. You can learn a few things from the Nerds’ experiences: Know when it makes sense to DIY or hire a pro, compare contractor bids carefully and build surprises into your budget. If you’re ready to dive into a project, start by learning how much the renovations and repairs will cost and know what your budget is. Even if you don't have any home improvement jobs planned, it’s smart to think about how you’d handle unexpected repairs and maintenance costs. A leaky roof or busted refrigerator may come knocking eventually. Related articles

item.title: 5 Ways to Slash Back-to-School Spending
item.description:
Source: NerdWallet Score: 3.89
Back-to-school shopping season always sneaks up on me. One minute, I’m planning trips to the pool on hot summer days, and the next I’m searching for a sturdy, yet stylish backpack. All the stuff we need to buy adds up quickly. NerdWallet’s annual back-to-school shopping survey found that back-to-school shoppers estimate they’ll spend an average of $611 on back-to-school expenses such as clothing, supplies and books. That large chunk of change can be hard to manage in an environment where prices are higher on many everyday items, including gas and groceries. Since prices are up across many categories, families have to search harder to find ways to fit back-to-school costs into their budget, says Andrea Woroch, a money-saving expert based in Bakersfield, California. So how can we parents plan for this predictable (yet stressful) time of year? I asked experts for their best strategies. Here’s how to cut costs without sacrificing quality. When you get the official school supply list, shop your home first, Woroch says. “Look to see what you already have. You can reuse pencil cases and binders,” she adds. Sometimes, a composition notebook from a previous year has only a few pages used, so you can simply remove those pages and reuse the notebook. You don’t need to buy the pricier items new every year either, says Kristian Brennon, an accredited financial counselor in the Kansas City area. If you know families with older children, you might be able to score gently used hand-me-downs and skip the stores altogether. Think backpacks, sports gear and shoes. Many communities have consignment sales, back-to-school fairs and freecycling events in advance of the new school year to help you save on supplies and clothes. Community members can trade items and pick up what they need for a low price or free, Brennon says. Sell or consign some of the stuff your kids have outgrown to generate some extra cash for this year’s back-to-school expenses, she adds. Another smart way to save? Band together with other caregivers in your grade to buy items — like notebooks and folders — in bulk at a lower price. “If you have a close-knit community, coordinating with other parents can be helpful,” Brennon says. The big-box stores like Walmart, Staples and Target are offering back-to-school sales comparable to the ones they’ve run in years past. Trae Bodge, a shopping expert based in the New York area, recommends taking advantage of those discounts to save as much as possible. “We’ll see tiered discounts like ‘buy one and get one free’ and loss leader prices like 25-cent notebooks,” she adds. Store-brand notebooks tend to be much cheaper than name-brand ones, Woroch says, even though the product is virtually identical. Plus, she says, some brands — like Hanna Andersson and Athleta Girl — offer pre-loved sections online, which makes it easier to snag lower prices on gently-used clothing. Stick to warm weather clothes for now, though. Bodge recommends waiting to purchase fall clothing because prices tend to drop in October. Plus, she says, kids often get to school, see what classmates are wearing and then have a better sense of the items they want. Since back-to-school expenses come around every year, we can prepare for them by setting money aside in advance, Brennon says. “We can treat it as an annual event like the holidays and set up some kind of sinking fund to prepare monthly for this big expense so we aren’t blindsided by it,” she says. A sinking fund is a savings account dedicated to a specific expense, like back-to-school. You deposit money into it regularly throughout the year so you can use it instead of your paycheck when it’s time to buy. Otherwise, it’s easy to forget the cost is coming up. “Especially in the summer, you’re out doing fun stuff. Who’s thinking about having to buy all this stuff?” Brennon adds. For some parents, figuring out how to budget for back-to-school shopping begins with a conversation with their kids about money. “Create a list together and set expectations,” Bodge says. “We might not be able to get everything our kids want.” That discussion can help kids build financial literacy. For preteens and teens, if they want a brand-name item, perhaps they can contribute to the cost through extra chores, their allowance or a summer job, Bodge says. “They should be spending some of their own money, because if there’s just an open wallet, they don’t understand the impact,” she says. I plan to embrace all of these techniques — especially that last one. Because teaching my kids to set their own budgets is a core curriculum in my house. Related articles

item.title: How the New Science of Social Energetics Explains the Magic of Group Exercise
item.description:
Source: Outside Magazine Score: 4.58
(Photo: Thomas Prior) Sometimes, thanks to work travel or a kids’ soccer game or some other conflict, I have to do my weekly tempo run alone. Most Saturday mornings for the last two decades, I’ve met up with a group of friends to perform this ritual. We chat and banter for a mile or two, then we lock in: an amoeba-like entity with 8 or 12 or 16 legs, united in purpose and moving as a single unit. What has always amazed me, on the days when I go through the same motions by myself, is how much harder it is to hit the usual pace. Some of the benefits of my Saturday morning routine, and of group exercise more generally, are fairly obvious: accountability (I can’t leave my friends hanging if they’re expecting me to show up), distraction, someone else to share the pace and block the wind, and so on. But some scientists believe there’s also something deeper going on—an idea sitting at the intersection of physiology, anthropology, and cognitive science that ties group workouts to ancient practices like music-making, dancing, and even religious rites. They call this emerging concept “social energetics.” Sign up for a ten-part email series from Alex Hutchinson on how to train, fuel, and recover. Each week, Alex covers a new topic, including strength training, supplements, and more! The first clue to social energetics came in a study published back in 2009, when Oxford University anthropologist Emma Cohen was assigned a new graduate student who happened to be captain of the university’s fabled rowing team. She and her student decided to test a theory that social bonding is related to the production of endorphins in the brain—the same euphoria-inducing neurochemicals thought to contribute to “runner’s high” during exercise. They put Oxford’s rowers through a hard workout on a rowing machine, testing their pain threshold before and after. As expected, exercise boosted pain threshold, presumably thanks to the pain-blocking effect of endorphins. But when the rowers repeated exactly the same workout alongside their teammates rather than alone in the room, their pain threshold increased twice as much. There was something about the act of communal exercise that altered the brain’s perception of discomfort. For rowers, this feeling grows out of the sense that they’re part of a larger whole moving in perfect synchrony. Cohen cites Daniel James Brown’s epic rowing book, The Boys in the Boat, which describes the magic of sixteen arms sliding back and forth together, oars entering and leaving the water at exactly the same instant: “Only then will it feel as if the boat is a part of each of them,” Brown writes. “Only then does pain entirely give way to exultation.” A few years later, Cohen supervised another elite student-athlete, this one captain of Oxford’s rugby team, which gave her an opportunity to test this idea more explicitly. They measured the team’s performance in a challenging running test after doing their warm-up routine alone, together, or together in synch with each other. Sure enough, the athletes performed best in the synchronized condition—an evolutionary relic, perhaps, of long-ago group hunts on the savanna. There are times, during my tempo runs, when my friends and I find that our strides have unconsciously synchronized. Indeed, research suggests that this happens more than you would expect from chance alone. But there’s more to the feel of a group run or ride than physical synchrony. Cohen studied participants in Parkrun, a free weekly 5K event held at locations around the world that is notably friendly and welcoming. Runners who felt a greater sense of social connection at the event also reported feeling more energetic, which in turn was associated with faster running times without any increase in effort. Most recently, a yet-to-be-published study from Cohen and her colleagues, led by Arran Davis, had competitive rowers row to exhaustion while viewing photos of either a stranger or a friend or family member. Remarkably, the rowers lasted 24 percent longer when viewing the supportive photo—even though their perception of effort was the same in both cases. There’s no synchrony here, since the other person was present only in the form of a digital photo, so something else must be happening. Cohen’s theory, which she has been developing alongside other scientists, including Chris Beedie, an expert in the placebo effect, and Herman Pontzer, an expert in human metabolism, is what they’ve dubbed social energetics. The basic idea is that the way you budget your body’s energy expenditure is influenced by your connections (or lack thereof) with the people around you. The feeling of fatigue is designed to keep us safe, to prevent us from pushing so hard that we collapse. When we’re surrounded by friends, we feel safer: we don’t need to hold as much energy in reserve to defend or take care of ourselves. Evolution has hardwired this instinct into our brains, so that cues that make us feel closer to others—synchronized movement, or even just a photo—alter the sensations that guide how we budget our precious energy stores. The original “rower’s high” study in 2009 assumed that these signals were mediated by endorphins, the body’s internal version of opioids. Cohen now thinks endocannabinoids, the body’s internal cannabis, are also involved. And there may well be other mechanisms. A recent stream of research, for example, suggests that the most famous social bonding hormone of all, oxytocin, is released during exercise and is responsible for at least some of exercise’s mental health benefits. The social energetics hypothesis and its associated neurochemistry helps explain why my tempo runs feel so much easier in a group. They also suggest an intriguing flip side: that these runs are, in turn, making my friendships better, thanks to the stew of social bond–promoting brain chemicals produced. I’m a big believer in the power of group workouts, and I’ve spent a lot of effort to maintain my Saturday morning ritual through the years: early wakeups, long commutes, a rotating cast of babysitters. I like being ten seconds per mile faster without trying harder—but my real motivation, now that I think about it, is that I love sharing the experience with my friends. This article is from the Summer 2026 issue of Outside magazine. To receive the print magazine, become an Outside+ member here. For more Sweat Science, sign up for the email newsletter and check out my new book The Explorer’s Gene: Why We Seek Big Challenges, New Flavors, and the Blank Spots on the Map.

item.title: What’s at Stake as Fires Threaten Mount Hood’s Historic Landmarks and Ski Areas
item.description:
Source: Outside Magazine Score: 4.38
Firefighters battle wildfires blazing across Oregon (Photo: Noah Berger/Associated Press) Every summer since 1924, U.S. Forest Service employees have worked inside the historic Flag Point Fire Lookout in Oregon’s Mount Hood National Forest (MHNF). On July 31, 2026, the high-alpine cabin burned to the ground. Flag Point is one of many beloved outdoor destinations in the Pacific Northwest to be destroyed or threatened by surging wildfires. The Grasshopper Fire burning east of Mount Hood destroyed the historic fire lookout, forced the evacuation of ski area Mt. Hood Meadows, and closed more than 50 trails across the mountain. “It’s been hot and dry this whole summer,” Heather Ibsen, an MHNF spokesperson told Outside. Nobody was inside the Flag Point Fire Lookout when it burned because the Forest Service evacuated staff as the fire got close, she said. But forests, fire lookouts, and recreation sites remain at risk. Officials shut down most of Mount Hood in the middle of its summer season. Mt. Hood Meadows, the largest ski resort on the mountain, is evacuated. Timberline Lodge, a historic landmark built in 1938 on the mountain’s south side, suspended hiking and mountain biking operations. Skibowl, a year-round recreational resort near the town of Government Camp, closed for smoke. Sparked by lightning on July 23, the Grasshopper Fire has burned nearly 35,000 acres as of August 5, officials said, and remains just 19 percent contained as of the publishing of this story. Roughly 1,300 firefighters and safety officials are currently battling the blaze. The lookout was one of three Forest Service watchtowers on Mount Hood, and it remained part of the fire detection network, working alongside forest patrols, cameras, and remote-sensing systems. Members of the public could also rent the lookout in the off-season. Though the Mount Hood community is already mourning the fire lookout, Ibsen told Outside that losing it doesn’t leave a hole in coverage—at least, not yet. “The in-person fire lookouts are really valuable, but they’re not the only tool we have,” said Ibsen. The Forest Service detects fires using a mix of staffed lookouts, remote cameras, satellite heat data, and firefighters patrolling by truck. Mt. Hood Meadows is roughly 60 miles from Portland. As the Grasshopper Fire pushed up against its boundaries, officials announced a “Go Now” evacuation—the most urgent—in the early morning of August 4. “Whelp, we hoped we wouldn’t have to post this, but here we are,” the ski mountain wrote on Instagram following the Level 3 evacuation. Mt. Hood Meadows President Greg Pack told local news outlet KPTV that a wind reversal caused the evacuation order. Typically, the mountain’s prevailing winds blow west, he said, carrying smoke and fire away from the resorts. But the area saw days of easterly winds instead. Officials placed the historic, nearly 90-year-old Timberline Lodge under a Level 1 “Be Ready” evacuation notice on August 3. “Be aware of danger, monitor local news, and start packing valuables or preparing family members and pets,” reads the notice. The lodge will remain open unless the evacuation order is raised to Level 2. On July 24, the Pacific Crest Trail Association (PCTA) announced the effective closure of the roughly 50 northernmost miles of the trail, including the northern terminus and access at Hart’s Pass, due to a wildfire burning to the east of the trail. Though the Pacific Crest Trail remains open in the Mount Hood area, as of the publication of this story, the PCTA listed the Grasshopper Fire as an alert. The fire is burning east of the trail. Hikers are advised to remember that conditions can change quickly and to check for updates. The Forest Service has closed more than 50 trails in response to the fires through December 31. These include the Timberline Trail, a 41-mile loop around Mount Hood, along with Elk Meadows, Umbrella Falls, Tilly Jane Ski Trail, Pollalie Ridge, Bluegrass Ridge, Lamberson Spur, Zig Zag, Lost Lake Butte and Surveyor’s Ridge. Reopening won’t happen quickly. Ibsen told Outside that once conditions stabilize, emergency teams will need to head into the burned area to assess the damage. “It’s usually scientists and specialists who come in to evaluate damage to soil and the geology and other natural resources, but they do evaluate recreation infrastructure as well,” she said. Forest staff then use that data to inventory recreation sites and trails, estimate repair costs, and request funding. How fast a trail is repaired depends on where it is. “How we manage wilderness areas is very different from how we might manage something that is very developed, around a busy campground on a lake,” she said. Some areas may open before the amenities that were there are repaired or replaced. “We want to open up areas to public access as soon as it’s safe to do so,” said Ibsen. Check before you drive. Current closures include a block of Highway 35, and evacuation levels shift daily. Consult both the county sheriff’s maps and the Forest Service closure order. You can check air quality at before heading outdoors.

item.title: What Is Bourbon Virus? Here’s What to Know About This Rare Tickborne Illness.
item.description:
Source: Outside Magazine Score: 4.06
(Photo: Ayana Underwood/Canva) Most hikers and campers are aware of the potential risk of getting Lyme disease, Rocky Mountain Spotted Fever, or similar diseases from a tick bite. But a May 2026 study published by Stony Brook University doctors and researchers in the American Journal of Tropical Medicine and Hygiene (AJTMH) suggested that a rare and potentially fatal tick-borne disease might be on the rise: Bourbon virus. The doctors confirmed New York state’s first-ever case of the virus in the AJTMH study, which detailed how two patients who developed a fever after a tick bite in Suffolk County, New York, had antibodies to Bourbon virus. Of those, one person had high-enough antibody levels that suggested they were recently infected. According to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), there is currently no known cure or vaccine for Bourbon virus. “The reality is, there is probably a lot more of this virus going around than we think,” Dr. Thomas Russo, an infectious disease doctor at the University at Buffalo in New York, told Outside. With that in mind, disease experts say that Bourbon virus is yet another tickborne illness that should be on your radar for people who spend significant time outdoors. Here’s what you need to know. Bourbon virus is a tickborne disease that was first detected in 2014 in Bourbon County, Kansas. The CDC says it likely spreads through the bite of an infected Lone Star tick. (Lone Star ticks are also responsible for alpha-gal syndrome, an allergy to red meat.) Since the initial case, the virus has been detected in Kansas, Oklahoma, and Missouri and some eastern and southern states. “The Lone Star tick’s geographic range seems to be increasing,” Russo said. “It’s possible that we may see more Bourbon virus as a result.” “Most tickborne diseases people think of—Lyme, anaplasmosis, ehrlichiosis, Rocky Mountain Spotted Fever—are bacterial, and babesiosis is a parasite,” Dr. Amesh Adalja told Outside. Adalja is a senior scholar at the Johns Hopkins Center for Health Security in Baltimore, Maryland. “All of those respond to antibiotics or antiparasitics,” he said. In other words, because Bourbon virus is a virus, none of the treatments that work against the diseases listed above will treat it. While cases of Bourbon virus are increasing across the country, this is still considered a rare disease, Russo says. “Clinically, I’ve never seen a case,” he said. But Bourbon virus can be fatal. “Not many confirmed human cases have ever been identified, and deaths have occurred,” Dr. Adalja says. “However, many cases are going undiagnosed, so the case fatality ratio will be skewed by the small number of reported cases.” Overall, Russo says you don’t have to stress too much about Bourbon virus, but heightened awareness that it exists will serve you well as you navigate the outdoors. Symptoms can include a fever, fatigue, rash, headache and body aches, nausea, and vomiting, per the CDC. “We see these symptoms with other infections as well, so these are not particularly discriminatory,” Russo said. “If someone came to me today that has those non-specific symptoms, I’m not sure I could make the diagnosis.” In other words, you would still need exact confirmation of which tick-related illness you have. There’s also no commercially available way to test for it, but your doctor can send your blood samples to health officials at the CDC for a diagnosis. However, it may take time to receive your results. Unfortunately, Bourbon virus isn’t easy to treat. “There’s no antiviral for it and no vaccine,” Dr. Adalja says. Instead, the virus is managed with supportive care, he said. Your doctor may suggest over-the-counter pain relievers for more mild symptoms. According to Adalja, if you’re receiving treatment for a tick disease and nothing is working, there’s a chance that you could be infected with Bourbon. The best way to lower the risk of Bourbon virus is to do what you can to avoid tick bites. “The prevention is identical to every other tickborne disease: use tick repellent, wear clothing that is not conducive to tick bites, do a full-body tick check after being outdoors, and remove any attached tick promptly,” Adalja said. While tick bites happen, doctors stress that they are often preventable. “The key for not only Bourbon virus, but all the other tickborne illnesses, is to try to not get bitten by ticks,” Russo said. Want more Outside health stories? Sign up for the Bodywork newsletter. And, for tips on how to train, fuel, and recover better, sign up for the Sweat Science 101 newsletter.

item.title: Former Ranger Melisa Dalley Left the National Park Service. Now She Gives Rogue Tours They Can’t Control.
item.description:
Source: Outside Magazine Score: 3.92
Melissa Dalley is a former NPS ranger who continues to document and share information she believes the federal government has censored (Photo: Melissa Dalley) In July, former National Park Service (NPS) ranger Melissa Dalley stood in a visitor center in Grand Teton National Park, next to a wall where a sign used to be, handing strangers a piece of paper with the missing words on it. “You could clearly see the ghost of the sign,” Dalley told Outside. “The language was still imprinted on the plinth.” The display she is referring to was once mounted beneath a statue of Gustavus Cheyney Doane, a 19th-century U.S. Army officer who explored parts of the Teton region and took part in the killing of more than 170 Piegan Blackfeet. Dalley documented the now-missing sign, and is sharing its information with visitors. Since April 2026, she has visited 18 parks, handing out such flyers. Dalley, 49, was a park guide at Martin Van Buren National Historic Site, an NPS-managed location in upstate New York for four years until she quit in 2026. She is now a volunteer organizer with America 433+, an education coalition named for the 433 sites in the NPS system. The group is petitioning Congress to stop what it calls the censorship of American history. “I determined that I could serve the Park Service much better right now from the outside,” she said. “I wouldn’t be muzzled, and I wouldn’t face retaliation.” Her decision to leave the NPS came a year after President Trump signed a March 2025 executive order directing federal agencies to review how the country’s past is presented at Park Service-managed sites. Secretarial Order 3431 followed in May of that year, requiring the agency to remove content that “inappropriately disparage[s] Americans past or living” and to emphasize instead the beauty and grandeur of the landscape. According to Dalley, the Doane at Grand Teton was one of dozens of signs the NPS said it has since removed. Dalley’s usual process involves standing near a removed sign and waiting for a visitor to stop and read the panels still posted. Then, she approaches them. “Hey, I see you’re reading these signs. Did you notice there was one missing? And here it is,” she says, handing them a copy of the sign’s text. Dalley is a member of the Resistance Rangers, a volunteer collective of off-duty and former employees. The mostly anonymous group was formed in response to the February 14, 2025 firing of some 1,000 workers across all 433 NPS sites. The courts ordered their reinstatement in March, but thousands more left voluntarily over the following months through buyouts and early retirements. Her work isn’t affiliated directly with the group, but she says that around that time, rangers across the country were having a version of the same conversation. “We were all talking about what’s our red line? What is the thing that is going to push us past our ability to tolerate? Because we all felt compromised morally and ethically,” Dalley said. The sign removals were her red line. By June 2025, park employees placed notices asking visitors to report signage they found negative about American history. Staff was required to flag their own materials. The first wave of removals began that September, and included signs referencing climate change, slavery and the massacre of Native Americans, among other topics. That’s when Dalley started tracking the removals herself. Soon, people at other parks began contacting her, and she became a hub of information. Sites that had never had reason to talk to each other were now comparing notes, from Alaska to Guam, she said. “People began to see the scope of it,” Dalley told Outside. “We could just start banging our drums and talking about it and trying to get the public to care.” In early 2026, Dalley drove west from New York, stopping at parks along the way. In May, she went to the President’s House in Philadelphia, the site that memorializes the enslaved people held by George Washington, where she had once given tours. She found that visitors had filled in missing information themselves, taping up photographs of the removed signs and printed articles describing the removals. Someone had strung up a roll of butcher paper with a Sharpie hanging from it, asking passersby to share their feelings on the perceived censorship. People from around the world responded in writing. “Basically, the public took on the mantle of what the Park Service should be doing,” she said. “They just spontaneously, grassroots, recreated an audience-centered interpretation.” She continued her mission with a Juneteenth teach-in at Harpers Ferry National Historical Park in West Virginia, then again at Grand Teton and Glacier National Parks while on vacation with her family. Some information is available only on NPS signs, Dalley said, while other details exist primarily in the institutional knowledge that park rangers have built over decades. “There is an irreparable loss associated with some of this information being censored,” she said. Signs at NPS sits also help visitors connect with the place where a historical event occurred, at a moment when they’re most likely to care, regardless of whether the “given history is flattering to Americans.” Dalley said her dedication to the mission of preserving the past is to inspire others to do the same. “I’m just one person, and I’ve been able to figure a lot of this out,” she adds. Next, Dalley plans to build a downloadable toolkit to catalogue removed signs. “Being a park ranger unlocked something in me,” she said. “I miss it so much.” For now, she’s sharing American history, standing next to the empty space where a sign used to be.

item.title: The AI hacking tests keep escaping the lab
item.description:
Source: PCWorld Score: 6.09
Once again, the most powerful Claude and ChatGPT models have been caught going rogue, with a pair of third-party cybersecurity teams spotting attempts by the models to hack real companies and even people. The UK government-backed AI Security Institute reports that during a series of cybersecurity evaluations, Anthropic’s Claude Mythos 5 and OpenAI’s GPT-5.6 Sol both took “autonomous, unsanctioned action on the live internet,” including an instance where an agent attempted to upload malicious code to GitHub using a phony identity. In another incident, an OpenAI model that had mistakenly been given internet access hacked a real website during a “capture the flag” exercise, according to third-party AI evaluator Irregular. AISI, the UK-based AI security firm, said it caught the suspicious activity before any damage was done, noting that it had deliberately given the models internet access and removed safety guardrails during its evaluations. Still, the actions of the agents demonstrated “signs of novel, potentially deceptive behaviors, and were to an extent and severity we did not anticipate,” according to the AISI report. The latest hacking attempts follow a series of other recent incidents involving “frontier” Anthropic and OpenAI models, which demonstrating a startling willingness to use both deception and brute force in their attacks on real targets. Late last month, OpenAI came clean about a hair-raising attack on AI repository Hugging Face by a trio of GPT models, which were intent on stealing data that could help them beat a cyber security benchmark. The unprecedented attack stunned AI experts, with Hugging Face’s security succumbing to the hack in a matter of hours. Only days later, Anthropic admitted that its own models had been involved in a trio of incidents in which they attacked outside organizations, with one of the models continuing its hack even after realizing its target was real. While the string of autonomous Claude and GPT hacks is unnerving, AISI sounded a note of optimism, noting that the GitHub attack was thwarted by a human reviewer who spotted the suspicious code and isolated it before it could cause any damage. “Standard good practice, human judgement, and caution around AI-generated code stopped the worst outcomes,” AISI concluded in its report. That said, “the margin between failure and success was narrow.”

item.title: Summer heat is coming for your PC’s performance. Here’s what actually helps
item.description:
Source: PCWorld Score: 6.06
In summary: - PCWorld explains how summer heat threatens PC performance through thermal throttling, where CPUs reduce speed at 100°C (Intel) or 95°C (AMD Ryzen) to prevent damage. - Essential solutions include cleaning dust buildup, monitoring temperatures with HWiNFO software, adjusting Windows power settings to disable Turbo Boost, and adding case fans for better airflow. - Laptop users benefit from cooling pads that reduce temperatures up to 20 degrees, while replacing thermal paste every 3-5 years maintains optimal heat transfer. When heatwaves strike in summer, any chance to cool down is welcome — whether at the lake, in an ice-cream parlor, or at home in front of a fan. What’s a relief for us is also something your computer desperately needs as soon as the thermometer hits the 30-degrees Celsius mark. After all, the hotter the ambient air, the harder the cooling system in your PC or laptop has to work. This puts the fans under constant strain: They get louder, use more energy, and wear out much faster. That’s why you should put your computer through a heat check: This way, you can ensure that it continues to run at its usual speed even under thermal stress and that the lifespan of its components isn’t reduced. First, use suitable tools to check just how hot your PC or laptop actually gets. These results will reveal whether your computer has a heat problem at all and whether you can solve it with free immediate help or additional internal and external cooling components. In most cases, a few measurements, targeted maintenance, and the correct Windows settings are enough to ensure you always keep your computer’s temperatures under control, even in the height of summer. Heat slows things down, but it doesn’t break anything First, the good news: An overheated PC does not, as a rule, crash immediately and without warning. Modern processors and graphics cards have built-in protection: If a chip approaches its maximum temperature, it reduces its clock speed and voltage — a process known as thermal throttling. This allows the components to reduce their power consumption, which in turn means less waste heat that the cooling system has to remove from the case. Thermal throttling is noticeable as a drop in speed: Programs start more slowly, copying large files takes longer, and the frame rate in games plummets. In an overheated laptop, the CPU clock speed can even drop by a quarter. Only when even this performance throttling is no longer sufficient does the hardware switch itself off as a last resort. However, this emergency shutdown (thermal shutdown) almost never occurs in practice, because users usually close computationally intensive applications or switch off the PC beforehand due to the significantly reduced performance. Regardless of the current loss of performance, prolonged exposure to heat also causes long-term damage to the hardware. When components are constantly operating at high temperatures, they age at an accelerated rate. This is due to accelerated chemical processes inside the components: In the fans, the vital lubricant in the ball bearings liquefies, while in the capacitors on the circuit boards, the electrolyte evaporates. The result is that they swell up or, in the worst case, even burst. In laptops, this primarily affects the battery: Lithium-ion cells age more quickly at higher temperatures, particularly when they remain fully charged for extended periods. Therefore, in summer, try not to leave the device permanently connected to power with the battery at 100 percent charge. It makes more sense to disconnect the laptop from the outlet from time to time or — if available — to activate a charge limit in the system settings. Checking the temperature with free tools To find out just how hot your computer really is, you’ll need specialized software. Windows’ built-in tools aren’t much help here. We recommend the comprehensive hardware analysis tool Hwinfo. After installation, select the ‘Sensors only’ option from the drop-down menu and click ‘Start.’ This opens the sensor list directly, without the full hardware system report. Friedrich Stiemer In the list, the readings are organized by individual component. Four columns show the current value, as well as the minimum, maximum, and average since the start of the measurement. For the processor, the ‘CPU Package’ row in the CPU section is particularly relevant; for AMD processors, this is labelled ‘CPU (Tctl/Tdie).’ Below this, under ‘Core Temperatures,’ HWiNFO also displays the temperature trends for each individual CPU core. Friedrich Stiemer For the graphics card, two values are of primary importance: ‘GPU Temperature’ for the average and ‘GPU Hot Spot Temperature’ for the hottest point on the graphics card. You can see how hot the SSD is under the ‘Drive Temperature’ entry. The clearest indication of an existing temperature problem in the computer is provided by the ‘Thermal Throttling’ line: If the ‘Maximum’ column shows ‘Yes,’ the processor has already throttled at least once during the measurement due to overheating. Core Temp presents the computer’s temperature readings in a less detailed, but clearer format. This mini-tool displays only the temperature of each core, the corresponding utilization, and the processor’s throttling limit under ‘Tj. Max.’ If desired, it can display the values in the Windows taskbar. Please note during installation: Be sure to deselect any additional programs offered. HWMonitor is ideal for a very quick overview: The program displays temperature readings in a table showing the current, minimum, and maximum values. An ad-free alternative is Libre Hardware Monitor. If you just want to keep an eye on your graphics card, the GPU-Z tool is all you need: Select the ‘Sensors’ tab to view the GPU temperature and the hot spot. If you want to see your computer’s temperature readings at all times so you can take immediate action, use the MSI Afterburner program: Here, you can enable an overlay view that remains in the foreground at all times. In the settings under the ‘Monitoring’ tab, you can enable the display of the desired values on the overlay screen. You’ll need to manually enable CPU temperature monitoring, as the program only monitors the graphics card by default. Friedrich Stiemer How hot can CPUs and other components get? Manufacturers specify temperature ranges within which processors and graphics chips should be operated. These depend on the manufacturing process, chip packaging, and build quality, and can therefore vary between different chip generations and even production batches. A CPU usually heats up to between 30 and 45 degrees Celsius when idle. Under heavy load with many active cores, it should ideally remain below 80 degrees. Thermal throttling generally kicks in at 100 degrees for Intel processors, at 95 degrees for AMD’s Ryzen 7000 chips, and at 89 degrees for the X3D variants with larger cache. Friedrich Stiemer These values have been deliberately chosen: They represent a compromise between performance and lifespan — they are designed to ensure that the chip does not suffer a heat-related fault under any circumstances during the warranty period and, beyond that, continues to function without problems until it is replaced for performance reasons anyway. Depending on the generation, Nvidia graphics cards throttle at between 90 and 93 degrees, whilst AMD Radeon cards are permitted to reach as high as 110 degrees at their hottest point, the ‘hot spot.’ An NVMe SSD throttles between 70 and 80 degrees to prevent the storage controller from overheating and to ensure no data is lost. With DDR5 RAM, things only become critical above 85 degrees — but RAM rarely reaches this temperature. This is because, before the RAM reaches these temperatures due to an inadequate cooling system, other components will already be causing problems. The rule for you is: If the temperatures remain below the specified limits even under load, everything is fine. If the temperature regularly rises above the limit and causes, for example, thermal throttling, you need to take action. Reducing heat via software Before making any hardware changes, you should try to get temperature issues under control using software settings. This is because every additional program running in the background uses processing power and therefore generates heat. So, first of all, open the Task Manager using Ctrl + Shift + Esc. In the ‘Startup’ tab, disable all programs that do not need to be active straight away — such as cloud services, update tools, or chat programs. In the ‘Processes’ tab, click on the ‘CPU’ column: Here you can see which programs are constantly generating CPU load — often it’s the browser with lots of tabs open. An unusually high load while the PC is idle, with fans running constantly, may indicate hidden mining malware: You can check for this using an antivirus scanner. The most effective way to reduce PC heat is via Windows’ power options: Here, for example, you can cap the processor’s Turbo Boost, which is responsible for a large proportion of the heat. Open the Windows Control Panel, go to ‘Power Options’ and, for the active plan, click on ‘Change power plan settings’ and then on ‘Change advanced power settings.’ Friedrich Stiemer Expand the ‘Processor power management’ section and change the value for ‘Maximum processor power state’ from 100 to 99 percent. For many processors, even this one percent is enough to switch off Turbo Boost, which briefly boosts the clock speed and consumes a disproportionate amount of power and generates excessive heat. In everyday use, you’ll hardly notice any loss of speed, but the temperature will drop significantly — often by several dozen degrees. On a well-cooled desktop PC, this is a stopgap solution; on an older laptop, however, it’s a very effective trick. It’s best to use this throttling in the ‘Balanced’ power plan and also keep a second plan set to full performance for situations where you need maximum processing power. In the same menu, it’s also worth taking a look at the system cooling policy: If this is set to ‘Active,’ Windows will initially increase the fan speed as the load rises, before the processor limits its performance by reducing its clock speed. Position your computer in the right place Simply moving your PC to a different spot can also provide quick relief. This is because every extra degree in the ambient temperature increases the thermal stress on fans and components. So don’t place the computer in direct sunlight or in the warmest room; keep it away from the wall, and don’t lock it away in a closed cupboard without ventilation. Furthermore, do not stack warm devices such as routers or consoles on top of it, and protect the laptop’s screen from direct sunlight. Free tip: This is the best way to combat heat Computers that have been in use for some time are particularly prone to overheating. In many cases, these can be resolved easily and completely free of charge: by dusting. Over the years, dust accumulates on cooling fins and fan blades, settling like a blanket over the cooling surfaces and obstructing the airflow. The result: The fans can no longer dissipate the waste heat as quickly as before; they have to spin faster — and therefore more noisily — and eventually, despite constant fan activity, thermal throttling sets in. To clean the computer thoroughly, switch it off and unplug the power cable. For a PC, remove one of the side panels of the case: It is usually secured to the back with two knurled screws. Once you have loosened these, you can pull the panel off towards the back. Now use a can of compressed air or a mini blower to blow the dust out in short bursts from a distance of a few centimeters. AF Utility Areas such as the processor cooler, the graphics card, the power supply’s air intake and the dust filters behind the front of the case are particularly important. When blowing out fans, you must block the fan blades with a finger or a toothpick to prevent them from spinning uncontrollably. Excessive speed can put strain on the bearing and, in the worst case, cause damage. You should not, however, use a vacuum cleaner directly on PC components, as this can cause static build-up. You can clean the removable dust filters at the front and bottom of the case under running water. It is important that they are completely dry before you reinsert them. A thorough cleaning of the PC is generally advisable every six to 12 months. However, in households with pets or smokers, it may be necessary to clean it more frequently. Check fans and replace thermal paste After cleaning, you should check whether all fans are still working properly or are already showing signs of wear and tear. Listen for grinding or rattling noises, which may indicate a worn bearing. You can also check the current speed using software such as HWiNFO: A 120- or 140-millimeter case fan usually operates at a few hundred to around 1,200 revolutions per minute (rpm) under normal conditions; under heavier load, this can rise to as much as 2,000 rpm. Smaller fans in laptops, on the other hand, spin significantly faster and often reach 2,000 to 5,000 rpm. A warning sign is a speed of 0 rpm displayed continuously, even though the system is warm and other fans are running. In this case, the fan may have stopped and is either faulty or not connected properly. Graphics card and power supply fans are an exception: Many models switch off automatically when idle or at low temperatures, which is why 0 rpm may be normal in these cases. Conversely, an unusually high speed during normal desktop operation may also indicate a problem, such as insufficient cooling or a faulty fan controller. If temperatures remain consistently too high despite cleaning and the fans working properly, you should replace the thermal paste on the CPU or GPU. For example, if an analysis program shows that a single CPU core is consistently 10 to 15 degrees hotter than the others, or if the average and peak temperatures at the hot spot on a graphics card differ by more than 25 degrees, this suggests that the thermal paste is outdated. Over the years, it dries out, becomes cracked, and is less effective at transferring heat to the cooler. High-quality thermal paste lasts three to five years, while the factory-applied paste in pre-built computers often lasts only two — so for a PC that’s four to six years old, replacing it is definitely worth it and costs next to nothing: A tube costs between $5 and $10. Thermal Grizzly To apply it, remove the cooler and wipe away the existing paste using isopropyl alcohol and a lint-free cloth. Then squeeze a pea-sized dot of fresh paste onto the center of the chip’s surface or the copper cover above it, and refit the cooler evenly in a criss-cross pattern. With laptops, this procedure is considerably more involved: The processor is located beneath a cover from which heat pipes lead to the fan. To apply new paste, you must therefore remove the entire cooling assembly and then refit it correctly. If in doubt, leave this to a specialist workshop. Fitting additional fans The next step towards lower temperatures is to fit additional case fans. Models with a diameter of 120 or 140 millimeters are common — the larger they are, the more air they move at the same speed and the quieter they operate. Bear in mind the airflow within the case: The fans draw in cool air at the front and bottom, and expel the waste heat from the components at the back and top. This creates a continuous flow that follows the natural rise of warm air. Friedrich Stiemer For a standard PC mid-tower, three to five fans are sufficient. Plug them into the motherboard connectors labelled ‘CHA_FAN’ or ‘SYS_FAN’; leave the ‘CPU_FAN’ connector free, as this is reserved for the processor cooler. If there aren’t enough connectors, an inexpensive fan hub will do the trick. The motherboard controls four-pin fans precisely via a pulse signal (PWM), while three-pin models are controlled via voltage; both fit standard connectors. You can then set the speed curves via the UEFI BIOS or a program such as FanControl. However, additional fans are only beneficial if part of a well-thought-out design. If there are more intake fans at the front than exhaust fans at the rear, this creates a slight overpressure inside the case. This pushes the air outwards rather than drawing dust in through every gap, provided that all intake vents are fitted with filters. Also ensure there is a clear airflow path and route cables behind the motherboard tray. A case with a fine mesh grille at the front cools significantly better than one with a solid glass front. Improving cooling in a laptop You cannot retrofit additional or larger fans into a laptop. Only small fans and thin heat pipes fit into the slim chassis; often, the processor and graphics unit share a single cooling solution. In this case, you’ll need to resort to external aids: The simplest measure is a stand that raises the rear end by two to three centimeters, so that the air intake vents on the underside can draw in more air. This reduces the temperature by five to 10 degrees under light to medium load. Targus A foldable aluminium stand costs around $25 to $30. Active cooling pads with their own fans offer more — but only the right ones: With cheap, open-sided models, the air escapes from the sides and does little to change the case temperature; sealed pads, on the other hand, force the air directly into the intake vents and reduce the temperature by up to 20 degrees. Simple pads with multiple fans cost around $20 to $35, while high-performance models with turbo fans cost $45 to $70. As a basic rule when using a laptop, always remember: Never place your laptop on a blanket, bed, or your lap, as soft surfaces block the lower ventilation slots and trap the heat. A hard, flat surface is essential. However, it’s also worth using short bursts of compressed air to clear dust from the ventilation slots on your laptop.

item.title: Your top PC fan might be making your CPU run hotter
item.description:
Source: PCWorld Score: 5.68
Many PC systems struggle with unnecessarily high CPU temperatures, even though they’ve got plenty of fans installed. Often, the problem isn’t insufficient cooling, but poor airflow. A particularly common approach is to configure all top-mounted fans as exhaust. While this may sound logical, in traditional PC cases with air coolers it can have the opposite effect. With a small adjustment to the fan orientation, the processor can often be run at a lower temperature at no extra cost. The crux of the problem lies in the interaction between the front and top fans. In most mid-tower cases, cool air flows into the case from the front. Ideally, this should reach the CPU cooler. However, if the front top-fan is configured as an exhaust fan, it immediately draws some of this fresh air back upwards before it reaches the CPU cooler. This short-circuits the airflow. Instead of flowing through the heat sink and fins, the cold air leaves the case virtually unused. The result is higher CPU temperatures, even though several fans are actively running. A simple fix is to configure the front-top fan as an intake rather than an exhaust, allowing more cool air to reach the CPU cooler before it exits the case. Noctua This ensures that the fresh air drawn in from the front is directed towards the CPU, rather than being pulled out of the case prematurely. The rear-top fan remains configured as an exhaust, allowing the heated air to be expelled in a controlled manner. Although this combination of intake and exhaust airflow in the top panel contradicts older rules of thumb, in practice it often means a more even and efficient airflow around the processor. It’s relatively easy to check whether this adjustment makes sense for your system. First, open the case and get an overview of the current fan orientation. Most fans have small arrows on the frame indicating the direction in which air flows. Alternatively, a piece of paper or smoke from an incense stick can help to visualize the direction of airflow. Next, rotate the front top fan so that it blows air into the case, while the rear-top fan continues to expel air outwards. For a meaningful comparison, measure the temperatures before and after the change under similar conditions. First, start Windows, let the system run for a few minutes to stabilize, and note the CPU temperature. Afterwards, perform a longer gaming test or a demanding application, as this provides a more representative test than a synthetic stress test. Monitor the average CPU temperature over several minutes. Gamemax In many cases, a reduction of one to two degrees can be observed, and occasionally even more, depending on the case, fan performance, and CPU cooler. It is important to note that this method applies to systems with a conventional air cooler. If the processor is cooled by a water-cooling system with a radiator, airflow around the CPU cooler plays a different role. If the radiator is mounted in the top panel, the fan orientation primarily determines whether the priority is lower processor temperatures or more effective overall heat dissipation from the case. There is no one-size-fits-all solution here, which is why conducting your own tests is useful. Caution is also advised if your case has additional fans in the bottom. In such configurations, a top intake fan can create unwanted turbulence that traps warm air inside the case or raises graphics card temperatures. In these situations, using a top exhaust fan is more reliable. The most important takeaway is that rigid airflow rules do not always produce the best results. Instead of automatically configuring all top fans as exhaust fans, it’s worth examining the actual airflow within your own case and adjusting accordingly.

item.title: Why uninstalling a Windows 11 app might not free up any storage
item.description:
Source: PCWorld Score: 5.66
In summary: - PCWorld notes that uninstalling Microsoft Store apps on Windows 11 may not actually free up storage space on your device. - This happens because MSIX-format apps use a staging and registration system, meaning uninstalling an app often just deregisters it rather than removing the underlying package files from your disk. - Users expecting to reclaim storage after removing apps may be surprised to find the payload files remain behind. If you planned to free up space on Windows 11 by uninstalling a few apps, you should know that it doesn’t always work, especially if you installed those apps via the Microsoft Store. When you download and install apps from the Microsoft Store, they come in a special format called MSIX. Microsoft created this format as a clean way to install apps, keep those apps update, and avoid registry bloat and leftover files when they’re eventually uninstalled. However, Microsoft does some funky magic behind the scenes when installing and uninstalling MSIX packages—sometimes, uninstalling an app doesn’t actually “uninstall” it in the traditional sense. Instead, Windows effectively makes it invisible to you even while keeping it on disk. That’s because the MSIX system design doesn’t recognize “install” and “uninstall” actions as we’ve come to know them. Instead, an app can be “staged” (downloaded and placed on disk), “registered” (associated with the user and made visible), “deregistered” (disassociated with the user and made invisible), and “destaged” (removed from disk). It’s all explained in a recent Inside MSIX blog post written by Howard Kapustein, Principal Software Engineer at Microsoft: Just as [this blog post] explained that Install is not truly an installation operation in MSIX, Remove is similarly not an uninstall operation. This can be surprising — sometimes even alarming — to developers coming from traditional installer technologies such as MSI, where uninstalling software typically implies: - binaries are deleted - directories are removed - registry entries are cleaned - runtime artifacts are purged In MSIX, that model simply does not exist. He later goes on to say: From the user’s perspective, the application is gone. From the operating system’s perspective, however, the package may still be present on disk — available for, and possibly in use by, other users. That distinction is crucial to understanding why Remove is not the same thing as Uninstall. Remove always unwinds registrations. Deletion of the package payload is conditional. When you uninstall an MSIX app, it’s guaranteed to be deregistered but not guaranteed to be destaged. It may be kept around for various reasons, just made invisible to you. It’ll appear as if it’s been removed, but it’s quietly existing on disk—and thus no regained storage space. By the way: If you’re using Windows 11 Home, you’re missing out on the many benefits of Windows 11 Pro. To learn more, see our comparison of Windows 11 Home and Pro. If you want to upgrade, snag it for cheap in the PCWorld Software Store: now just $59 instead of $99.

item.title: HP OmniBook X Flip 14 review: A luxurious 2-in-1 held back by aging graphics
item.description:
Source: PCWorld Score: 4.85
At a glance Expert's Rating Pros - Good build quality and attractive “deep espresso” color option - 360-degree hinge design makes laptop and tablet use convenient - Attractive OLED touchscreen - Good mix of USB-A and USB-C connectivity Cons - CPU performance doesn’t stand out - Integrated Radeon GPU is behind Intel Arc - Moderate battery life Our Verdict The HP OmniBook X Flip 14 isn’t the most portable or powerful 14-inch 2-in-1, but it provides a luxurious experience and lots of connectivity. Price When Reviewed This value will show the geolocated pricing text for product undefined Best Pricing Today Best Prices Today: HP OmniBook X Flip 14 There was once a time, just after the reveal of the iPad, when every laptop maker seemed a bit ashamed to be selling laptops instead of tablets. That time has long passed, and the OmniBook X Flip 14 is the evidence. Though technically a 2-in-1, it focuses so much on the laptop experience that it’s easy to forget the tablet mode even exists. This decision ultimately works to the Flip’s advantage. HP OmniBook X Flip 14 2-in-1: Specs and features as-tested The HP OmniBook X Flip 14 2-in-1 is available in a variety of configurations that stretch from entry-level models with AMD Ryzen AI 5 and 16GB of memory to high-end configurations with AMD Ryzen AI 9 and 32GB of memory. The model I reviewed was a high-end configuration with almost every option, though it did lack an optional upgrade to a 2880×1800 OLED display. - CPU: AMD Ryzen AI 9 465 - Memory: 32GB LPDDR5x-8533 - Graphics/GPU: AMD Radeon 880M - NPU: AMD Ryzen AI NPU up to 50 TOPS - Display: 14-inch 1920×1200 60Hz OLED touchscreen - Storage: 2TB PCIe Gen 4.0 NVMe M.2 SSD - Webcam and microphones: 5MP IR webcam with HDR, dual microphone array - Connectivity: 2x USB-C 40Gbps with Power Delivery and DisplayPort 2.1, 2x USB-A with 10Gbps data, 1x HDMI 2.1, 1x 3.5mm combo audio - Networking: Wi-Fi 7, Bluetooth 6.0 - Biometrics: Windows Hello facial recognition - Audio: Downward-firing speakers with HP Audio Boost - Battery capacity: 59 watt-hours - Dimensions: 12.25 x 8.6 x 0.57 inches - Weight: 3.09 pounds - Operating System: Windows 11 Pro - Price: $2,529.99 MSRP as configured While an entry-level model has an MSRP of $1,299.99, the model I reviewed was quite a bit more expensive at $2,529.99. With that said, sale pricing is frequent and can offer significant discounts. The model I reviewed is currently available on sale at $2,279.99 and entry-level configurations can dip below $1,000. HP OmniBook X Flip 14 2-in-1: Design and build quality Foundry / Matthew Smith The most notable aspect of the HP OmniBook X Flip 14 I reviewed was obvious from the moment I took it out of the box. It’s brown—or, to be more specific, “Deep Espresso.” I must say, I quite like it. This sort of deep chocolate-coffee hue is uncommon among laptops from any manufacturer. It helps the laptop look unique while remaining professional. HP also provides an “Atmospheric Blue” colorway which, from photos, also looks attractive but is more conventional. Aside from the color, the OmniBook X Flip 14 is a simple but attractive laptop. The exterior is made of aluminum and feels sturdy, yet the laptop is still reasonably light at just 3.09 pounds. I saw little flex when opening the laptop or picking it up from one corner. The hinge is nicely tuned, too. The laptop can be opened with a single finger, yet it remains firmly closed in a bag. The OmniBook X Flip 14 is a 2-in-1 with a 360-degree hinge. That means the display folds all the way back, effectively turning the laptop into a tablet. The Flip 14 is both too large and too heavy to be used exactly like a dedicated tablet, but the versatility is helpful and makes it useful in a wide variety of situations. HP also offers an active stylus, though it’s optional and wasn’t included with my review sample. Importantly, the OmniBook X Flip 14 offers its 2-in-1 versatility with absolutely zero downside. It otherwise looks and feels exactly like a conventional laptop. It doesn’t even try to squeeze power or volume buttons on the sides, a move that some 2-in-1s make in an effort to enhance the tablet mode, but which can cause accidental activation when plugging in peripherals. I think the focus on laptop mode is the right call. The tablet mode is a nice bonus, but not how the OmniBook X Flip 14 is meant to be used most of the time. HP OmniBook X Flip 14 2-in-1: Keyboard, touchpad Foundry / Matthew Smith A spacious keyboard can be found in the HP OmniBook X Flip 14’s interior. Most keys are large. However, a few keys, like the left-side Control key, the Alt keys, and the Tab key, are slightly smaller than usual. On the other hand, the primary alphanumeric keys are large, and I like the beveled keycap design. Key feel is good, as keys provide significant travel and bottom out with a firm action. There’s a slightly hollow sound to the keyboard which I don’t love, but that’s a minor point. The keyboard also benefits from significant palm rest space that will comfortably accommodate most users. Below the keyboard is a typical touchpad that measures about five inches wide and a little over three inches deep. This is a typical size for a 14-inch laptop touchpad and generally offers enough room for multi-touch gestures, though swiping can feel tight at times. The touchpad doesn’t have a glass surface or other premium texture and also lacks haptics, though it does offer a shallow physical click action. HP OmniBook X Flip 14 2-in-1: Display Foundry / Matthew Smith HP offers three display options for the OmniBook X Flip 14: a 1920×1200 IPS-LCD, a 1920×1200 60Hz OLED, and a 2880×1800 120Hz OLED. All three are touchscreens. My review unit had the middle option, a 1920×1200 60Hz OLED touchscreen. HP quotes a maximum brightness of 300 nits, and while the display reached a little above that in testing, it’s not a bright display and often loses the fight with glare caused by the reflective panel coating. It’s also not an impressive display for the price in terms of resolution and refresh rate. On the plus side, however, it benefits from the rich contrast and superb color gamut that most OLED displays share. Movies, photos, and games have a vivid, alluring look. And while the resolution of 1920×1200 isn’t incredible for the price, it’s still very sharp when spread across a compact 14-inch screen. It’s worth mentioning that the display upgrades are affordable. Upgrading from the IPS-LCD to OLED is just $50, and upgrading from the 1920×1200 OLED to the 2880×1800 panel adds $130 more. That’s not nothing, but in a world where you can expect to pay through the nose for any memory or storage upgrade, you may find that choosing a display upgrade delivers more bang for your buck. HP OmniBook X Flip 14 2-in-1: Audio The HP OmniBook X Flip’s maximum volume is sufficient for use in a home office and audio clarity is good. The OmniBook X Flip doesn’t deliver the dynamism and passable low-end performance that you can find from an Apple MacBook and most Lenovo Yoga 9i alternatives, but the speakers are fine for listening to music at low volumes or enjoying a podcast. HP OmniBook X Flip 14 2-in-1: Webcam, microphone, biometrics The HP OmniBook X Flip 14 has a 5MP webcam and a dual microphone array. This is a typical arrangement for a Windows laptop at nearly any price point, and it delivers typical performance. A physical privacy shutter is included and can fully obstruct the webcam when it’s not in use. Video quality is sharp in good light and benefits from good color reproduction, but it can look grainy in darker situations. The microphone picks up crisp, loud audio but also sounds hollow and distant. Overall, it’s a usable combination that works well for video calls and conferences. Biometric login is supported through an IR camera and Windows Hello facial recognition. A fingerprint reader was not included. HP OmniBook X Flip 14 2-in-1: Connectivity Foundry / Matthew Smith The star of the HP OmniBook X Flip 14’s connectivity is its pair of USB-C ports with 40Gbps of data bandwidth, power delivery, and DisplayPort 2.1. These are great modern ports and provide a lot of options for connecting docks, displays, and high-speed external storage. There’s more good news on connectivity, as the laptop also has two USB-A ports that promise 10Gbps of data bandwidth. The inclusion of both USB-C and USB-A offers a wide variety of options for connecting devices. Additional physical connectivity includes HDMI 2.1 and a 3.5mm combo audio jack. The only port that might be considered missing is Ethernet, but it’s very rare to see any modern 14-inch laptop offer Ethernet. That ship has sailed. To make up for that, the HP OmniBook X Flip 14 provides modern wireless connectivity in the form of Wi-Fi 7 and Bluetooth 6.0. This is about as good as wireless connectivity gets, and I had no problems with the laptop’s wireless networking performance during my time with it. HP OmniBook X Flip 14 2-in-1: Performance The HP OmniBook X Flip 14 covers a wide variety of price points. To do that, it offers a wide variety of AMD hardware. The model I reviewed, though, is a fully equipped configuration with an AMD Ryzen AI 9 465 CPU that has 10 cores and 20 threads. It’s paired with 32GB of RAM and 2TB of solid-state storage.
