This is the top-end hardware configuration. The only option not included in the model I reviewed is the 2880×1800 120Hz OLED display. Foundry / Matthew Smith Let’s start with PCMark 10, a holistic system benchmark. Here we see the HP OmniBook X Flip 14 provides a mid-range result of 8,226. That wedges it between the OmniBook Ultra 14 and the MSI Prestige Flip 14 AI+. If the Acer Swift X 14 AI’s result has you scratching your head, there’s a reason for it. The Swift X 14 AI has an Nvidia GeForce RTX 5060, which helps boost the result. That’s because this test includes graphics benchmarks. Foundry / Matthew Smith Cinebench 2024 is a heavily multi-threaded CPU benchmark. The AMD Ryzen AI 9 465 in the HP OmniBook X Flip provides healthy, but not incredible, results in this benchmark. It’s able to defeat some Intel Core Ultra X7 laptops, but it falls behind the HP OmniBook Ultra 14 with an Intel Core Ultra X9 388H. It’s also interesting to see the AMD Ryzen AI 7 350 in the Acer Swift X 14 AI take a win, too. That laptop has a larger power adapter, and it seems to take advantage of that to deliver more power to the CPU, resulting in better performance. Foundry / Matthew Smith Handbrake is another heavier multi-threaded test and, once again, the HP OmniBook X Flip 14 provides a solid yet unsurprising result. The AMD Ryzen AI 9 465 ends up a bit behind the Core Ultra X9 388H—at least as it exists in the similar HP OmniBook Ultra 14. On the whole, the AMD Ryzen AI 9 465 doesn’t look all that strong here, but its performance is adequate at the least. Foundry / Matthew Smith GPU performance, as it turns out, is the HP OmniBook X Flip 14’s weakness. That’s because it relies on AMD’s Radeon 880M integrated graphics, which was great when it debuted a couple years ago but is now less competitive against Intel’s new Arc graphics. The difference isn’t small, either. Compared to the Intel Core Ultra Series 3 alternatives with Intel Arc B390 graphics, the OmniBook X Flip 14 with Radeon 880M is roughly 15 to 40 percent behind the Intel competition. That’s enough to be extremely noticeable in real-world use. HP OmniBook X Flip 14 2-in-1: Battery life and portability Most HP OmniBook X Flip 14 configurations, including the one I reviewed, ship with a 59 watt-hour battery. A 70 watt-hour battery is available, but only with the 2880×1800 OLED display. Foundry / Matthew Smith A 59 watt-hour battery is toward the lower end for this category of laptop, and the graph shows that it does have an impact. However, I think the real boat anchor dragging down the laptop’s battery life is the AMD Ryzen AI 9 chip. AMD’s Ryzen 300 and 400 series chips have generally failed to match Intel Core Ultra Series 3 and Qualcomm Snapdragon alternatives on battery life. The HP OmniBook X Flip 14 is no exception. Yet it would be wrong to call the OmniBook X Flip 14’s battery life bad or short. It still endured over 14 hours in our standard video playback test. This, as the graph shows, is not exceptional—but 14 hours is still a respectable result and the OmniBook X Flip 14’s battery life will be enough to get most people through an eight-hour workday. HP OmniBook X Flip 14 2-in-1: Conclusion The HP OmniBook X Flip 14 is an attractive, luxurious 2-in-1 that is mostly meant for laptop use. It provides a sturdy chassis, nice keyboard, lots of connectivity, and respectable all-around performance—though the aging Radeon 880M integrated GPU ends up the weak link. Battery life is also unimpressive, though it remains adequate. HP prices the model I reviewed at an MSRP of $2,529.99. That’s not inexpensive, but in 2026, with escalating memory and storage pricing, I think it’s a reasonable value for what the laptop offers. However, the real value is arguably found in the less expensive configurations. While these won’t perform as well, they will retain key traits including the 2-in-1’s attractive design.

item.title: Dreame D20 Air Plus review: A $270 self-emptying vacuum that delivers where it counts
item.description:
Source: PCWorld Score: 4.60
At a glance Expert's Rating Pros - Good vacuum performance for the price - Gets close to edges and under low furniture - Good value at $269.99 Cons - Basic mopping system - No self-washing mop feature - Can struggle with lightweight rugs and mats Our Verdict The Dreame D20 Air Plus is focused on doing the basics well. It’ll vacuum your floors, empty debris into the base station, and (mostly) stay out of your way. Price When Reviewed This value will show the geolocated pricing text for product undefined Best Pricing Today Price When Reviewed $269.99 Best Prices Today: Dreame D20 Air Plus The Dreame D20 Air Plus is the type of robot vacuum that’s focused on doing the basics really well. It’ll vacuum your floors and navigate well around corners and coffee tables. It doesn’t have the Roborock Saros 20’s fancy mop-washing system, but it does mop…. sort of. I tested the D20 Air Plus in my split-level home on both hard floors and rugs, amid furniture like a low entertainment center, a coffee table, and a game table with metal legs. While it has limitations common in a budget model, it gets the important stuff right and that’s exactly what I want to see. Dreame D20 Air Plus: Setup Getting the D20 Air Plus up and running was refreshingly simple. The hardware setup involved basically just snapping into place the side brush, which sweeps debris toward the main brush, and plugging in the base station. I didn’t feel tripped up at any point here. The base station itself is much smaller than the one that came with the premium Roborock model I tested, which I appreciated. Some base stations are big and bulky, and can take up a lot of space. This one doesn’t. There’s a dust box and a filter inside of the robot — it’s a wedge-shaped piece that slides out of the back. This is where the debris goes until the robot returns to the base station, where the dust gets sucked into a disposable bag. Everything is pretty straightforward here. There was one tiny hiccup during setup, though. I plugged in the base station and assumed it wasn’t working because nothing happened (usually a base station will start chattering away after you’ve plugged it in). Turns out, there’s a physical power switch on the back that you’ve got to turn on first. It’s obvious, I know. I did spend a few minutes wondering if I had gotten a dud. Once everything was powered on, the app walked me through the rest of the setup process. Dreame D20 Air Plus: The app The app is pleasantly simple. A lot of robot vacuum apps throw a million different cleaning modes and settings at you. The D20 Air Plus keeps things much more streamlined (thankfully!). For the D20 Air Plus, you can choose between vacuuming, mopping, vacuuming and mopping at the same time, or a custom mode where you can adjust things to your liking. You can change the suction power, too. Just be careful if you’re going to turn up the suction power because it drains the battery faster. The options for suction power are Quiet, Standard, Intense, and Max. I mostly stuck with the standard setting for everyday cleaning, but it’s nice to have a little extra oomph sometimes. During testing, the D20 Air Plus built the map while it cleaned the floor. It didn’t have to map the floor first. Speaking of, the map view is pretty useful while the robot is cleaning. It shows the vacuum’s current location in real time, along with the areas it already vacuumed (areas with lines indicate they’ve been vacuumed). I like being able to see the robot’s progress. It also makes it easier to spot areas it missed. Dreame D20 Air Plus: Navigation Like most robot vacuums, the D20 Air Plus moves in a back-and-forth pattern. The lines are straight and parallel, and there’s no random bouncing around. It slowed down around table legs instead of bumping into them at full speed. It also got surprisingly close to corners and edges. This robot uses several sensors to help it see the room. It uses a Laser Distance Sensor (LDS) for mapping and navigating around furniture, a bumper for detecting walls and corners, a return-to-base sensor for finding the charging station, and cliff sensors so it doesn’t go tumbling down the stairs. One thing that surprised me was how well it got underneath my small entertainment center, which doesn’t have a lot of clearance. It slid right under there, even with the LiDAR (aka the LDS system) turret sticking out on top, adding height. I half expected it to skip that area, but it cleaned underneath it without any trouble. That said, it did have one annoying habit: moving the mat by my sliding glass door. The robot consistently pushed the mat around while it cleaned instead of smoothly driving over it. Not a huge deal, but I did have to walk over and reposition it a few times. It’s the kind of thing that makes you realize robot vacuums aren’t completely “set it and forget it” devices yet (though I think the tech is definitely going there). Sometimes they still need a little human supervision. Dreame D20 Air Plus: Vacuuming Vacuuming is where the D20 Air Plus shines. It finished cleaning my downstairs in about 33 minutes, and it still had 77 percent battery remaining. That’s plenty of power left over for larger spaces. It also picked up my greyhound’s hair, as well as the dirt and bits of leaves he tends to bring in. For suction power, the D20 Air Plus has 20,000Pa, which is pretty good for a $269.99 budget model (and for getting the stuff out of carpets). That’s more than enough for the usual suspects: pet hair, dirt, leaves, crumbs, etc. The Roborock Saros 20, a premium model costing over $1,000, has a suction power of 36,000Pa. The vacuum itself is a little louder than I expected. It’s definitely not as loud as a traditional upright vacuum, but compared to the premium Roborock model I tested, the difference was noticeable. It gets louder when it detects carpet, but that’s by design. The vacuum will automatically ramp up suction, and you can actually hear the motor kick into a higher gear. Noise aside, the D20 Air Plus isn’t trying to reinvent the wheel here. It’s just trying to reliably clean your floors without making the experience overly complicated. That’s where it succeeds. Dreame D20 Air Plus: Mopping The mopping system is where you start seeing the difference between budget and higher-end models. It feels more like an afterthought, really. The D20 Air Plus uses a single mop pad that slides along the floor. It doesn’t spin or lift up when going over carpets. The base station also doesn’t wash the mop or empty the dirty water into a separate container like we’ve seen more expensive models do. You’ve also got to wet the mop yourself. That means the mopping is more of a maintenance feature than a deep clean. It can help with everyday dust and light marks, but it’s not going to scrub away tougher messes. You’ll also need to manually deal with the mop pad when you’re done. For me, that’s not necessarily a dealbreaker. I think most people buying a robot vacuum are probably buying it for the vacuuming power anyway. The D20 Air Plus is much better at vacuuming than mopping, and that’s where I’d put my expectations. Should you buy the Dreame D20 Air Plus? If you want the convenience that a robot vacuum brings but don’t want to drop a ton of money on one, the Dreame D20 Air Plus is a good fit. I mean, not only does it vacuum well, it also deftly moves around furniture. For just $269.99, that’s very good The compromises are pretty clear, though. The mopping system is basic, the robot can be a bit noisy, and it doesn’t have the advanced self-cleaning features you’d get in a more expensive model.

item.title: Optery review: A free scan showed how exposed my personal data really was
item.description:
Source: PCWorld Score: 4.44
At a glance Expert's Rating Pros - Clear dashboard with profile screenshots and broker links - Useful free scan and Exposure Report - Strong privacy standards Cons - Dashboard “View” links are not guaranteed matches - Like all data-removal services, verification is difficult at scale Our Verdict Optery gives users a clear, useful look at where their personal information is exposed online, but its real cleanup value depends on upgrading to a paid plan and trusting its removal process. Price When Reviewed This value will show the geolocated pricing text for product undefined Best Pricing Today Best Prices Today: Optery Most people don’t know how many data brokers have built profiles on them until a service like Optery shows them the list. Names, addresses, phone numbers, and other personal details can end up scattered across people-search sites, public records, and data-broker databases. Removing that information yourself is possible, but it can mean chasing dozens—or hundreds—of opt-out forms, confirmation emails, and follow-up requests. Optery tries to turn that messy opt-out process into something more organized and trackable. It scans data-broker and people-search sites for exposed personal information, shows users where their profiles may appear, and provides tools for requesting removals. What Optery does Optery’s basic job is simple: Find where your personal information is showing up online, then help you get it removed. After you create an account and enter enough profile details for Optery to identify likely matches, the service scans data brokers and people-search sites for exposed records. The main dashboard is organized around three scan areas: Primary Scan, Custom Scan, and Expanded Reach. Primary Scan is the default check for exposed profiles. Custom Scans let users run more targeted checks, such as a specific name and city-state combination, or a custom scan of Google search results. Expanded Reach extends paid-plan removals to broker sources that may not publish profiles openly or meet Optery’s usual verification standards. Michael Ansaldo/Foundry Optery also generates a downloadable Exposure Report. This gives users a snapshot of the matched profiles Optery found, including screenshots. The report turns an otherwise abstract privacy problem into something visible: broker names, profile pages, and exposed details you can inspect. What happens next depends on the plan. Free users can investigate profiles and submit opt-out requests themselves. Paid subscribers can have Optery submit removals, track progress, and follow up with brokers on their behalf. Higher tiers add broader broker coverage, human-assisted opt-outs, custom removal requests, before-and-after screenshots, Expanded Reach, and outdated-content removal submissions to Google and Bing. Plans and pricing Optery has a Free Basic plan, plus three personal paid plans: Core, Extended, and Ultimate. Core is the paid plan most people should consider first. It costs $3.99 per month, or $39 per year, and adds automated removals from 367+ sites, monthly scans, opt-out progress reporting, and automatic opt-outs from newly supported brokers. Michael Ansaldo/Foundry Extended costs $14.99 per month, or $149 per year, and raises coverage to 545+ sites. It also adds unlimited name variations, unlimited past cities and states, human-assisted opt-outs, and before-and-after removal reports every 90 days. Ultimate costs $24.99 per month, or $249 per year, and covers 641+ sites. It adds unlimited custom removal requests, Google and Bing outdated-content removal submissions, and priority email support. Family discounts are available, starting at 20 percent off when two family members have paid plans. Getting started with Optery Getting started with Optery is straightforward, though it requires handing over enough personal information for the service to identify you accurately. During signup, Optery asks for the usual account details along with information such as your state or region, city, year of birth, optional month and day of birth, and middle name. The more information you supply, the better, since Optery needs enough detail to tell you apart from people with similar names and avoid filling your dashboard with bad matches. Optery says it queues the Exposure Report scan for about 20 minutes after signup so users can add more profile details, then typically delivers the report within about an hour. Users can also postpone the initial scan for up to 24 hours. In my case, the scan finished in about 35 minutes. Michael Ansaldo/Foundry What Optery found in testing The scan results came back with two different levels of detail. In the dashboard, Optery listed 404 sites that may expose personal information. That number is useful for getting a sense of the scale, but it should not be read as 404 confirmed exposures. Optery’s own help material says its “View” links are a best initial attempt to point users toward possible broker pages. A link may lead to your profile, someone else with a similar name, or a dead page. The Exposure Report was more concrete. My report found 61 matched profiles and included screenshots from individual sites. The profiles included the kinds of details people-search sites commonly collect: names, ages, or birthdate clues, current and past locations, phone numbers, relatives, and snippets that connect those details together. Optery also divides the found profiles by the paid plan that covers them, which makes the upgrade path obvious. I found the report more useful than a simple broker count. A plain list of broker names can feel abstract; seeing profile pages with personal details boxed in red makes the exposure easier to understand and harder to shrug off. The next step is to decide how to tackle the problem: Upgrade and let Optery submit removals, or use the dashboard’s opt-out links and do the work yourself. For DIY removals, Optery recommends using a burner email address, since contacting data brokers directly can add you to their lists. Privacy and trust When you use a data-removal service, you’re handing over many of the same personal details you want removed from broker sites, so the service needs to explain what it collects, why it needs it, and how it protects it. Optery does a solid job on that front. Its help material says it does not sell or rent customer personal information to third parties. It also says its products run on AWS infrastructure in the United States, with TLS used for data in transit, AES-256 encryption for data at rest, MFA and 2FA support, access controls, and SOC 2 security controls. Michael Ansaldo/Foundry Optery also names third-party vendors that it uses for things such as analytics, support, email, payments, and business operations, which is more useful than a vague “we take privacy seriously” statement. To handle some removals, Optery may ask paid users to grant a Limited Power of Attorney. Optery says some data brokers require proof that the service is authorized to submit opt-out requests on a user’s behalf. The authorization is optional, can be revoked, and is limited to data-rights and opt-out requests, not broader legal, financial, or personal matters. What to expect from paid data removal After I upgraded to Optery’s Ultimate plan, the service moved from discovery to active removal. The dashboard began tracking broker-by-broker removal status, with labels such as Removed, Submitted, Not Found, Pending, and In Progress. The dashboard also added a Maximize Removals section that flags missing information that some brokers may require before accepting opt-out requests. In my account, Optery asked for a ZIP code, street address, and Limited Power of Attorney, and showed how many brokers each item affected. Don’t expect the process to be instant. Under my Ultimate plan, I received monthly removal-progress emails, and after two months, the latest update showed 179 records marked removed, 75 not found, 55 pending, and 90 still in progress. The reality is that data removal can take weeks, and even then, search engines may continue showing cached results for a while, and some broker profiles can reappear over time. Michael Ansaldo/Foundry It’s a good idea to double-check any data-removal service’s work and Optery made this easier than it otherwise would be. Each removed profile includes a direct link back to the original broker site, which made verifying removal easier than trying to recreate each search myself. The results were mixed. Some matched profiles were no longer visible at the linked pages, while others appeared only partially cleaned up. Some of that was caused by my own profile setup. When I created my Optery account, I had entered my two most recent addresses, but no addresses going back more than 15 years, which limited how well the service could match and target older listings. But the removals I checked also revealed a messier problem: Records for people with the same name can expose related information even when they are not cleanly “your” profile. In my case, one listing appeared to mix my details with my late father’s, who had the same name, and another record for him named me, my sister, and my mother as relatives. So even when a matched profile is removed or reduced, related family records can still leave a trail back to you. It is a reminder of the uncomfortable tradeoff behind data-removal services: To get your personal information off broker sites, you may have to give the removal service more of it first. I’ll be fine-tuning my Optery profile with a longer address history and other identifying details to see whether that improves matching and removal accuracy. Is Optery worth it? Optery is a strong option for seeing where your personal information is exposed because it gives you a meaningful look at the problem before asking you to pay for the fix. Manual opt-outs are tedious, and Optery’s Core plan is affordable enough that automated removal doesn’t require a big financial leap. Extended and Ultimate are better fits for people who want wider coverage, human-assisted opt-outs, custom removal requests, and help cleaning up stale Google and Bing results. The paid-removal process isn’t perfect, and users should still check sensitive listings themselves. But Optery makes that easier than it could be. For most people, the best move is to start with the free scan, see what it finds, and then decide whether the cleanup is worth outsourcing.

item.title: Geekom’s all-day laptop with 16GB RAM hits a new low price: $809
item.description:
Source: PCWorld Score: 4.25
Laptops have gotten pricey thanks to the global AI-driven memory and storage shortage, and great laptop deals have (unsurprisingly) dried up. Gone are the days of punchy budget laptops for under $500. But if you temper your expectations, you can still get a laptop with enough RAM and solid performance for about $800—like with this deal. The Geekom GeekBook M16 is a great all-day productivity laptop that launched earlier this summer, and it just got its first price cut. On Amazon, you can now clip the on-page coupon to score $90 off, bringing it down from $899 to $809. That’s a new low price and nothing to sneeze at given the current eye-watering market conditions. What the Geekom GeekBook M16 offers The GeekBook M16 is powered by an Intel Core Ultra 9 185H, a Meteor Lake series chip with 16 cores and up to 5.1GHz clock speed. Key highlights include an NPU for AI applications, integrated Intel Arc graphics for 1080p gaming and video work, and excellent power efficiency for over all-day battery life with everyday tasks. That makes it a great daily driver machine, whether for office work or personal use. With 16GB of LPDDR5 RAM, it packs enough memory to handle Windows 11 without slowing to a crawl, and that’s about as much RAM as you can expect these days in a sub-grand laptop. The 512GB PCIe 4.0 SSD is fast for quick startups and app launches, although we do wish it had at least 1TB of capacity (again, hard to expect with the global shortage). That’s at least enough storage for daily use, but not enough if you’re regularly working with huge video files or projects. It feels pretty premium too thanks to its aluminum alloy unibody design. It weighs about 3.8 pounds, neither light nor heavy for a 16-inch laptop. The screen has a 1920×1200 IPS panel but leaves a bit to be desired in other areas: only 60Hz refresh rate and 300 nits of brightness. Don’t expect to use it outdoors and don’t expect fluid visual responsiveness—it merely gets the job done, as that’s what it’s designed to do. No worries if you travel a lot either. The GeekBook M16’s battery has a 99.9 Wh capacity, which puts it just within TSA and FAA limits for flights. You can expect up to 24 hours of video playback under benchmark conditions, or about 13 hours of real-world use while doing office work, active Wi-Fi, video calls, web browsing, etc. Why this deal is worth it It may not seem like a large discount, but that’s just the time we’re living in now—laptop deals won’t be knocking our socks off for a few years. That’s why this Geekom GeekBook M16 for $809 is good, down from its original $899 for the first time since it launched in June. The battery is its key selling point. With 13+ hours of real-world use, it serves well for commuters, remote workers, travelers, and anyone who just hates being tethered to a power adapter. With a 4.6 rating across 75+ reviews (not bad for a laptop that released so recently), it’s consistently well-received. Users praise it for its premium build quality, overall performance, and long battery life. If there’s criticism, it’s mainly for the below-average display and the soldered RAM, which means it isn’t repairable or upgradeable.

item.title: Microsoft warns hotel/airport Wi-Fi is being hijacked to steal your login
item.description:
Source: PCWorld Score: 4.02
In a recent Microsoft Security Blog post, the company has raised awareness of a widespread attack campaign called CaptiveCrunch. In short, Russian hackers are using manipulated DNS queries to redirect users to phishing sites that mimic Microsoft’s official online services. As a result, Microsoft is warning against the use of public Wi-Fi networks. With these fake phishing sites, the attackers are attempting to intercept and steal login credentials for Microsoft accounts. Some security researchers previously published a warning to this effect back in July, and now Microsoft is supplementing that report with its own new information based on what it has been monitoring since May 2026. According to the report, the attackers redirect users—for example, those who are logging into their Microsoft accounts via a hotel Wi-Fi network—to imitation phishing sites. There, the attackers capture device and OAuth codes, which they can use to take over said Microsoft accounts. In addition, the attackers are believed to be installing malware on victims’ devices, including Trojans that record keystrokes, eavesdrop on device activity, spy via hijacked cameras, and forward sensitive files and passwords. Furthermore, the malware sets up remote access for the attackers to the infected devices. It’s apparently made possible by compromised public Wi-Fi networks, like the ones you’d rely on in hotels and airports. The key question, of course, is how the attackers gain access to those networks, which Microsoft is currently investigating. It’s possible that the captive portals, where users agree to terms of use, play a role. Microsoft states the following on this matter: Although our investigation into the initial compromise vector for the captive portal networks is ongoing, we have observed notable commonalities in the equipment and management systems used across multiple affected networks. These similarities suggest that the activity might not be limited to isolated compromises of individual venues and could reflect access to shared services within portions of the captive portal ecosystem. Microsoft believes the hacker group Storm-2945 is responsible for this wave of CaptiveCrunch attacks. This group is associated with Midnight Blizzard, which in turn is believed to be part of the Russian Foreign Intelligence Service. What you can do to stay safe Public Wi-Fi networks are risky. Not only is there a non-zero chance for your data to be intercepted, but Wi-Fi hotspots can be exploited to track your physical location and even identify your physical body. The safest thing you can do is to never use public Wi-Fi. Of course, that isn’t always the way to go—who can deny the convenience of Wi-Fi at coffee shops, hotels, and airports, especially if you don’t have unlimited mobile data to use as your own personal hotspot? If you are going to use public Wi-Fi, make sure your devices are protected with a VPN. A good VPN encrypts your network activity, hiding it from the network and making it virtually uncrackable by hackers. Just make sure you don’t settle for a free VPN, which comes with its own issues. Choose one from PCWorld’s roundup of the best VPNs and you’ll be golden. Microsoft warns: “When traveling, users should treat hotel, conference, airport, and other guest wireless networks as untrustworthy.” You should opt for private connections (like your own mobile hotspot) when you can, and never download software updates, certificates, or apps that are presented through public Wi-Fi captive portals and web prompts. Further reading: I use public Wi-Fi despite the risks. Here’s how I stay safe

item.title: Best laptops under $500: Affordable picks that will satisfy your needs
item.description:
Source: PCWorld Score: 3.51
Finding a great laptop for under $500 isn’t impossible. It just takes knowing what to pay attention to and what to ignore. For most people, I’d recommend opting for a laptop with a 1080p display and at least 8GB of RAM. If you spot a model with 16GB of RAM in this price range, scoop that up. It’s worth it for the long-term usability. At a glance | | | | View Deal | | Show Pros & Cons Pros Cons Hide Pros & Cons | | | | | | | | View Deal | | Show Pros & Cons Pros Cons Hide Pros & Cons | | | | | | | | View Deal | | Show Pros & Cons Pros Cons Hide Pros & Cons | | | | While you shouldn’t expect premium features at this price point, there are plenty of laptops that offer excellent day-to-day performance. Here are the best ones we’ve found so far. Why you should trust PCWorld for laptop reviews and buying advice: It’s in our name! PCWorld prides itself on laptop experience and expertise. We’ve been covering PCs since 1983, and we now review more than 70 laptops every year. All of our picks have been personally tested and vetted by our experts, who’ve applied not only performance benchmarks but rigorous usability standards. We’re also committed to reviewing PC laptops at every price point to help you find a machine that matches your budget. MacBook Neo (2026) – Best laptop under $500 overall Pros - Distinguished and sturdy design - Excellent single-core CPU performance - Great-looking display - Nothing feels cheap Cons - Different USB implementations on the two ports - Trackpad lacks pressure-sensitivity - Multi-core performance lags - No P3 color gamut support Who should buy the MacBook Neo (2026)? If you can stretch your budget just a tiny bit, the MacBook Neo (2026) is easily the best cheap laptop you can buy right now. We know it goes over our $500, but the jump in quality and performance… well, it’s just too good to ignore. It simply doesn’t feel like a budget laptop. You’re getting the full MacBook experience. The all-aluminum build feels as premium as more expensive models, and the A18 Pro chip delivers fast, responsive performance for everyday tasks like writing and streaming. In our review, we noted that apps open quickly and multitasking feels smooth. Battery life is another big win, lasting well over a full workday in real-world use. The 13-inch Liquid Retina display is also sharp at 2408×1506 resolution and bright at 500 nits–a strong combination at this price point. MacBook Neo (2026): Further considerations The MacBook Neo is pretty much the complete package as far as budget laptops go. You don’t get the premium extras like Thunderbolt connectivity or a high-end webcam, but that’s not wholly unsurprising for a laptop at this price point. What really matters is that it feels fast and is well-built. It’s reliable in a way most Windows laptops aren’t. Read our full Apple MacBook Neo review Asus Chromebook CX15 – Best Chromebook under $200 Pros - Compact form factor - Good everyday performance - Long battery life - Great keyboard and mouse Cons - Screen quality is mediocre - Noisy fans Who should buy the Asus Chromebook CX15 ? If you need a laptop that won’t make your wallet cry, the CX15 does the basics really well. It handles web browsing, streaming, and email like it’s nothing, and the 15.6-inch 1080p screen plus the full-sized keyboard actually make it feel more solid than the price suggests. Asus Chromebook CX15 : Further considerations The Intel Celeron N4500 with 4GB of RAM handles the basics fine–web browsing, streaming, email, all that. But try to do too much at once and it’ll start dragging. Battery life’s also fine, a little over 10 hours on a single charge, so you’ll probably get through a full day. Not record-breaking by any means, but it does the job. Read our full Asus Chromebook CX15 review Asus Chromebook Plus CX34 – Best Chromebook under $500 Pros - Zippy processor performance - Nice keyboard - A wide array of connectivity options - Chic design Cons - Battery life isn’t competitive - The display’s 16:9 aspect ratio feels a little cramped Who should buy the Asus Chromebook Plus CX34? If you’re not running Photoshop or playing AAA games, the Asus Chromebook Plus CX34 absolutely gets the job done. The Intel Core i5 and 8GB of RAM keep everything zipping along, even with a dozen tabs open and a video call going. It’s lightweight, looks clean with that white finish, and has a 1080p display that’s easy on the eyes. The webcam’s full HD too, which makes a real difference on Zoom or Google Meet. No weird lag or blurry faces here. Asus Chromebook Plus CX34: Further considerations The CX34 keeps it simple and just works. It boots fast, stays responsive, and doesn’t run hot or loud. Chrome OS has come a long way, and if you mostly live in a browser, this setup is kind of ideal. Read our full Asus Chromebook Plus CX34 review Other laptops under $500 we tested - Acer Chromebook Plus 516: The Acer Chromebook Plus 516 isn’t much to look at, but it benefits from an Intel Core i3 chip with solid performance and, at times, low sale pricing. - Acer Chromebook Plus 514: Offers good performance and lots of storage for the price ($399.99, by the way!). - Asus Chromebook Plus CX14: Edges out models with Celeron processors and is currently on sale for $299.99 at Walmart. How we test laptops The PCWorld team puts each and every Windows laptop through a series of benchmarks that test GPU and CPU performance, battery life, and overall usability. The idea is to push the laptop to its limits and then compare it against others we’ve tested. Chromebooks, on the other hand, go through a series of web-based tests. For a much deeper look at our review methodology, check out how PCWorld tests laptops. Who curated this article? Hi, I’m Ashley Biancuzzo, and I oversee all laptop and Chromebook coverage at PCWorld. While you’ll see me review Chromebooks on occasion, I’m also really into the broader world of consumer tech. I spend a lot of time writing and thinking about where laptops are headed–from AI and sustainable designs to long-term trends. When I’m not deep in the world of tech, you’ll probably find me gaming, getting lost in a good book, or chilling with my rescue greyhound, Allen. How to choose the best laptop under $500 Ah, here we are at the billion dollar question. Do you spring for a basic Chromebook or go for a Windows laptop with more features? Honestly, it mostly comes down to your lifestyle and what you’re expecting from a laptop under 500 bucks. You’re not gonna get some super-powerful beast at that price, but if you just need something for the basics, there are a lot of decent options out there. Chromebooks, for example, are super budget-friendly and the battery life is awesome. I actually use one myself for work (writing, editing, all that) and it does the job just fine. If you travel a lot, it’s worth going for something that’s nice and light — under three pounds, if possible. Still not sure what to get? No big deal, take your time figuring it out. I’ve put together a list of quick buying tips below. - Laptop type: There are many different laptop types that fall in the sub-$500 category: clamshells, 2-in-1s, Chromebooks, and much more. The displays on convertible laptops (aka 2-in-1s), for example, can swing around 360 degrees. This allows you to use the laptop like a tablet. They can also be propped up like a tent for viewing movies or participating in video calls. Chromebooks come in various shapes and sizes, and exclusively run Google’s web-focused Chrome OS. With a Chromebook, all you need is a Gmail account and, boom, you’re in. - CPU: When it comes to the sub-$500 Windows laptops, you can expect to find Intel Core i3 or i5 processors. An i5 processor obviously provides a little more oomph. That said, basic office and web work does just fine on a Core i3. For AMD stuff, Ryzen 3 is fine for everyday stuff like web browsing, and Ryzen 5 is a solid all-rounder—kind of like Intel’s i5. On Chromebooks, Snapdragon and Pentium chips usually beat out MediaTek ones. - Graphics: Don’t expect great graphics at this price. You’ll mostly get integrated graphics, which is totally fine unless you’re trying to game or do 3D work. - RAM: RAM-wise, go for 8GB if you can—it just makes everything smoother. Most Chromebooks come with 4GB, which works, but 8GB is way better if you can swing it. - Display size: For screen size, 13 to 14 inches is the sweet spot. Big enough to work on, small enough to carry around. Bigger screens mean more weight (and usually a higher price). - Resolution: Don’t settle for less than 1080p resolution. Anything lower just looks kinda blurry, even for basic stuff like Netflix or spreadsheets. - Battery life: Battery life? Look for 10 to 12 hours. That’ll get you through most of the day without hunting for an outlet. - Ports: It’s nice to have a bunch so you don’t need extra adapters. Look for USB-C and USB-A, and HDMI is cool if you want to hook up to a screen. FAQ What is the best laptop under $500? MacBook Neo (2026) is the best cheap laptop you can get right now, hands-down. Performance is fast and reliable, and battery life is surprisingly good at 13+ hours. It doesn’t cut corners in many areas either, a rarity in a budget machine. What is the best Chromebook under $500? If you want a solid Chromebook under $500, the Asus Chromebook Plus CX34 is fast, smooth with tabs and video calls, has a sharp 1080p screen, and a good HD webcam. It’s just plain simple and reliable. Can I upgrade the RAM or storage on these laptops later? Most laptops under $500 don’t let you upgrade RAM because it’s soldered on, but some do let you swap or add storage. Check before you buy if that stuff matters to you. What’s the difference between a regular laptop and a Chromebook? When people say “laptop,” they usually mean a PC or a Mac. But Chromebooks are laptops too, they just run Google’s Chrome OS instead of Windows or macOS. So, yeah, all Chromebooks are laptops, but not all laptops are Chromebooks. They’re mostly built for Google apps like Drive and Docs, so they work best when you’re online. Are Chromebooks good for gaming? Eh, not really. If gaming’s your thing, you’ll probably wanna look at a Windows laptop or a Chromebook designed for cloud gaming. Both will be more expensive than a basic Chromebook. Most Chromebooks are fine for web games and Android stuff, but that’s about it. With a gaming Chromebook, you will need to subscribe to a cloud gaming service such as GeForce Now and have a reliable internet connection. Can you use integrated graphics for gaming? Yes, some of the latest processors with integrated graphics can run modern PC games at decent enough settings. For example, we found that in our tests, Intel’s latest Iris Xe line of processors with integrated graphics can run some of the latest games at 1080p and 30fps. Unfortunately this is not the case for all integrated graphics and your mileage may vary drastically with older tech. Intel and AMD’s integrated graphics have made huge leaps in recent years with regard to gaming performance. If you’re on a budget or looking for an ultra-thin laptop with integrated graphics you need not worry, you can still game on.

item.title: Hold up. Is the year of Linux actually happening?
item.description:
Source: PCWorld Score: 3.43
The “year of Linux” has been a thing for literally decades, but never delivered. Yet 2026 seems to be an indication that it’s finally gaining traction. Before now, the gains have been anecdotal, largely borne out of the frustration users had with Microsoft’s Windows operating systems, and their myriad flaws. Now, the numbers are starting to indicate that the gains are real: in the last two months, the market share of Linux has tripled, cresting the 10 percent mark to 11.87 percent in the United States. That figure, compiled by StatCounter, isn’t replicated in other areas of the world. Yet. Still, StatCounter (which gathers its data from reports from at least 1 million websites which allow it to track data) indicates steady growth since April, which showed that Linux was at 2.91 percent of the market StatCounter tracks and 3.71 percent in May. Foundry / Statcounter (According to the StatCounter data, it even looks like Linux is passing “macOS,” currently at about 8 percent by StatCounter’s data. It’s really not, since StatCounter breaks the data out into macOS — or 8.25 percent — and OS X, at 21.7 percent. Realistically, those two should be combined to put Apple’s OS share at about 30 percent of U.S. users, versus 56 percent for Windows.) No metric is perfectly accurate, and StatCounter’s data can only track the sites it monitors. ZDNet also didn’t quite see the same enthusiasm for Linux on the U.S. government’s data tracker, either. Nevertheless, the market share of Linux has been largely flat for decades at about 3 percent, StatCounter found, and over the last few months it’s begun to take off. Why? StatCounter doesn’t say, of course. Some of this can might be attributed to Linux-based gaming handhelds like the Steam Deck — which have been around for months at this point. Still, StatCounter accumulates its data from websites, not devices, and it seems unlikely that the sharp price increase of the Steam Deck actually attracted users who decided to browse the web rather than play games. Others have suggested that the increased surge in Linux market share might be something else altogether: bots, or specifically AI agents running on behalf of a user but via a Linux-based server. There could be some truth to that, as most “deep thinking” algorithms at least touch several websites as they search. That could indicate a false positive, or not! Agents have also been around for several months, giving time for StatCounter to filter them out. Still, whether the surge signal is a false positive or not, there are clearly reasons why it could be true. Here, Windows takes the blame: pushing Copilot into every corner of the OS, pervasive advertising, the improved efficiency of running Linux on older PCs. Simply choosing a Linux distro has never been easier, and the fervor for which enthusiasts have begun to push Bazzite or more productivity-oriented distributions rivals those who have adopted electric vehicles — most never want to go back. Microsoft has seen the writing on the wall, of course, and its latest efforts address that last point: with memory prices soaring, Windows simply must be made to run more efficiently. That’s Microsoft’s priority for the remainder of 2026. Of course, the rise of Linux could suddenly reverse. Still, after years of writing Linux off as just a hobbyist OS, it does appear that “the year of Linux” could be 2026. Maybe… even beyond?

item.title: Samsung’s brand-new 990 SSD just hit its lowest price yet: $370 for 2TB
item.description:
Source: PCWorld Score: 3.38
It’s a rough time for anyone who’s looking to upgrade their PC hardware. The AI-driven shortage has spiked the prices of memory and storage, doubling or even tripling in some cases. If you need better and/or more internal storage and can’t wait around for prices to fall back down (if they ever do), here’s a deal worth jumping on. Samsung released its new baseline 990 SSD last month with an MSRP of $530. It’s currently available on Amazon for $370, a hefty 30 percent discount and $160 savings. Not bad for a powerful drive with 2TB of capacity, at least for the market conditions we find ourselves in. If you need one right now, it could be worse. What the Samsung 990 SSD offers The new 990 SSD comes in both 1TB and 2TB capacities, although this deal is for the 2TB option. It uses the PCIe 4.0 x4 interface and, according to Samsung, achieves read speeds up to 7,250 MB/s and write speeds up to 6,450 MB/s, plus up to 1.1 million IOPS for random write operations. That’s faster than the 990 EVO, which peaks at 5,000 MB/s for reading, 4,200 MB/s for writing, and 800K IOPS for random writes. It’s easy to slot into any available M.2 2280 slot, and the 2TB capacity is plenty for pretty much everyone except photographers, video editors, gamers with enormous libraries, and data hoarders. The Samsung Magician software assists with firmware updates, performance optimization, data migrations, and monitoring the drive’s status. With the SSD 990, Samsung has opted for an energy-efficient design intended to support longer battery life, particularly in laptops. The SSD is compatible with PCIe 4.0 but also works in systems with PCIe 3.0. It’s compatible with laptops, desktop PCs, and some handheld consoles. One thing to note, though, is that this new 990 SSD uses QLC NAND instead of the TLC NAND that’s used in the 990 EVO line. That means the 990 can’t write as much data before the drive wears out, which is reflected in its 3-year warranty versus the 990 EVO’s 5-year warranty. The 990 also has worse write performance when its cache is full. Why this deal is worth it It hasn’t even been a month since the 990 SSD was released, so this marks its first significant price drop and the lowest it’s ever been. If you need a high-performance internal SSD and don’t want to skimp, this is a solid option that’ll serve you well for a few years—longer if you don’t abuse it with too much heavy writing to its cells. Given its newness, it doesn’t have many user reviews to go off. It’s currently sitting at 5 stars on Amazon across 12 ratings, and buyers praise its everyday performance, its cool and energy-efficient operation, and how easy it is to install. Samsung Magician is also praised for its simple firmware updates and smooth drive management. If there’s any criticism, it’s mainly for the 990’s lesser performance during very long, continuous write operations. It’s the kind of thing you’ll notice when transferring huge amounts of data—like for professional 4K video editing—but not when gaming or doing everyday tasks.

item.title: This Grainy Photo of Earth Captured on Mars Is Way Cooler Than It Looks
item.description:
Source: PetaPixel Score: 7.25
NASA’s Perseverance Mars rover used its Mastcam-Z instrument to photograph Earth as it passed behind the Martian moon, Phobos. The Mastcam-Z instrument is primarily designed to photograph things on Mars itself, rather than peer up into the sky at Earth, about 140 million miles (225 million kilometers) away. Unsurprisingly, then, Perseverance’s composite photo of Earth is not exactly beautiful in and of itself. It’s really noisy, and given Earth’s distance, the planet is but a speck in the frame, not unlike Voyager 1’s legendary photo of Earth, “Pale Blue Dot.” But behind the grain and relatively low visible resolution is something truly special. Perseverance’s new image is the first time Earth has been photographed hidden behind another astronomical object from the surface of another planet. How NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory (JPL) created the final image is interesting, too. Perseverance’s Mastcam-Z instrument captured a series of images for the final composite, showing Earth at different locations near and behind Phobos. The team then performed special image processing to make the background black, which “removed extraneous light in the background to enhance detail.” The image below is a composite of nine images taken by Mastcam-Z on July 2, 2026, and the inset portion shows five images of Earth passing behind Phobos. The black rectangle shows the area that was imaged to see Earth, comprising a very small portion of the overall frame. Meanwhile, the image below shows annotations with the local solar time on Mars when each frame was taken. In both cases, image processing has been performed to closely approximate the true color of the Martian sky during twilight when the images were captured. The photos were shot about 40 minutes after sunset on Mars, when the sky is blue-gray near the horizon and reddish-gray farther above. It was just over 22 years ago that NASA’s Mars Exploration Rover Spirit captured the first ever photo of Earth from the surface of another planet. Unsurprisingly, Earth was mighty small in the photo back then, too. 10 years later, Curiosity delivered its own, arguably superior, take on a photo of Earth from Mars. Image creditsNASA/JPL-Caltech/ASU/MSSS/SSI Affiliate Disclosure PetaPixel articles may include affiliate links; we may earn a commission if you buy through one.

item.title: Astronomers Capture ‘Exceptionally Rare’ Star Explosion for Only the Second Time in 20 Years
item.description:
Source: PetaPixel Score: 6.32
In March, the Einstein Probe, a satellite made by the Chinese Academy of Sciences in partnership with the European Space Agency, detected a very brief flash of “soft X-rays” emitted by a galaxy about 500 million light-years away. Within an hour, ground-based telescopes, including several at National Science Foundation (NSF) NOIRLab facilities, began investigating the region, getting a front-row seat to bombastic and very special star death. Telescopes like the U.S. Department of Energy’s Dark Energy Camera, the U.S. National Science Foundation’s Nicholas U. Mayall 4-meter telescope, and the NSF-DOE Vera C. Rubin Observatory all turned their telescopes toward the flash, named EP260321a. Within an hour of monitoring the region, scientists discovered that the source of the soft X-ray detected by the Einstein Probe was a “rapidly brightening supernova,” later named SN 2026gzf. “Two teams of scientists utilized several NSF NOIRLab facilities to observe the event and monitor its evolving light profile,” NOIRLab explains. “The teams were led by Brendan O’Connor, astronomer and McWilliams Fellow at Carnegie Mellon University, and Jillian Rastinejad, a NASA Einstein Fellow at the University of Maryland, College Park.” The teams have just published the results of their studies in The Astrophysical Journal Letters. O’Connor’s team’s paper is “EP260321a/SN 2026gzf: The Faintest Shock Breakout Associated with a Broad-lined Supernova,” while Rastinejad’s is “A Multi-Wavelength View of the First Type Ic-BL Supernova with an Einstein Probe X-ray Shock Breakout.” Both teams independently arrived at a similar conclusion about the nature of the initial burst of X-rays. They each identified it as a “shock breakout,” which is the precise moment when a powerful shock wave from a stellar explosion breaks through the star’s surface and releases the first light of a supernova, or “colossal explosion of a star,” as the Department of Energy puts it. Scientists believe that these shock breakouts typically occur in all supernova explosions, but they are “notoriously difficult to observe” because they last only seconds or, if lucky, hours. In the past two decades, scientists have confidently identified an X-ray shock breakout just one other time. EP260321a is “exceptionally rare.” Each team also identified that the explosion was a “broad-lined Type Ic supernova.” “These supernovae typically possess jets of relativistic material — material that is moving close to the speed of light — and they are commonly linked to gamma-ray bursts, which are the brightest and most powerful class of explosions in the Universe,” NSF explains. That said, SN 2026gzf is special for a few reasons. The initial shock breakout was the faintest ever associated with an Ic-BL supernova, although the explosion itself was not weak. Scientists also surprisingly found no evidence of a gamma-ray burst after the supernova itself, which is very unusual. “SN 2026gzf looks remarkably similar to other energetic supernovae that have been previously linked to gamma-ray bursts. Yet multi-wavelength follow-up observations using the most sensitive facilities found no evidence for a relativistic jet or an afterglow, which are typically seen in those events,” says O’Connor. “One possibility is that the jet was ‘choked,’ either by the surface of the star or by circumstellar material surrounding the star.” To investigate this “puzzling event,” O’Connor and his team used the 570-megapixel Dark Energy Camera (DECam) mounted on the NSF Victor M. Blanco 4-meter Telescope in Chile. The team used new images and compared them against archival data taken by the DECam 10 years ago. In both cases, the high-res camera revealed a blue light source at the same location, “offering rare clues about the progenitor system and its environment before the star died.” The new Vera C. Rubin Observatory supplied additional multi-band images of the area, as did the Dark Energy Spectroscopic Instrument. Scientists are especially excited about Rubin, which can deliver high-resolution images very often, providing detailed, long-term records of the supernova as it evolves. O’Connor and his team also acquired observational data from NASA’s Chandra X-ray Observatory, the National Radio Astronomy Observatory’s Very Large Array, the Fraunhofer Telescope at Wendelstein Observatory, Caltech’s Palomar Observatory, the Hobby-Eberly Telescope, and the Southern African Large Telescope. Rastinejad and her team used multi-wavelength observations from the Gemini Multi-Object Spectrographs, the International Gemini Observatory, and the Goodman spectrograph. Between the two teams of researchers, the hunt for information about EP260321a and SN 2026gzf was a truly global affair. The scientific community can be very cooperative, and it’s inspiring to see how quickly everyone came together to contribute. “Our observations allowed us to study the physics of three pieces of this explosion: the X-ray shock breakout, the accompanying supernova, and the interaction of the supernova with material previously cast out by the dying star,” says Rastinejad. “With this information we were able to map out the structure of the material surrounding the star and understand the star’s violent lifestyle before it collapsed.” Rastinejad’s team determined that the progenitor is a Wolf-Rayet star. This type of star is born with about 20 times the mass of the Sun and burns through its stock of hydrogen in its early life. Before this star blew up spectacularly, it had irregular episodes of mass loss, ejecting its hydrogen and helium. This meant the stripped remains comprised mostly carbon and oxygen. “The turbulent mass loss created multiple shells of material around the star: a nearby, compact shell of low-mass material that emitted the initial X-ray signal, plus an extended, non-symmetric shell of material that emitted the optical supernova signal,” NSF explains. “This is the first time we’ve mapped out the pre-explosion environment of a star that has been stripped of hydrogen and helium,” says Gokul Srinivasaragavan, a recent PhD graduate from the University of Maryland and a member of Rastinejad’s team. Srinivasaragavan is the second author on the team’s paper. “Going forward, I’m excited to observe more shock breakout events in similar detail to test if all stripped stars have a similar ‘lifestyle’ prior to collapse and what, if any, differences we see.” Thanks to the Einstein Probe’s initial observation and a very rapid response in the astronomy community, scientists have now learned that massive stars can die in more diverse ways than previously realized. “The result also demonstrates the growing power of coordinated time-domain astronomy, where space missions and ground-based observatories work together to capture transient cosmic events in real time. By combining observations from Einstein Probe, NSF NOIRLab facilities, and partner observatories around the world, researchers were able to reconstruct a rare explosion in unprecedented detail,” NSF concludes. Image creditsNSF–DOE Vera C. Rubin Observatory/NOIRLab/SLAC/AURA. CTIO/NOIRLab/DOE/NSF/AURA.
