It sounds so self-defeating and, more than that, depressing, that it’s impossible to imagine people still doing that. But we can see that people are still doing that. And while many countries are entering into explicit contracts with visitors to meet the challenges of the climate crisis, not all of these are particularly helpful. In Palau in the western pacific, you will receive a pledge stamp in your passport that will give you special access to places if you buy reef-safe sunscreen. In Denmark, there’s a trial initiative called Copenpay, in which tourists might get a free boat trip for picking up litter, or a free drink if you cycle to a bar instead of driving. It’s a creative way to connect tourists to the place they’re in, but it all underlines how hard it is to truly mitigate your carbon footprint as a tourist: cycling through Copenhagen won’t make a lot of difference if you arrived there by plane. McClanahan is more plausible than most tech-optimists on the aviation front. “The technology for carbon-free travel already exists,” she says. “It’s not being deployed at anything like the scale needed, and we all need to educate ourselves, as consumers and as voters, about the transformation and the speed that we need. Whether it’s through electric flight, whether it’s hydrogen-powered flight, whether it’s through a hydrocarbon fuel that is made from carbon dioxide, extracted from the atmosphere, this technology exists, these planes have flown. It’s a question of being able to do it at the scale required to make an actual impact on the atmosphere.” On the climate crisis, as with all the ethical challenges tourism faces, McClahanan urges us to consider the counter-factual. There isn’t a simple fix, such as “stop doing it”. As the old TomTom satnav adverts used to say, you’re not in traffic, you are traffic. If you’ve travelled somewhere where you can see overtourism, you’re an overtourist. Yet “there’s a wonderful amount of humility that we gain from getting out of our comfort zone”, McClanahan says. “We just need to learn to do it differently.” The New Tourist by Paige McClanahan is out now published by Simon & Schuster.

item.title: My slow Swedish summer on the tranquil islands of Östergötland
item.description:
Source: The Guardian Travel Score: 3.76
At 5am on Arkösund bay, it is so light it could be midday. I slip out of the pretty clapboard Arkösunds hotell, opened in 1895, as a small boat putters into the Baltic Sea, the sun sparkling on its calm waters. A wooden boardwalk invites me on to a string of tiny islets as geese arrow overhead and a mother swan coaxes her fluffy cygnets into a nook under a bridge. I’m on Sweden’s east coast to explore the Östergötland archipelago, a sprawl of about 9,000 islands scattered across the Baltic Sea a few hours south of Stockholm. Quieter and less crowded than the better-known isles off Stockholm or Gothenburg, it covers several pockets of coastline and smaller archipelagos: Arkösund, Sankt Anna, Gryt and Tjust. The larger islands are flecked with traditional red timber summer houses, and are home to seals, sea birds, and dense, verdant forests of alder, cedar, oak and pine. I’d arrived in a suitably slow fashion. My journey to Arkösund – a 45-minute drive from Norrköping station along a road locals call the End of the World – started 24 hours earlier, with an early morning Eurostar from London to Brussels, then on to Hamburg via Cologne, where I boarded the SJ EuroNight Train to Norrköping. I slept while we slipped across the Danish border in the early hours and crossed the Øresund Bridge into Sweden. Dawn unfolded in pink, dusky waves as we shuddered out of Malmö towards Östergötland. Visitors navigate the region’s islands in sailboats, small motorboats or kayaks, spending elongated summer days swimming, fishing and hiking. From Arkösund jetty, I take to the water with Åsa, a local guide, in a motorboat belonging to Kauko Lindstedt, a Finn who has spent 40 years living on the island of Aspöja, a four-mile crossing away. There is an unspoken rule, Åsa says, that if you spot a moored kayak or boat, move on. In the Swedish spirit of allemansrätten – the national law to roam and sleep freely in nature – there are enough islands for everyone. Aspöja is one of the few inhabited islands and Lindstedt, as with many islanders I meet, is industrious: building, hunting, smoking fish, running boating tours, and eager to share his home, where just 25 people live year-round. We land at his jetty and walk across grassy meadows dotted with lumps of granite and teeming with butterflies. There are no cars, though the jetty has a communal wheelbarrow for groceries and post. We meet Helen, who farms sheep and cattle, knits, tans sheepskins, keeps bees, grows vegetables and runs the only restaurant, Forsmans på Aspöja, with her daughter. Lunch is smoked fish and boiled potatoes heaped with fresh dill, alongside a glass of Baltic seawater, filtered through the island’s small desalination plant. On the trip back to the mainland, we pass an island stacked with fishing nets, buoys and wooden crates. A pair of craggy-faced men wave – brothers in their 70s, the final vestiges of a once thriving fishing industry, Åsa tells me. They are the last two fishers legally able to catch eels; the licence can only be passed on through family, and with none it ends with them. The next day, Åsa and I drive further along the coast to the Sankt Anna archipelago, stopping for lunch at Mauritzberg Castle, a 400-year-old manor house rebuilt in pastel rococo splendour after the Russians burned it down in 1719. At the bay of Sankt Anna, I meet a German tourist packing his kayak for a 10-day solo adventure. He tells me he paddles for days from island to island without seeing a single soul and adores it – it’s his third trip here. From the shore I clamber into a kayak alongside Andreas, my guide, another Finn who works for outfitter Kajakparadiset, and we paddle into the languid, liquid landscape. We stop for fika – hot coffee and something sweet – on one islet, stretching out on sun-scorched granite as a sea eagle soars above. That night I sleep at Skärgårdsbyn Mon, a hotel on the mainland shore, after a meal of buttered sea bream and potatoes eaten on the wooden balcony of the Boathouse restaurant, overlooking the marina, with the islands spilling out behind. I wonder enviously which one the German kayaker has chosen to sleep on underneath the barely darkened sky. I wake to rain. But with temperatures averaging around 23C, summer here is comfortable. Driving south with Åsa, I learn that about 70% of the country is forested, and it’s crossed by hiking and biking trails. At Fyrudden, a hamlet on the south-eastern end of a narrow peninsula in the Gryt archipelago, Magnus Lindkvist, a boat captain, is waiting in his grandfather’s wooden boat to take us across eight miles of open water to the island of Harstena. It’s where his grandparents once lived and he spent every summer of his childhood, and continues to go there today with his family. A cluster of 18th-century cabins still stand. The old schoolhouse is a museum, depicting the history of these wild islands, where herring, eel fishing, seabird eggs and seal blubber were once the means of the islanders’ survival. A 1641 census registers two households, and a family tree traces local names back to their two families – including Magnus, and now his son. Back on the mainland, we drive north and inland to spend the night in Söderköping, where in 1281 King Magnus Ladulås’ wife, Helvig, was crowned in its medieval church. This tiny town is steeped in history, standing at the eastern end of the Göta Canal, which the Swedes, in a bid to avoid Danish taxes, began building in 1810, connecting Gothenburg to the Baltic Sea. I spend the next morning cycling alongside it, stopping to sample ice-cream from the Smultronstället cafe and handmade chocolates from Jolla. By evening, I am back in Norrköping, an industrial city once booming with textile and paper mills powered by water. Today, the mills have been restored into a stylish district of bars, apartments and offices. The streets are alive at night as students celebrate the end of term and city revellers gear up for a weekend of national celebrations. From the train window the following day, as I head back to the UK, I watch the fields and forests unfurl as Norrköping station slides away behind me, the summer light filtering through the trees and across the red weatherboard farmsteads. A skein of geese flies overhead in a V, and I imagine the kayaker searching for his perfect island to camp tonight, and Magnus teaching his son to fish for herring from his great-grandfather’s boat – the delicate balance of nature and visitor continuing in harmony. The trip was provided by Visit Sweden. The writer travelled by rail from Eurostar London to Brussels (from £39 one-way), then to Cologne/Köln (from £16.50 one-way), and on to Hamburg (from £16.50 one-way). The SJ EuroNight train from Hamburg to Nörrköping costs from £40 one-way. Elite Grand hotel Norrköping has doubles from £80 B&B; Söderköpings Brunn from £93 B&B; Skärgårdsbyn Mon from £100; and Arkösunds hotell from £170 B&B Comments (…) Sign in or create your Guardian account to join the discussion

item.title: A break from the accommodation mega-sites: the best alternative booking platforms
item.description:
Source: The Guardian Travel Score: 3.71
Accounts of tenants illegally subletting rental properties by listing them on Airbnb and Booking.com, without the permission of their landlords, have hit the headlines in recent months. While there’s no denying that the convenience of these accommodation booking platforms has transformed holidays – making independent travel more accessible and affordable – that convenience often comes at a cost. In tourism hotspots like Barcelona, which banned short-term rentals in 2021 (and will ban all apartment rentals to tourists by late 2028), platforms such as Airbnb are being blamed for driving up rents and house prices for residents. However, there are alternatives to these search engine and booking monoliths, with an increasing number of smaller websites offering hand-picked owner-run, independent B&Bs, home swaps, or rental properties that are primary homes (rather than fuelling a second home market). With a focus on passionate, local hosts who know their patch inside out, using these platforms can also take some of the pain out of researching a destination. Better for locals and better for your holiday; it’s often a win-win. Fairbnb A direct challenger to Airbnb, Fairbnb is a cooperative short-term rental platform that started in Venice with a mission to “redefine tourism”. It claims to do this in two ways: by only listing places to stay that are owned and lived in by local people, and by donating 50% of the commission earned on each booking to community projects chosen collectively by hosts. Today, the platform has about 2,000 listings in 10 countries across Europe. In 2023, Fairbnb launched fairUP, listing experiences that support underrepresented local businesses. For example, half of the commission earned on bookings for this flat sleeping up to six in Mouraria, a vibrant neighbourhood near the centre of Lisbon (£221 a night), will be donated to local homeless charity Centro de Apoio ao Sem Abrigo. Socialbnb Initially developed as a student project in Cologne, Socialbnb connects travellers with social and ecological projects across the world. Many of these projects have rooms to rent, providing travellers with engaging experiences while funding important grassroots projects. It lists over 400 experiences and places to stay worldwide. Stay in a restored water mill surrounded by 60 miles of hiking and biking routes in a biosphere reserve in Förstgen, Germany, (from £60 a night), or book a room at PitaSana, an organic farm 15 miles inland from Spain’s north coast (doubles from £42). Ecobnb Once an award-winning blog for green travel, Ecobnb now lists about 3,000 sustainable places to stay in more than 55 countries. Each of these – primarily small hotels and self-catering properties in rural locations – must submit data across 10 sustainability criteria, including organic produce use, wastewater recycling and renewable energy. Independently owned and run, these B&Bs often use local suppliers and experience providers, making sure locals benefit from tourism as well. A 90-minute drive from Milan, Valtidone Verde is a bio-agriturismo with a pool and sweeping views offering two nights for one at weekends (from £168 for two people for two nights). Kindred Most travel companies bandy around the term “living like a local”, but one way to guarantee doing just that is house swapping. Unsurprisingly, this way of travelling is on the rise – it’s affordable, offers a home away from home, and reduces tourism’s environmental impact. Kindred is one of the newer platforms, with 80,000 homes available, 90% of which are primary residences. The platform has differentiated itself by taking away traditional home-swapping pain points like inconsistent cleaning and not having a 24/7 point of contact. Hosts must apply to join and, once approved, must host someone before booking a home swap for themselves. Hole up in a colourful loft studio in Berlin’s creative Neukölln district, or enjoy mid-century style in Amsterdam. A credit system means you don’t have to do a direct swap, but you do have to pay a cleaning and service fee for each stay, which is about £250 a week. Landfolk This Danish start-up is on a mission to get people into nature, drawing on the concept of friluftsliv, which translates as “living in the free air”. Launched by a group of seven former Airbnb colleagues, Landfolk prioritises personality, access to nature and enthusiastic hosts (each host has to write a local guide for guests). It now operates in six European countries, but the majority of the properties listed are in Scandinavia. Typical properties include a cosy wooden fisherman’s house overlooking the fjord at Mjosundet, about 93 miles west of Trondheim in Norway, which has been the holiday home of host Lars since 1959 (from £128 a night), and a traditional holiday cottage surrounded by forest in southern Jutland, Denmark (from £173 a night). Sawday’s and Canopy & Stars One of the highest-scoring B Corp travel companies in the UK, Sawday’s (which owns the glamping site Canopy & Stars) takes active steps to overcome the social and environmental cost of tourism. By introducing caps on listings in places suffering from overtourism, (including the Isle of Skye, Lake District, St Ives and Palma de Mallorca), the company won’t solve overtourism, but it might help mitigate demand and highlight the need for action. Sawday’s also offers discounts on designated “Community Champion” listings that give money back to social causes. Yaffle and Dumbledore are two cabins set among the trees at Wilderness Wood in East Sussex (from £167 a night sleeps two, with extra space for two children). Proceeds from the accommodation help to fund community access to woodland craft and adventure in the vicinity. Coolstays Focused on unique places to stay, from converted grain stores to rail carriages, Cool Stays offers thousands of properties across Europe. A comprehensive search function makes it possible to pick out its more sustainable accommodation, such as off-grid cabins or converted historical buildings, which are less likely to take away from local housing stock. Find properties with high green credentials in the eco-friendly collection. Coety Bach is an off-grid hideaway handcrafted from repurposed materials for two in mid-Wales’ Radnorshire Hills (from £110 a night, sleeps two), and Magic Wood is an ecocabin in the Peak District national park (from £150 a night).

item.title: 10 of Britain’s best piers for dining, nightlife and good old seaside fun
item.description:
Source: The Guardian Travel Score: 3.60
Perched in our glass-fronted eyrie, 300 metres out to sea, we watch a murmuration of starlings rise and fall and swoop around us. When the show is over, we turn our attention to the food. I have a bespoke vegan menu based on the best early summer ingredients: jersey royals, asparagus, strawberries. My boyfriend orders off the weekly changing à la carte: slow-cooked beef dumplings followed by butter-poached halibut. We are at Ebb, a restaurant at the end of the pier in Worthing, West Sussex, which opened in May. Its art-deco design and fine-dining dishes are a far cry from the fish-and-chip shops and ice-cream parlours more commonly found on seaside piers. But traditionalists need not despair: downstairs at Perch on the Pier, fish and chips – as well as tofish (tofu) and chips – are always on the menu, with a knickerbocker glory to round things off in fine retro style. Worthing pier, which opened in 1862, is one of Britain’s surviving 19th-century pleasure piers. “The seaside piers around the coast of Britain stand as a powerful reminder of the achievements of Victorian engineers and entrepreneurs,” says the National Piers Society website. “However, of the 100 piers that once graced our coastline, only half survive, and several of these face an uncertain future.” The society campaigns to preserve the piers for everyone’s enjoyment, and has saved several that were at risk of demolition. Worthing may well be the foodiest pier in the UK, but they all have their charms. Here are 10 well worth a stroll out to sea. Best for overnight stays: Garth pier, Bangor, Gwynedd Bangor’s 458-metre (1,500ft) pier stretches out halfway across the Menai Strait, backdropped by the Eryri mountain range (Snowdonia). To coincide with its 130th anniversary this year, the Pier Master’s House at the entrance has been turned into a holiday let (from £140 a night, sleeps six). The pavilion at the far end is now a cafe, and the smaller Victorian kiosks dotted along the pier house independent businesses selling gifts, artworks and local food. There is a programme of weekend events over the summer, from busking and children’s fun days to a dog parade. Best for adventure: Bournemouth pier Bournemouth pier (first opened 1856, current structure 1880) boasts the world’s first pier-to-shore zip wire, a 250-metre dual line starting from the end-of-the-pier tower. As well as the PierZip, it has RockReef, an indoor climbing centre with 28 climbing walls, an aerial obstacle course, a vertical slide, a “leap of faith” and caving tunnels. The pier is the best place to watch Bournemouth’s Friday fireworks (10pm, until 28 August), and there is regular live music at its Key West restaurant (until 28 August). The town’s other pier, Boscombe (opened 1889), is next to free bouldering obstacles and slacklines, and near the beach volleyball courts. Best for traditional seaside fun: Britannia pier, Great Yarmouth Britannia pier won the coveted 2026 Pier of the Year award, taking over from last year’s winner Llandudno, and beating runners-up Herne Bay and Swanage. The 250-metre pier was built in 1858, but as with many of the original Victorian piers, it has been damaged, demolished, rebuilt (in 1901), burned down and reconstructed over the years. The current owners bought it in 2022 and have spent £2.2m restoring and upgrading it. Its attractions include a theatre, fun fair, arcades, fish and chip shop, pub and nightclub. Holidaymakers can also visit the town’s Wellington pier, further south along the seafront, which opened in 1853 and has a bowling alley, arcade and ice-cream parlour. Best for culture: Penarth pier, Glamorgan While Penarth pier dates back to 1894, as a landing jetty for the steamships in the Bristol Channel, its art-deco pavilion wasn’t built until 1929. This former dancehall has recently been restored and is now a cinema and arts centre, with year-round film screenings, art exhibitions, live music, workshops and talks. Coming up this month is a jazz brunch, a drawing workshop, and a knitting and crocheting social, alongside summer blockbusters The Odyssey and Minions & Monsters. There is a cafe in the pavilion, and a coffee shop, ice-cream parlour and chippy elsewhere on the pier. Best for exploration: Roker pier, Sunderland Roker pier is distinctive for its red-and-white striped granite lighthouse, completed in 1903. After extensive restoration, and closures due to storm damage, pier and lighthouse are now open for guided tours (£14 adults/£10 children, to 27 August). Visitors walk the length of an underground tunnel to reach the lighthouse – the route the keeper used in bad weather – then climb to the top to take in the views. For post-tour refreshments, the pier’s former toilet block is now a gin bar, Tin of Sardines, with brunch and tapas menus served on the terrace in the summer. Best for beauty: Clevedon pier, north Somerset England’s only Grade I-listed pier opened in 1869 to receive paddle steamer passengers from Devon and Wales. It is made from discarded wrought iron railway lines shaped into eight arches, nearly 15 metres high. In 1980, during a campaign to save it from demolition, the then poet laureate John Betjeman described it as “the most beautiful pier in England”. “Clevedon without its pier would be like a diamond with a flaw,” he said. The pier was duly saved, and now its Victorian pagoda is a cafe, its toll house is a museum and gift shop, and there is a modern restaurant, the Glass Box. The sea view from the porthole room is streamed live 24/7. Best for nightlife: Royal pier, Aberystwyth The oldest pier in Wales (1865) was designed by Eugenius Birch, a renowned seaside architect best-known for Brighton’s now-ruined West pier. Today, Royal pier is billed as “the number one destination for competitive socialising in Aberystwyth”, with three bars and a nightclub. There is a host of activities in the Billiard Bar, including shuffleboard, augmented-reality darts, footpool and interactive mini golf; the Upstairs Bar has seven pool tables; and the Inn on the Pier is a restored Victorian boozer, with stained glass and custom tiles. DJs play chill-out tunes in the pier garden over the summer, and the Pressure Nightclub is open until 4am on Fridays and Saturdays. Best for variety: Blackpool Blackpool is the proud home of three piers: Blackpool North (1863), Blackpool Central (1868) and Blackpool South (1893). The Grade II-listed north pier is the oldest surviving Birch pier, and has an art-deco theatre, a two-tier carousel, bars and an arcade. It was sold in June and is open until at least the end of the year before a promised £10m refurbishment. The central pier has Blackpool’s Big Wheel, a funfair and a show bar with live performances. The south pier has a more high-octane funfair, with a rollercoaster, a freefalling swing and a reverse bungee ride, and is next to Blackpool’s Pleasure Beach for more adrenaline-fuelled fun. Its many food and drink options include the Gin House and a loaded jacket potato stand. Best for history: Gravesend pier, Kent Gravesend’s pier opened on the Thames in 1834, and is the oldest surviving cast-iron pier in the world. It was once a hub for steam packets to London – more than 3 million passengers used it between 1835 and 1842 – and today there are still occasional summer sailings to the capital with Uber Boat by Thames Clippers. Just by the entrance to the pier is the ancient Three Daws pub, which was licensed in 1565 as the Three Cornish Choughs and renamed in 1745. This old smugglers’ haunt, which has three underground tunnels, now hosts a summer beer and music festival (7-9 August) and an Oktoberfest (18 September). Best for rainy days: Sandown pier, Isle of Wight The Isle of Wight once had an incredible 11 piers, and four still survive: Ryde (the second-longest in the UK, after Southend-on-Sea in Essex), Sandown, Totland (for sale) and Yarmouth. Sandown (1879) is a particular paradise for families, whatever the weather. There is the Aztec-themed Lost World indoor crazy golf, with lighting and sound effects; the Magic Island indoor adventure play area; and Superbowl 10-pin bowling. The end of the pier has rides such as dodgems and teacups (Easter to September only); there is a cafe, ice-cream kiosk and burger bar; and Scruffy Jacks bar shows live sport. Comments (…) Sign in or create your Guardian account to join the discussion

item.title: Summer on the Baltic: a laidback coastal adventure in Lithuania
item.description:
Source: The Guardian Travel Score: 3.30
The water off Palanga’s sandy white beach is tinged pale green – the colour of the feathery clouds of Furcellaria lumbricalis that occasionally brush against my calves. Underfoot, the Baltic seabed is ridged, the sea so clear and shallow that every ripple is visible. The water deepens very gradually – making it ideal for families. I’m quite far from the coast, but still only thigh deep, the sea still cool as I duck beneath the surface. Elsewhere in Europe, another heatwave has prompted health warnings and school closures. But here in Lithuania, children scamper on the sand and splash in the shallows as temperatures remain, if not cool, bearable. I’ve come to explore some of the Baltic beaches – here and on the Curonian Spit – which are fast gaining popularity as the Med heats up and prices in southern Europe remain stubbornly high. Palanga has been drawing Lithuanian holidaymakers since the wealthy Tiškevičiai family transformed it into a seaside resort in the mid-19th century. Today, there is a certain rowdy seaside vibe in parts: the central beach can get crowded and the promenade is on the kitsch side too, with many of the historic wooden buildings – demolished or damaged in the Soviet era – replaced by brash signage, entertainment venues and raucous restaurants. Nonetheless, the main beach is reassuringly devoid of construction and characterised primarily by its distinctive 19th-century L-shaped pier, a popular sunset-catching spot. Away from the shore, you need only stroll the 100-hectare (250-acre) botanical garden, home to the 19th-century Tiškevičiai Palace and amber museum, with its thousands of prehistoric exhibits, to witness a different past. A bronze sculpture of Feliksas Tiškevičius stands just outside the park; legend has it that if you rub his foot with yours and kiss his cheek, good luck will follow. Just a 10-minute cycle ride away from the pier, my hotel, the Gradiali (B&B doubles from €118), is another peaceful oasis. From here, a 500-metre walk through aromatic pine forest leads to an uncrowded section of Palanga beach, where €75 (£64) gets you all-day use of a curtained cabana, complete with a bottle of prosecco and a mountain of ice-cream. (I’ve paid at least double that on the Greek island of Mykonos – and that was just for the bed.) There are other ways to get into the water around Palanga, including wakeboarding at the 313 Cable Park (from €20), about 2.5 miles (4km) from the town, or plunging into one of the 16 leisure and mineral pools at the Atostogų Parkas complex (from €30), about 4 miles away. But I’m on a mission to explore Lithuania’s more untamed side – the Curonian Spit, a protected 61-mile stretch of dense forest and Blue Flag beaches accessed only via the modern port city of Klaipėda, a half-hour drive away. Trains run to Klaipėda from the capital, Vilnius, too – and electrification of the train line next year will reduce the 205-mile journey time by 30 minutes to four hours. With its waterfront setting, compact old town and restored castle complex, Klaipėda makes for a pleasant afternoon stop – but I’m eager to board the ferry (approximately €1.70), which has me on the spit within 10 minutes. Threaded by bike and walking trails, this narrow stretch of sand peninsula – flanked by the Baltic Sea on one side and the Curonian Lagoon on the other – is occupied in the south by Russia. Observation decks near the border allow glimpses of a similarly forested landscape, but one punctuated by watchtowers. As fascinating as this off-limits area is, it’s the older stories about the spit that bewitch me. Legend has it the giant Neringa formed it by pouring sand from her apron to create a protective break between the irascible Baltic Sea and her people. The amber fragments, which still wash up on the peninsula’s beaches, are said to be the debris from an underwater amber castle, shattered in rage by the thunder god Perkūnas when Jūratė, goddess of the sea, fell in love with a mortal. But some of the area’s most haunting tales are not mere myth. On an evening trip in a traditional flat-bottomed fishing boat from the harbour in Nida – the spit’s largest town – our skipper Aurelijus Armonavičius speaks of the vagaries of shifting sands and the 18th-century felling of forests, which led to the slow burial of 14 villages and two cemeteries on the spit. Only through the building of a sand ridge and concerted reforestation efforts has this – now Unesco-listed – landscape been preserved. My accommodation, Hotel Nidus (B&B doubles from €119), lies between lagoon and beach, and features basic, comfortable rooms and expansive gardens. I head to the harbour for dinner at Nidos Prieplauka, watching the sunset and sampling the cold, kefir-based beetroot soup – a traditional Lithuanian dish so adored that there’s an annual springtime festival held for it in the capital. The following day, I meet Angelina Ivanova, from Nida’s tourism centre, to bike to Vecekrugas Dune. At 67 metres (220ft) above sea level, it is the spit’s highest point: the flatness of the landscape, as well as its pine needle-strewn bike paths, make it manageable for even the least experienced cyclists. As we walk from our bikes to the peak, the ground is scarred with furrows of dark earth; the work of wild boar. Clusters of mushrooms stud the soil; foraging is a beloved Baltic activity – although the protected status of the Curonian Spit means that it is off limits in certain areas, such as the Nagliai nature reserve, about 11 miles from Nida. The area is also a migratory path for millions of birds such as peregrine falcons and red kites. This being high summer, we see mostly gulls and cormorants. “The shoulder seasons are our busiest for twitchers,” says Angelina, as we reach the top of the dune. And, with water on both sides – at points separated by as little as 400 metres – the spit sustains not only these migratory birds, but also the fishing traditions that have traditionally shaped life here. We continue on to Preila, about a mile away. A tiny village on the lagoon, it is home to a row of smoke-fishing shacks. “Everybody has their favourite,” says Angelina, as we peruse that day’s offerings: hers is Rimo Žuvis, owned by the parents of her schoolfriend. Eel, considered a delicacy, is the most expensive dish on the menu, but we opt for sea perch and turbot, which we eat at picnic tables overlooking the water, accompanied by bread, fresh tomatoes and cold beer. Later, we will end the day back in the sea at Nida, with the midsummer sun hanging high in the sky and temperatures still hovering pleasantly in the 20s. The trip was provided by the Neringa, Klaipėda, Palanga and Kretinga tourism offices, with accommodation at Hotel Nidus and Hotel Gradiali Comments (…) Sign in or create your Guardian account to join the discussion

item.title: The best new cycling and ebike trails in Melbourne and surrounds
item.description:
Source: The Guardian Travel Score: 3.25
Ebike sales are surging in Australia – and retailers are struggling to keep up. “We’ve sold three times as many ebikes for the first months of this year than we did last year,” says Tony Morgan, manager of The Electric Bicycle Company in Melbourne. “This is absolutely in response to the fuel price spikes.” Compared with manual bicycles, ebikes can travel faster and further, allowing riders of all ages and abilities to sail over hills or into strong headwinds. As a longtime cyclist and recent ebike user myself, the latter unlocks a whole new sense of freedom. But much like electric cars, range anxiety is still an issue with ebikes and I’ve learned the hard way that you need to ensure your bike has adequate power for longer journeys, or know where public charging facilities are. Fortunately, in Victoria, infrastructure is improving quickly. With public transport half price in Victoria for the rest of the year, it’s a good time to take your ebike on the train and explore those new bike paths in Melbourne and further afield. You can take ebikes on all metro and regional trains in Victoria without charge, but it’s worth arriving early as spots are limited. Just don’t rely on Google Maps for cycling – in most cases it simply hasn’t kept up with bike trail upgrades and will try to direct you on to highways or trafficked streets. Instead, use local bike trail websites with up-to-date maps such as those provided by the Bicycle Network. If you’re keen to hit the new and improved bike trails in Victoria, here are some good places to start. Dixon Veloway Opened in December 2025, the 2.5km Dixon Veloway Bridge, named after the late trailblazing Australian cyclist Iris Dixon, is the jewel of Melbourne’s cycling upgrades. Elevated above Footscray Road with the sounds of semitrailers echoing below, it’s quite a sensation to ride. The veloway, part of the West Gate Tunnel project, provides a safe bike-only connector from Melbourne’s west to the CBD. For riders, it also connects to the Federation trail and Docklands from the Maribyrnong River, which previously required cycling through heavy traffic. Cycling the four-metre-wide, fluoro green Veloway for the first time brings to mind riding on Beijing’s bike highway. It’s a glimpse of what future city bicycle infrastructure can and should look like in Australia. Trail length 2.5km. Difficulty Easy – fairly flat and smooth. Charging facilities There is free charging available at Library at the Dock or the Myrtle cafe beside the Maribyrnong Creek. The cross-city caterpillar Historically, cycling in Melbourne could be frustrating. Bike paths weren’t interconnected and would often dump riders out into notorious arterial roads and intersections, including black spots such as Footscray Road in the west and the beginning of St Georges Road, Northcote. But recent improvements have made cycling safer. Since April 2025 it has been possible to cycle from the southern to northern suburbs of Melbourne completely on designated paths, via a new cable-stayed bridge, dubbed “the green caterpillar”. The 220-metre bike and pedestrian bridge, which was also part of the West Gate Tunnel works, connects Docklands to the Capital City trail and Moonee Ponds Creek trail – a gamechanger for folks wanting to ride safely from suburbs like St Kilda to Brunswick. Other notable recent improvements include separated bike lanes along the southern part of Wellington Street in Collingwood; Heidelberg Road between Clifton Hill and Station Street; St Kilda Road between the CBD and St Kilda Junction; Arden Street between Moonee Ponds Creek and the Wreckyn Street/Chetwynd Street roundabout; and Macaulay Road between Moonee Ponds Creek and Boundary Road. These improvements mean cyclists no longer have to share the road with cars travelling at high speed or along narrow roads. Trail length Melbourne has more than 2,000km of bike trails stretching across the city and suburbs. Difficulty Mostly easy. Melbourne is a relatively flat city and most trails are built around creeks, waterways and former rail lines. Charging facilities If you have a detachable battery some cafes will allow you to charge it as a paying customer, just like you’d charge your phone. There are dedicated ebike charging stations in Lilydale trail head and Frankston foreshore. Local libraries are also a good option. Kororoit Creek trail If you’re looking for a great bike ride close to the city, take the train to Sunshine, Albion or Ardeer stations and ride through the backstreets to the Kororoit Creek trail, which stretches about 15km north-west to Deer Park. Recent upgrades as part of the West Gate Tunnel project include the completion of missing links between Altona North and Brooklyn, and a new underpass at Geelong Road, providing a safer direct connection to the Federation trail. The moderately easy shared-use path crisscrosses Kororoit Creek, winding through regenerated bushlands, basalt cliffs and rocky outcrops, interspersed with semi-industrial areas. You’ll ride near river red gums and blackwood trees and pass Mount Kororoit, an ancient volcanic hill. The path is also teeming with native birds and plant species. Keep a lookout for water and woodland birds such as pelicans, black swans, rainbow lorikeets and black-faced cuckooshrikes that are returning to the area after years of regeneration work from Friends of Kororoit Creek volunteers. Trail length 22km. Difficulty Easy, mostly flat. Charging facilities You will need to go off-trail. The Sunshine library or the Kororoit Creek Neighbourhood House are good options. Lilydale to Warburton bike trail Often referred to as the “Warby trail”, this excellent recreational ride through the Yarra Valley has had significant improvements to intersection safety, connectivity to the Yarra Valley trail loop, and the addition of ebike charging stations, a public bike pump and bike repair station. Take the train to Lilydale; the bike path starts near the train station car park and follows the former train tracks, with extended brick veneer back yards making way to a lush, forested trail. The 40km path between the Dandenong Ranges and Great Dividing Range passes through the towns of Wandin, Seville, Yarra Junction and finishes in the artsy town Warburton. One of the prettiest stretches is around Mount Evelyn, where the path is lined with wildflowers and tree ferns, and offers glimpses of the mountain ranges. This route also doubles as a kind of history lesson – riding alongside the decommissioned tracks, there’s a sobering realisation that Melbourne once had much better train connections to its outlying areas. Trail length 40km. Difficulty Moderate – its a bit of climb up to Warburton although most of the gradients are gentle. Charging facilities The ebike charging stations at the Lilydale trail head are equipped with universal charging ports. There are also many cafes along this path that will let you charge, including the Trail cafe in Mount Evelyn and Carriage cafe in Seville. Murray to Mountains rail trail One of Victoria’s most beautiful bike trails is worth an overnight stay while transport is cheaper. Take the train to Wangaratta to see its $8.5m “enhancement”, completed in September 2025, which added a 31km extension from Beechworth to Yackandandah and improved safety – including nine new bridges and an elevated boardwalk – across the 180km trail network. The trail starts at the northern end of town, beside the Ovens River. The many paths are relatively flat and, depending on which route you choose, will take you past farms, ramshackle country homes, wheatfields and the odd pack of roaming sheep before reaching more forested areas. The most popular route is Wangaratta to Everton and then on to the historic township of Beechworth. Unless you arrive in peak season (weekends in autumn and spring), you’ll feel almost completely alone on this ride, with a well-paved pathway stretching nearly 30km to Everton, where you turn towards Beechworth (altitude 550m) for another 17km ride, mostly uphill. There are many good options to stay in Beechworth, such as the Tanswell’s Commercial hotel (from $95 per night, twin share). Then you can look forward to a blissful early morning downhill to Mount Everton. Consider riding back through the eucalypt and wattle forests to the Milawa Cheese Company, an excellent lunch stop that offers free cheese and wine tastings. Trail length 130km total, through the heart of north-east Victoria, linking the flatlands of the Murray River to the foothills of the alps. Difficulty Moderate. Depending where you go, expect some uphill riding as these paths are in the foothills of alpine country. Charging facilities There are no public chargers on the actual rail trail, so you’ll need to detour to a cafe or bar in high country towns such as Bright, Myrtleford, Beechworth or Wangaratta. Omeo mountain bike park For those wanting to take cycling to the next level, the new 114km Omeo mountain bike park in Victoria’s alpine region offers off-road adventure riding for all levels. There’s no straightforward way to take public transport from Melbourne to Omeo town, especially with a bike in tow; however from Omeo’s main street, you can book a third-party shuttle service to get to the bike park. Officially opened in December 2025, the snaking dirt paths offer freeriding, stomach-flipping descents, scenic adventure rides and climbs through the foothills of Victoria’s alpine national park. Daniel Norris, a local dirt bike rider and tour guide for Gravity Dirt Co, says there are enough options to keep riders occupied for three to four days. “As far as I’m aware, there is not a park within Australia that has gravity trails anywhere near as long as what we have in Omeo.” Trail length 114km of paths. Difficulty The park has easy, moderate and difficult trails. Charging facilities There are no charging facilities at the park. However in Omeo there are several public charging points including next to the Golden Age hotel and behind the East Gippsland Shire Council building. Comments (…) Sign in or create your Guardian account to join the discussion

item.title: £600 for cheese? The Brazilian beach scams that cost visitors dear
item.description:
Source: The Guardian Travel Score: 3.10
When Lisa Selby* used her debit card to pay for two slices of barbecued cheese from a beach vendor in Rio de Janeiro, she expected to pay 40 reais (£5.90) for the snack. But shortly after the payment had gone through, she realised that she had been charged 4,000 reais (£590) after the vendor added two extra zeros to the card reader. “He showed me the right number on the contactless terminal, but then turned it round to face him and, unbeknownst to me, added two zeros just as I was about to tap with my phone,” she said. “He then gestured that there was no paper for a receipt and walked away.” Holidaymakers have been warned to beware of the crime in Rio. Last month a beach vendor was arrested after a British man was duped into paying £1,500 for a kebab, while an Argentinian tourist discovered a £3 corn on the cob had cost her £3,000. What it looks like Unscrupulous traders take advantage of tourists who are unfamiliar with the local currency and are less likely to notice a doctored sum. A common ploy is to ask the customer to confirm the correct figure on the card reader, then to alter it surreptitiously before the card is presented. Some scammers thrust their card reader at the customer’s card or phone to complete the payment before the customer has checked the total. What to do The scam exposes a gap in UK consumer protection. Customers who are tricked into sending money to criminals by bank transfer in what’s known as authorised push payment fraud are usually entitled to a refund from their bank. However, victims of face-to-face vending scams are unlikely to get their money back unless they can produce evidence that they were overcharged. Selby discovered the fraud shortly after the payment and immediately alerted her bank, Monzo. An agent told her that since the transaction was still pending it would be returned to her. Monzo later admitted that she had been wrongly advised and said that authorised payments cannot be reversed. Her attempts to claim the money via her card issuer’s chargeback scheme, which allows a dispute to be raised with a trader who is in breach of contract, failed because she did not have an invoice or receipt showing the agreed price. Monzo refunded her as a goodwill gesture after contact from Guardian Money. It said that reports of beach vendor scams are increasing but that Selby’s experience is classed as a buyer/seller dispute rather than fraud because she had authorised the card payment. A spokesperson said: “We understand this was a very frustrating experience for the customer. While our reasons for rejecting the claim were correct, we recognise that our communication fell short of our usual high standards.” The Financial Conduct Authority, which regulates UK banks, confirmed that pending transactions cannot usually be reversed, and that chargebacks are a voluntary service offered by card issuers, which are free to decide their own criteria and processes. It said victims may be able to submit a claim to their bank for an unauthorised transaction since they had not consented to the amount that was debited and that they can complain to the Financial Ombudsman Service if they are unhappy with the response. To avoid being caught out, holidaymakers are advised to pay mobile vendors in cash, or to insist on holding the card reader to insert or swipe their card themselves to prevent a last-minute alteration to the price. * Name has been changed

item.title: Mushroom trip: a mycologist’s tour of the Tarkine
item.description:
Source: The Guardian Travel Score: 3.00
Revered as one of Australia’s last true wilderness areas, Takayna/Tarkine is a place of legends. Freshwater crayfish that can reach almost a metre in length lurk in the shade of 2,000-year-old Huon pines, and every few years a rumour emerges that thylacines still prowl the dense Gondwanan rainforest of north-west Tasmania. For 65m years, this landscape has sheltered all manner of astonishing creatures. But some of the most fascinating life forms found here are even older. Before animals walked the Earth or trees began converting carbon dioxide into oxygen, fungi helped to create the conditions necessary for complex life on our planet. “People often say that fungi grow in the forest,” Dr Alison Pouliot, a mycologist, tells me as we inhale cool air perfumed with the gentle spice of sassafras. “But there wouldn’t be a forest without fungi. Fungi are the ecosystem engineers that created the foundation for the forest.” Joining me on a three-day fungi workshop led by Pouliot are toxicologists, botanists and ecologists, but everyone seems united by a sense of wonder when it comes to fungi. After a few hours in their company, it’s easy to see why. Long considered plants by taxonomists, fungi were finally given their own kingdom about 50 years ago, but they remain woefully understudied. Researchers estimate that there are 2-3m species, of which just over 205,000 have been identified, and mushrooms are merely the most visible part of complex organisms connected by vast webs of underground threads called mycelium. These networks, all 100 quadrillion kilometres of them, allow fungi to form life-sustaining symbiotic relationships with as many as 70% of plant species on the planet. “Fungi can be so small they’re invisible to the human eye or inconceivably big,” Pouliot says, citing a specimen in Oregon in the US that covers more than 9 sq km and weighs as much as 30,000 tonnes. But she is not here merely to impart interesting facts. Her interdisciplinary approach explores the vital role fungi play in ecosystems around the world and their importance in environmental restoration. We listen to a Sylvia Plath poem, take “sporeprints” that create photonegative imprints of a mushroom’s underside and examine how language affects the way we view fungi – why does love bloom, but crime mushrooms? In the afternoons, we set out on foraging trips from Corinna Wilderness Village, a former mining town deep in the rainforest that has been converted into a charming eco village. We follow the tannin-stained Pieman River, which flows so slowly the inky black surface forms a perfect mirror, and admire ancient Huon pines bowed low over the water. Pushing through giant ferns that spread across the paths, we walk through stands of majestic leatherwoods, celerytop pines and myrtle beeches whose trunks are completely hidden beneath glistening cloaks of dew-flecked moss, lichen and liverwort. And everywhere we go, the gentle thrum of birdsong is interrupted by cries of delight whenever the group spots a new type of fungi. There are delicate blue pixie’s parasols and fields of ruby bonnets that look like bright red berries scattered across the forest floor, slime-covered earth tongues that resemble worms pushing up through the ground, giant bracket fungi the size of dinner plates and echidna fungi with thousands of spiky teeth beneath their caps. The wild variety of shapes and colours is matched by the incredible density of fungi, and we often cover less than 200 metres an hour. “It’s hard to believe there’s so much diversity in a tiny space,” says Liz Davis, a workshop attender from Orange, who has been foraging for 30 years and started the Mycology May festival in regional New South Wales. “Fungi hunting anywhere else is never going to compare.” Because much of the fungal life remains invisible below ground, Pouliot says we could come here another 100 times and still find different species on each visit. It’s easy to get wrapped up in the joy of spotting these weird and wonderful species, especially given my newfound appreciation of their role as architects of the rainforest. To use the parlance of the group, I quickly become “fungally infected”. And yet part of the shared passion is a sense of outrage that this vital kingdom of life remains so undervalued. Fungi are essential to the survival of almost every ecosystem on the planet, but there is not even an agreed-upon collective noun for fungi (as opposed to mushrooms). My mind goes back to Sylvia Plath’s poem Mushrooms, which celebrates the resilience, strength and sheer inevitability of fungi, seeing in them a metaphor for gender equality. In its conclusion, she declares: “We shall by morning/ Inherit the earth/ Our foot’s in the door.” After three days in a rainforest built on fungal foundations, I’m grateful for our own bountiful inheritance of fungi. Guardian Australia travelled as a guest of Tourism Tasmania and Corinna Wilderness Village Comments (…) Sign in or create your Guardian account to join the discussion

item.title: Best low-annual-fee credit cards with no foreign transaction fees
item.description:
Source: The Points Guy Score: 5.60
Best low-annual-fee credit cards with no foreign transaction fees If you're planning an international trip, one of the easiest ways to save money is by using a credit card that charges no foreign transaction fees. Many credit cards add foreign transaction fees of around 3% every time you make a purchase abroad. While that might not sound like much, those charges can add up quickly over the course of a vacation. Spend $3,000 internationally, for example, and you could end up paying about $90 in extra fees. Fortunately, you don't have to pay a premium annual fee to avoid them. Here are our favorite low-annual-fee credit cards with no foreign transaction fees. How we chose these cards We've selected these cards based on a few key factors: - No foreign transaction fees - Annual fees of $100 or less - Competitive rewards rates and welcome offers - Strong overall value for travelers or everyday spending While there are plenty of premium travel cards that charge no foreign transaction fees, we've focused on affordable options that deliver excellent long-term value without paying a high annual fee. Top cards at a glance - Chase Sapphire Preferred® Card (see rates and fees): Best overall - Capital One Venture Rewards Credit Card: Best for simplicity - Wells Fargo Autograph® Card (see rates and fees): Best no-annual-fee option - Ink Business Preferred® Credit Card (see rates and fees): Best for small business owners - Capital One Savor Cash Rewards Credit Card: Best for dining and entertainment purchases - Discover it® Student Cash Back Credit Card: Best for students - Chase Freedom Flex®* (see rates and fees): Best for rotating bonus categories *No foreign transaction fees on the Chase Freedom Flex begin Sept. 20. The information for the Discover it Student Cash Back has been collected independently by The Points Guy. The card details on this page have not been reviewed or provided by the card issuer. Chase Sapphire Preferred Annual fee: $95 Welcome offer: Earn 75,000 bonus points after spending $5,000 on purchases in the first three months from account opening. Who it's for: The Sapphire Preferred is ideal for travelers seeking a well-rounded rewards card that combines valuable travel perks, such as an up to $100 annual hotel statement credit, with flexible points. Why we picked it: The Sapphire Preferred continues to set the standard for low-annual-fee travel cards. It earns bonus points on travel and dining, offers valuable travel protections and allows cardholders to transfer points to Chase's airline and hotel partners, such as United Airlines, Southwest and Marriott, for potentially outsize value. For travelers who want a single card that does almost everything well, it's hard to beat. To learn more, read our full review of the Chase Sapphire Preferred. Apply: Chase Sapphire Preferred Capital One Venture Rewards Annual fee: $95 Welcome offer: Earn 75,000 bonus miles after spending $4,000 on purchases in the first three months from account opening. Who it's for: The Venture Rewards is best for travelers who prefer earning the same rewards rate on nearly every purchase (instead of tracking bonus categories). Why we picked it: The card earns at least 2 miles per dollar on every purchase, making it one of the simplest travel rewards cards available. It also allows cardholders to redeem miles toward travel purchases or transfer them to Capital One's airline and hotel partners, including Air Canada Aeroplan, Air France-KLM Flying Blue and Wyndham Rewards, giving users flexibility without adding complexity. Like all Capital One credit cards, the Venture Rewards charges no foreign transaction fees, making it a strong option for international travel. To learn more, read our full review of the Capital One Venture Rewards. Wells Fargo Autograph Annual fee: $0 Welcome offer: Earn 20,000 bonus points after spending $1,000 on purchases in the first three months from account opening. Who it's for: The Wells Fargo Autograph is a great fit for travelers who want to avoid both annual fees and foreign transaction fees while still earning bonus rewards. Why we picked it: It's uncommon to find a no-annual-fee card that also charges no foreign transaction fees. The Autograph stands out by earning bonus rewards across several everyday spending categories — including restaurants, travel, transit, gas stations, streaming services and phone plans — making it one of the strongest no-fee travel cards available. To learn more, read our full review of the Wells Fargo Autograph Card. Apply: Wells Fargo Autograph Ink Business Preferred Annual fee: $95 Welcome offer: Earn 100,000 bonus points after spending $8,000 on purchases in the first three months from account opening. Who it's for: The Ink Business Preferred is ideal for small-business owners who regularly travel internationally or make purchases from overseas vendors. Why we picked it: Despite its relatively modest annual fee, the Ink Business Preferred offers premium-style benefits, including valuable travel protections and the ability to transfer Ultimate Rewards points to Chase's travel partners. It's a solid choice for entrepreneurs who want to separate business expenses while incurring no foreign transaction fees. To learn more, read our full review of the Ink Business Preferred. Apply: Ink Business Preferred Capital One Savor Rewards Annual fee: $0 Welcome offer: Earn a $250 cash bonus after spending $500 on purchases in the first three months from account opening. Who it's for: The Capital One Savor Rewards is a strong pick for food lovers, concertgoers and frequent diners who want to maximize everyday rewards without paying an annual fee. Why we picked it: The Savor card shines for dining, entertainment and grocery purchases while charging no annual fee and no foreign transaction fees. Since dining often represents a significant portion of travel spending, it's also a surprisingly solid companion for international trips. To learn more, read our full review of the Capital One Savor Rewards. Discover it Student Cash Back Annual fee: $0 Welcome offer: Earn a $100 statement credit after spending $300 on purchases in the first three months from account opening. Plus, Discover will match all the cash back cardholders earn during their first year with the card. Who it's for: The Discover it Student Cash Back is a top choice for students, those planning to study abroad and first-time credit card users. Why we picked it: The Discover it Student Cash Back combines beginner-friendly features with no annual fee and no foreign transaction fees. It also earns 5% cash back (on up to $1,500 in purchases each quarter; activation required) in rotating bonus categories, which frequently include popular spending categories like restaurants, grocery stores and entertainment (plus 1% cash back on all other purchases). Students traveling internationally or studying abroad can avoid unnecessary fees while building credit and earning rotating cash-back rewards. To learn more, read our full review of the Discover it Student Cash Back. Chase Freedom Flex Annual fee: $0 Welcome offer: Earn a $200 bonus after spending $500 on purchases in the first three months from account opening. Who it's for: The Freedom Flex is best suited for people willing to activate rotating quarterly bonus categories to maximize rewards. Why we picked it: Starting Sept. 20, the Freedom Flex will no longer charge foreign transaction fees, making it an even more compelling no-annual-fee option. Its rotating 5% bonus categories** can deliver exceptional value throughout the year, with past categories including restaurants, grocery stores and gas stations — all of which can come in handy while traveling. It's an especially strong choice for cardholders who already earn Ultimate Rewards points with another Chase card. **On up to $1,500 spent each quarter, then 1%; quarterly activation required. To learn more, read our full review of the Chase Freedom Flex. Apply: Chase Freedom Flex How to pick the right card for you The best no-foreign-transaction-fee card for you depends largely on how you spend. If you want one card for nearly everything, the Chase Sapphire Preferred is hard to beat thanks to its mix of rewards, travel protections and flexible redemption options. Travelers who value simplicity may prefer the Capital One Venture Rewards card, while those looking to avoid annual fees altogether should consider the Wells Fargo Autograph or Capital One Savor. Students and first-time cardholders may find the Discover it Student Cash Back to be the easiest entry point, while business owners should consider the Ink Business Preferred. Related: How to choose a no-foreign-transaction-fee credit card Bottom line Foreign transaction fees are an unnecessary expense that can increase the cost of international travel. Fortunately, you don't need to pay hundreds of dollars each year for a premium travel card to avoid them. Several cards with annual fees under $100 — or no annual fee at all — charge no foreign transaction fees while still offering valuable rewards. Choosing one of these affordable cards means you can spend confidently abroad, avoid unnecessary fees and continue earning rewards on every purchase. Related: 9 types of cards you should pack for your next trip abroad Frequently Asked Questions Foreign transaction fees are extra charges that some credit card issuers add when you make purchases outside the United States or process a transaction in a foreign currency. They're typically charged as a percentage of each purchase. Most foreign transaction fees range from 2% to 3% of the purchase amount. For example, if your card charges a 3% foreign transaction fee, you'd pay an extra $30 on a $1,000 purchase. Yes. Even if you're earning points or cash back, foreign transaction fees can easily outweigh the value of the rewards you earn on international purchases. When a transaction qualifies for a foreign transaction fee, the issuer automatically adds the fee to your statement. If your card doesn't charge foreign transaction fees, you'll simply pay the converted purchase amount.

item.title: How to use the $500 American Airlines Vacations credit on the Citi AAdvantage Executive Card
item.description:
Source: The Points Guy Score: 5.56
How to use the $500 American Airlines Vacations credit on the Citi AAdvantage Executive Card Editor's Note The Citi® / AAdvantage® Executive World Elite Mastercard® (see rates and fees) is adding a new perk that could help offset a significant portion of its annual fee: up to $500 in annual statement credits on eligible American Airlines Vacations purchases. Beginning Aug. 23, cardholders can earn up to $250 in statement credits from January through June and another up to $250 from July through December when booking eligible American Airlines Vacations packages or experiences. The new credit arrives alongside a broader refresh to the card, including an increase in the card's annual fee from $595 to $695, meaning cardholders who maximize the benefit can recoup much of the added cost. Unlike a straightforward airline credit, this perk comes with specific booking requirements. So what qualifies, and how can you get the most value from the credit? Here's what you need to know. What is the American Airlines Vacations credit? Beginning Aug. 23, cardholders of the Citi / AAdvantage Executive can receive up to $500 in annual statement credits on eligible American Airlines Vacations purchases. Rather than one annual credit, the benefit is split into two six-month periods: - Up to $250 in statement credits on eligible purchases made from Jan. 1 through June 30 - Up to $250 in statement credits on eligible purchases made from July 1 through Dec. 31 To receive the credit, you'll need to pay with your Citi / AAdvantage Executive and book an eligible American Airlines Vacations travel package or experience through AAVacations.com. According to Citi, statement credits will typically appear on your account within eight to 10 weeks after the qualifying purchase posts. To be eligible for the benefit, your card must be open and in good standing at the time the statement credit is fulfilled. Related: Is the Citi / AAdvantage Executive World Elite Mastercard worth it? What counts as an eligible purchase? It's important to note that this isn't a general American Airlines travel credit. Purchases made directly through AA.com, including airfare booked on its own, won't qualify. According to the benefit terms, eligible travel packages must include at least two travel components, such as: - A flight and hotel - A flight and rental car - A hotel and rental car The benefit also applies to eligible American Airlines Vacations Experiences booked through the platform. These can include destination activities and excursions, though availability varies by destination. When is this credit actually worth using? The credit is likely most valuable if you: - Already book vacation packages. If you typically bundle your flight and hotel (or rental car), you may be able to earn the credit without changing your travel habits. - Take at least two vacations each year. Since the benefit is split into two $250 biannual credits, travelers who book one eligible trip in each half of the year are best positioned to maximize the full $500. - Don't mind booking through a portal. If American Airlines Vacations offers pricing that's comparable to booking directly with airlines and hotels, the statement credit can provide meaningful savings. However, it's probably less valuable if you: - Usually book flights, hotels and rental cars separately. Bundling isn't always the cheapest option, so forcing yourself to book a package just to earn the credit could erase much of its value. - Primarily travel for business. Many business travelers book airfare and hotels separately or through corporate travel portals, making this benefit harder to use. - Loyal to a hotel or car rental program. Booking through American Airlines Vacations may not offer the same points, elite-night credit or elite benefits as booking directly, so compare the tradeoffs before using the credit. Tips for maximizing the American Airlines Vacations credit Although the new benefit is designed for American Airlines Vacations packages rather than stand-alone flights, there are plenty of ways to incorporate it into trips you may already be planning. Here are a few ideas: - Book a weekend getaway: Bundling your airfare and hotel through American Airlines Vacations could qualify for the statement credit while simplifying your travel planning. If the package is priced competitively, the credit can further reduce your out-of-pocket cost. - Offset the cost of a bigger vacation: If you're already planning a longer trip, booking through American Airlines Vacations could help offset part of the overall cost. Since the credit applies to eligible vacation packages, it can be especially valuable on higher-priced itineraries. - Pair your flight with a rental car: If you'll need a rental car, compare the cost of booking an eligible flight-and-car package through American Airlines Vacations with reserving each component separately. In some cases, packaging your trip may save money once the statement credit is factored in. - Add an experience to your trip: If you're already planning a vacation, check whether an eligible American Airlines Vacations Experience qualifies for the statement credit. Just be sure to compare prices with booking the activity directly, since third-party platforms aren't always the cheapest option. To get the full value of the benefit, remember that it's split into two six-month periods. Book one eligible vacation package between Jan. 1 and June 30 and another between July 1 and Dec. 31 to earn both statement credits. If you only book one qualifying package each year, you'll forfeit the other half of the benefit. As always, compare the package price with the cost of booking flights, hotels, experiences and rental cars separately. American Airlines Vacations packages can sometimes offer competitive pricing, but booking directly may provide better value or additional loyalty benefits. Related: The best travel credit cards Bottom line The new American Airlines Vacations credit is one of the biggest additions to the soon-to-be-refreshed Citi / AAdvantage Executive. While it requires a little more planning than a straightforward airline credit, travelers who already book vacation packages — or are willing to bundle a flight with a hotel or a rental car — could offset up to $500 of the card's annual fee. Just remember that the benefit is split into two biannual credits, so you'll need to use one before June 30 and another before Dec. 31 to unlock the full value. For more information, read our full review of the Citi / AAdvantage Executive World Elite Mastercard. Related: Monthly checklist: Credit card perks and benefits you should be using in August Frequently Asked Questions No. The American Airlines Vacations credit doesn't apply to flights booked directly through AA.com. Instead, you'll need to book an eligible American Airlines Vacations package or experience through AAVacations.com and pay with your eligible card to qualify for the statement credit. No. The benefit is split into two six-month earning periods: up to $250 in statement credits on eligible purchases made between Jan. 1 and June 30, and another up to $250 on eligible purchases made between July 1 and Dec. 31. Even if you book a more expensive vacation package, you can only earn the credit available during the applicable six-month period. To receive the full $500 in annual statement credits, you'll need eligible purchases in both earning windows. Yes. There's no enrollment required to receive the benefit; you can simply pay for an eligible American Airlines Vacations package or experience with your eligible card. According to Citi, statement credits will typically appear within eight to 10 weeks after the qualifying purchase posts, provided your account remains open and in good standing when the credit is issued.

item.title: Book international award flights for 50% off: Alaska Airlines releases August Atmos Rewards Global Getaways deals
item.description:
Source: The Points Guy Score: 5.12
Book international award flights for 50% off: Alaska Airlines releases August Atmos Rewards Global Getaways deals Alaska Airlines offers a little-known way to save up to 50% on award tickets to places like Australia, Fiji, Italy, Japan and French Polynesia. Through the carrier's monthly "Atmos Members Day" promotion, Alaska Airlines Atmos Rewards members have access to special perks, including recurring "Global Getaways" offers. With these, members can score some spectacular deals. Should you take advantage of one (or more) of this month's Global Getaways offers? Here's everything to know about the promotion and how to quickly rack up points for future Global Getaways deals. What are Atmos Rewards' August Global Getaways offers? Routes: Economy award fares are available on flights between the U.S. and select cities in Europe, Asia and the South Pacific, among other destinations. Cost: Short-haul economy awards start at 20,000 points each way. Business-class and premium economy awards are not eligible. Travel dates: Exact dates vary by deal, though some are available on select dates through Feb. 28, 2027. Book by: Aug. 8, 2026. August Global Getaways from the US Alaska Airlines Atmos Rewards' Global Getaways deals for August include transatlantic routes between the U.S. and the following cities (each way): - Edinburgh (from 20,000 points each way in economy) - Madrid (from 20,000 points each way in economy) - Budapest, Hungary (from 25,000 points each way in economy) - Papeete, Tahiti, in French Polynesia (from 25,000 points each way in economy) - Rome (from 25,000 points each way in economy) - Osaka, Japan (from 27,500 points each way in economy) - Nadi, Fiji (from 30,000 points each way in economy) - Hong Kong (from 34,000 points each way in economy) - Sydney (from 35,000 points each way in economy) If any are of interest, you'll need to act fast. You have until Aug. 8 to book. Before booking, remember that the Alaska Airlines Atmos Rewards program offers the ability to add a stopover of up to 14 days for free, so you can essentially get two trips for the price of one. And you can fly with Alaska Airlines' extensive list of partner airlines, too. For example, say you're flying from Seattle to Sydney. A stopover would allow you to stop for a few days (or longer) in a city where you make a connection. So, in this case, a stopover could let you visit Honolulu on your way to Sydney. Here's another example, this time from Los Angeles International Airport (LAX) to Sydney Airport (SYD). It includes a stopover at Fiji's Nadi International Airport (NAN) and requires just 35,000 Atmos Rewards points plus $158 in taxes and fees. That's a fantastic deal for an international trip if you are willing to fly in economy. How to book Atmos Rewards flights Booking Atmos Rewards tickets is fairly straightforward. Simply visit the Alaska Airlines or Hawaiian Airlines website, then log in to your account and click the "Use points" box on the home screen. After, enter your desired itinerary before clicking "Search flights." As you can see in the example below, I was able to quickly find an award on Alaska Airlines' new flight from Seattle-Tacoma International Airport (SEA) to Rome Fiumicino Leonardo da Vinci Airport (FCO) for just 25,000 Atmos Rewards points plus $6 in taxes and fees. That is an incredible value. How to earn Atmos Rewards points There are multiple ways to earn Alaska Airlines Atmos Rewards points. You can, of course, earn them by flying Alaska Airlines or Hawaiian Airlines. The carriers also partner with over 30 airlines, including (but not limited to) members of the Oneworld alliance. Another quick way to accumulate points is to open one of Atmos Rewards' cobranded credit cards: - Atmos™ Rewards Ascent Visa Signature® credit card: Earn 3 points per dollar spent on eligible Alaska Airlines and Hawaiian Airlines purchases; 2 points per dollar spent on cable, at electric vehicle charging and gas stations, on local transit and ride-hailing services, and on select streaming services; and 1 point per dollar spent on all other eligible purchases. - Atmos™ Rewards Visa Signature® Business Card: Earn 3 points per dollar spent on eligible Alaska Airlines and Hawaiian Airlines purchases; 2 points per dollar spent at EV charging and gas stations, on local transit and ride-hailing services, and on shipping purchases; and 1 point per dollar spent on all other eligible purchases. - Atmos™ Rewards Summit Visa Infinite® credit card: Earn 3 points per dollar spent on eligible Alaska Airlines and Hawaiian Airlines purchases, eligible dining purchases and foreign transactions; and 1 point per dollar spent on all other eligible purchases. You can even transfer Bilt Points to Atmos Rewards at a 1:1 ratio. I'm particularly fond of earning points through Alaska Vacations bookings. Atmos Rewards members can access exclusive pricing on hotels, car rentals and more and earn 1 point per dollar spent at nearly 1 million properties worldwide. You'll also earn 1,000 status points for every 3,000 points earned from Alaska Vacations purchases (excluding airfare). Best credit cards to book Atmos Rewards award flights Aside from the cards mentioned above, we also recommend using the following cards for Alaska Airlines purchases, as they offer elevated earnings on airfare purchases, including the taxes and fees charged on award tickets: - American Express Platinum Card®: Earn 5 points per dollar spent on airfare booked directly with the airline or through American Express Travel® (on up to $500,000 on these purchases per calendar year, then 1 point per dollar). - Chase Sapphire Reserve® (see rates and fees): Earn 4 points per dollar spent on flights booked directly with the airline. - Wells Fargo Autograph Journey℠ Card (see rates and fees): Earn 4 points per dollar spent on airline purchases. - American Express® Gold Card: Earn 3 points per dollar spent on airfare when booked directly with the airline, through amextravel.com or via the Amex Travel App™. - Chase Sapphire Preferred® Card (see rates and fees): Earn 2 points per dollar spent on travel purchases made outside of the Chase Travel℠ portal. Related: Which credit card should you use for Alaska Airlines flights? Bottom line Alaska Airlines is really stepping up its recurring Atmos Members Day promotion with monthly Global Getaways that can offer terrific value on award redemptions. If you've had your eye on some of the incredible destinations on offer this month, including Rome, Budapest and Sydney — and are willing to fly in economy — jump on this offer before it ends Aug. 8. item.title: Up to $1,600 in value: Marriott Bonvoy credit card welcome offers ranked
item.description:
Source: The Points Guy Score: 4.84

Below, we break down the current offers and help you decide which Marriott card might be worth it. Comparison of Marriott credit card welcome offers Marriott Bonvoy loyalists can choose from card options issued by American Express and Chase. There are multiple personal cards and one business card available. Make sure you're eligible for a business card before applying.
