The information for the Marriott Bonvoy Bountiful Credit Card has been collected independently by The Points Guy. The card details on this page have not been reviewed or provided by the card issuer. Related: Which credit card should you use for Marriott stays? Marriott Bonvoy Boundless The Marriott Bonvoy Boundless Credit Card is one of Chase's two mid-tier Bonvoy cards. Annual fee: $95 Welcome offer: Earn four free night awards (valued at up to 50,000 points each) after spending $3,000 on purchases in the first three months from account opening. Additionally, you can receive up to $100 in statement credits (up to $50 biannually) after spending $500 on eligible airline purchases. Certain hotels have resort fees. If you maximize the free night award and earn the statement credits for airline purchases, this bonus is worth up to $1,600. This is one of the better offers we've seen on the card, the only better welcome bonus we've tracked included five free night awards (no longer available) making this an excellent time to apply if you've been considering the card. THE POINTS GUY Earning rates: Cardholders earn: - 6 points per dollar spent at Marriott hotels (Earn up to 17 points per dollar spent on eligible Marriott stays: 10 points from being a Bonvoy member, 6 points from this card and 10% bonus points from the Silver elite status the card provides, which equates to a total 12.8% return on spending based on TPG's valuations) - 3 points per dollar spent on the first $6,000 spent in combined purchases each year on dining and at gas stations and grocery stores - 2 points per dollar spent on all other purchases Why we like it: The Boundless gives you great Marriott perks without paying a high annual fee. With this card, you'll get automatic Bonvoy Silver Elite status and 15 elite qualifying nights every year. You'll also earn one elite night credit toward the next level of elite status for every $5,000 spent, and you can reach Gold Elite status by spending $35,000 on the card in a calendar year. Perhaps the most valuable perk is the annual free night award (worth up to 35,000 points) at each account anniversary, though Marriott's lack of award charts could hinder your ability to use this benefit. Fortunately, this free night award can be topped up with up to 25,000 points from your Bonvoy account for a total of 60,000 points per night. Certain hotels have resort fees. To learn more, read our full review of the Marriott Bonvoy Boundless card. Apply here: Marriott Bonvoy Boundless Credit Card Marriott Bonvoy Business The Marriott Bonvoy Business American Express Card is Marriott's only business card currently available to new applicants. Annual fee: $125 Welcome offer: Earn up to 125,000 bonus points: 75,000 bonus points after spending $6,000 on purchases in the first six months of card membership, plus 50,000 bonus points after spending an additional $3,000 ($9,000 total) on purchases in the first six months of card membership. According to TPG's valuations, this bonus is worth up to $938. This matches one of the better offers we've seen on the card, so now is a good time to apply if you've been considering it. Earning rates: Cardmembers earn: - 6 points per dollar spent on Marriott hotels (Earn up to 18.5 total points per dollar spent on eligible Marriott stays: 10 points from being a Bonvoy member, 6 points from this card and 25% bonus points from the Gold elite status the card provides, which equates to about a 13.9% return on spending based on TPG's valuations) - 4 points per dollar spent at restaurants worldwide and U.S. gas stations and on wireless telephone services from U.S. service providers and U.S. shipping purchases - 2 points per dollar spent on all other purchases Why we like it: With this card, you'll get automatic Gold Elite status with Marriott Bonvoy and a 7% discount on eligible bookings made directly with Marriott through an eligible channel at participating properties with this card's rate. The card also comes with 15 elite night credits annually (which can be stacked with a Marriott Bonvoy consumer card) and a free night award annually after your card renewal month (worth up to 35,000 points and can be topped up with up to 25,000 points from your Bonvoy account for a total of 60,000 points per night). In addition, you can earn a second free night (also worth up to 35,000 points) after $60,000 of purchases on your card in a calendar year. Certain hotels have resort fees. Marriott's use of dynamic pricing may make it hard to use these awards. Still, you should be able to find a participating property that can cover your annual fee (and then some), as our data indicates there's still significant value in the program. To learn more, read our full review of the Amex Marriott Bonvoy Business. Apply here: Marriott Bonvoy Business American Express Card Marriott Bonvoy Brilliant The Marriott Bonvoy Brilliant American Express Card is Marriott's top-tier card. Annual fee: $650 Welcome offer: For a limited time, earn 150,000 bonus points and a $250 statement credit after spending $6,000 on purchases in the first six months from account opening. Offer ends Sept. 30. Based on TPG's valuations, this offer is worth $1,375, including the statement credit. This is better than the standard offer we typically see in the card's history, but we'd recommend waiting for a higher offer of at least 185,000 points. Earning rates: Cardmembers earn: - 6 points per dollar spent at Marriott hotels (Earn up to 21 total points per dollar spent on eligible Marriott stays: 10 points from being a Bonvoy member, 6 points from this card and 50% bonus points from the Platinum elite status the card provides, which equates to a 15.8% return on spending based on TPG's valuations). - 3 points per dollar spent at restaurants worldwide and on flights booked directly with airlines - 2 points per dollar spent on other eligible purchases Why we like it: The card also has valuable perks, such as automatic Platinum Elite status, an annual free night award (worth up to 85,000 points; certain hotels have resort fees) after card renewal month, up to $300 per year (up to $25 in monthly statement credits) for eligible purchases at restaurants worldwide, Priority Pass™ lounge access and 25 elite qualifying night credits per year. Enrollment is required for select benefits. Remember that Marriott uses dynamic pricing, so you may need to work harder to find a property where you can use your free nights. But you can top up free night awards with up to 25,000 points now, which allows you to book a night worth up to 110,000 points. To learn more, read our full review of the Amex Marriott Bonvoy Brilliant. Apply here: Marriott Bonvoy Brilliant American Express Card Marriott Bonvoy Bevy The Marriott Bonvoy Bevy American Express Card is Bonvoy's mid-tier card from American Express. It has earnings, benefits and an annual fee that mirror the Bountiful. Annual fee: $250 Welcome offer: For a limited time, earn 125,000 bonus points and a $150 statement credit after spending $5,000 on purchases in the first six months from account opening. Offer ends Sept. 30. This bonus is worth $1,088 (including the statement credit), per TPG's valuations. This is better than the standard offer we see in the card's history, but we'd recommend waiting for a higher offer of at least 155,000 points. Earning rates: Cardmembers earn: - 6 points per dollar spent at Marriott hotels (Earn up to 18.5 points per dollar spent on eligible Marriott stays: 10 points from being a Bonvoy member, 6 points from this card and 25% bonus points from the Gold elite status the card provides, which equates to a 13.9% return on spending based on TPG's valuations). - 4 points per dollar spent on the first $15,000 per calendar year in combined purchases at restaurants worldwide and U.S. supermarkets (then 2 points per dollar spent thereafter) - 2 points per dollar spent on other eligible purchases Why we like it: This card also offers mid-tier perks, including complimentary Gold Elite status, a solid earning rate at Marriott properties and elite night credits. However, it lacks several benefits that you might expect from a mid-tier card. For example, you must spend $15,000 in a calendar year to earn a free night (worth up to 50,000 points; certain hotels have resort fees). Other Marriott cards with lower annual fees include a similar perk with no spending requirement, making this card tough to justify holding beyond earning the welcome offer in the first year. To learn more, read our full review of the Amex Marriott Bonvoy Bevy. Apply here: Marriott Bonvoy Bevy American Express Card Marriott Bonvoy Bountiful The Marriott Bonvoy Bountiful is the other mid-tier Bonvoy card from Chase. Annual fee: $250 Welcome offer: Earn 85,000 bonus points after spending $4,000 on purchases in the first three months from account opening. Based on TPG's valuations, this offer is worth $638. This is typically the standard welcome offer we see in the card's history. Unless you absolutely need this card now, you're better off applying when the offer is higher. Earning rates: Cardholders earn: - 6 points per dollar spent at Marriott hotels (Earn up to 18.5 points per dollar spent on eligible Marriott stays: 10 points from being a Bonvoy member, 6 points from this card and 25% bonus points from the Gold elite status the card provides, which equates to a 13.9% return on spending based on TPG's valuations) - 4 points per dollar spent at restaurants and grocery stores (on the first $15,000 per calendar year in combined purchases, then 2 points per dollar spent thereafter) - 2 points per dollar spent on all other purchases Why we like it: While American Express issues the Bevy, the Bountiful comes from Chase. The two cards offer mostly the same benefits, making it hard to justify the Bountiful's $250 annual fee. However, the welcome bonus may be of interest to you. To learn more, read our full review of the Marriott Bonvoy Bountiful card. Marriott Bonvoy Bold The Marriott Bonvoy Bold Credit Card is Chase's entry-level card for Bonvoy enthusiasts. Annual fee: $0 Welcome offer: Earn 45,000 bonus points after spending $1,000 on purchases in the first three months from account opening. The bonus points are worth $338, according to TPG's valuations. This is slightly higher than the standard welcome offer we've seen on the card, but we'd still suggest waiting for a more rewarding bonus if your timeline is flexible. Earning rates: Cardholders earn: - 3 points per dollar spent at Marriott hotels (Earn up to 14 points per dollar spent on eligible Marriott stays: 10 points from being a Bonvoy member, 3 points from this card and 10% bonus points from the Silver elite status the card provides, which equates to a 10.5% return on spending based on TPG's valuations) - 2 points per dollar spent at grocery stores and on ride-hailing services, select food delivery, select streaming, internet, cable and phone services - 1 point per dollar spent on all other purchases Why we like it: The card offers automatic Bonvoy Silver Elite status and five annual elite night credits. It also charges no foreign transaction fees. Additionally, the Bold features Chase's Pay Yourself Back, allowing you to redeem points toward eligible travel purchases made directly with airlines or Marriott Bonvoy hotels (up to $750 in total redemptions per year). This is a solid set of perks for a card with no annual fee. However, frequent Marriott guests may do better with a card that offers more perks during each stay. To learn more, read our full review of the Marriott Bonvoy Bold card. Apply here: Marriott Bonvoy Bold Credit Card Can you apply for more than one Marriott card offer? If multiple Marriott card offers intrigue you, you can indeed have more than one open Marriott card. Some TPG staffers have two or three. It can make sense to leverage the annual anniversary award nights and stack the 5 to 25 elite nights awarded by carrying both a personal and a small-business Marriott card. However, with six Marriott cards available to new applicants, there are several restrictions on who can earn the welcome offers across the cards, especially since Marriott cards are issued by both Amex and Chase. Note that these restrictions are all in addition to Chase's 5/24 rule (which applies to new applicants for the Bold, Boundless and Bountiful cards) and Amex's one-bonus-per-lifetime rule (which applies to the Bevy, Brilliant and Business cards). Make sure you're eligible for these offers before applying. Related: Here's how to calculate your Chase 5/24 standing Bottom line Marriott credit cards regularly rank among the best hotel credit cards thanks to the long-term value they offer through perks such as elite status and annual free night awards. Several Marriott credit cards are currently offering compelling welcome bonuses, making now an excellent time to apply if you've been considering one. The Boundless boasts the strongest offer of the bunch, while the Brilliant and Bevy are also available with above-average bonuses (through Sept. 30). Unless you need them right away, we'd wait for better offers on the Bountiful and Bold. Apply here: Marriott Bonvoy Boundless Apply here: Marriott Bonvoy Business Amex Apply here: Marriott Bonvoy Brilliant Apply here: Marriott Bonvoy Bevy Learn more: Marriott Bonvoy Bountiful review Apply here: Marriott Bonvoy Bold For rates and fees of the Marriott Bonvoy Business card, click here. For rates and fees of the Marriott Bonvoy Brilliant card, click here. For rates and fees of the Marriott Bonvoy Bevy card, click here.

item.title: Wells Fargo Travel portal: What to know before booking
item.description:
Source: The Points Guy Score: 4.33
Wells Fargo Travel portal: What to know before booking If you're a Wells Fargo cardholder, you may want to get familiar with the Wells Fargo Travel portal. The Wells Fargo Travel portal provides cardholders with access to book flights, hotels, car rentals and activities. You can redeem your Wells Fargo Rewards points, use your card to pay or combine the two. You can also earn bonus points when you book certain types of travel through the portal, depending on the card you hold. We found a few pleasant surprises and a few quirks you'll want to know about before booking. What is the Wells Fargo Travel portal? The Wells Fargo Travel portal is an online booking platform for eligible Wells Fargo cardholders. The Wells Fargo Travel portal operates similarly to competitors' portals and includes a lesser-known version of a luxury hotel program that offers cardholders additional perks at select high-end properties. Which cards can access the Wells Fargo Travel portal? Any Wells Fargo credit card that earns Wells Fargo Rewards points or cash rewards can access the portal. Eligible cards that are open to applicants now include: - Wells Fargo Active Cash® Card (see rates and fees) - Wells Fargo Autograph® Card (see rates and fees) - Wells Fargo Autograph Journey℠ Card (see rates and fees) - Wells Fargo Signify Business Cash® Card (see rates and fees) Related: A guide to the Wells Fargo Trifecta: Maximize earnings with 3 cards What can you book in the Wells Fargo Travel portal? The Wells Fargo Travel portal allows you to book flights, hotels, rental cars and activities. To access it, simply log in to your Wells Fargo account, navigate to your rewards dashboard and launch the Travel portal. Here's what stood out during our testing. Flights TPG editor in chief Nick Ewen and contributing editor for credit cards Matt Moffitt noted some challenges when searching for flights on the Wells Fargo Travel portal. First, the initial search results for a flight didn't clearly identify the type of fare class you're booking (basic economy, regular economy, business, etc.). To see different fare options, travelers have to click "View Details," then "Fare Options" to compare what's available. As Nick navigated the portal, he didn't initially see Delta Main Classic as an option for a flight from Orlando to New York, but it appeared later in the booking process. Once Nick reached the "Review Your Trip" page, he noticed the two nonstop flights were booked into Delta Main Basic. This was the first time he noticed that the fare class was explicitly listed. Nick noticed a "View Upgrade Options" button, which led him to the full list of fare classes. Until now, it was hit-or-miss whether each fare class would be displayed. As both Nick and Matt navigated the booking process, they noticed that a random Known Traveler Number was automatically populated. In both cases, the number shown was not close to their actual KTN. It's worth double-checking this information before completing your booking. Hotels The process for booking a hotel proved to be much smoother. Once you've selected a hotel you'd like to book, you can view the price in cash or points, as with flights. Like flights, hotels can be booked with cash, points or a combination of the two. Wells Fargo Rewards points are worth a flat 1 cent each when redeemed through the portal. There is a field to enter your hotel loyalty program number for your booking, but it's untested whether or not it actually links your stay to your loyalty account. One pleasant surprise was Wells Fargo's Preferred Partner Hotels collection. Nick noticed 23 hotels listed as a "Preferred Partner Hotel." These properties tended to be higher-end luxury hotels, such as Langham, Nobu, Pendry, Ritz-Carlton, St. Regis and Waldorf Astoria. If you book with these hotels through the Wells Fargo Travel portal, you receive benefits such as: - Complimentary breakfast for two - Room upgrades (subject to availability) - Early check-in (when available) - Late checkout (when available) Nick was especially surprised to find that his no-annual-fee Wells Fargo Autograph included access to the issuer's luxury hotel program. Matt, who carries the $95 Wells Fargo Autograph Journey, also had access to these bookings. Car rentals and activities You can also book car rentals and activities in the Wells Fargo Travel portal. Searching and pricing these travel purchases is similar to flights and hotels. The booking process is straightforward, but as with any third-party travel portal, it's worth comparing prices with booking directly. If you normally receive elite benefits with companies like National or Enterprise, those perks may not apply when reservations are made through the portal. Related: 6 key tools and tips to find the cheapest airfare Should you book with points or cash? Whether paying with points or cash makes more sense depends on your travel goals. Wells Fargo Rewards points are worth 1 cent each when redeemed through the Wells Fargo Travel portal. For example, a $200 flight would cost 20,000 points to redeem. This may not always be the best return for your rewards. TPG's August 2026 valuations place Wells Fargo Rewards points at 1.75 cents apiece when you leverage the issuer's transfer partners. These partners include Air France-KLM Flying Blue, British Airways Club and Virgin Atlantic Flying Club. We generally recommend transferring your points to partners to get maximum value. However, if you're sitting on a large haul of points or you're looking for the simplest redemption option, going through the Wells Fargo Travel portal may be worth it for you. If you book through the Wells Fargo Travel portal with an eligible Wells Fargo card, you may earn bonus points on that purchase depending on the card's bonus categories. For example, with the Wells Fargo Autograph, you'll earn 3 points per dollar spent on travel booked through the portal (including airfare, hotels and car rentals). If maximizing rewards is your goal, you're generally better off paying in cash through the portal and saving your Wells Fargo Rewards points for redemptions with transfer partners. Related: Wells Fargo Rewards adds Cathay Pacific Asia Miles as a transfer partner Bottom line The Wells Fargo Travel portal is an easy way to book flights, hotels, rental cars and activities using either cash or Wells Fargo Rewards points. Our testing uncovered a few quirks, particularly around flight bookings and fare selection, but we were pleasantly surprised by the portal's Preferred Partner Hotels collection, which delivers luxury hotel perks even on some no-annual-fee Wells Fargo cards. If you value simplicity, the Wells Fargo Travel portal is a solid option, offering a fixed redemption value of 1 cent per point. And if you pay with an eligible Wells Fargo card instead of redeeming points, you'll continue earning rewards based on your card's bonus categories. However, if maximizing the value of your Wells Fargo Rewards points is your priority, you'll generally get more by transferring them to one of Wells Fargo's airline partners rather than redeeming them through the portal.

item.title: 7 years in the making: Delta will return to former Tokyo Narita hub in 2027
item.description:
Source: The Points Guy Score: 4.25
7 years in the making: Delta will return to former Tokyo Narita hub in 2027 Seven years later, Delta Air Lines is returning to Narita. Next spring, Delta will bring back nonstop service to the Tokyo airport from Seattle-Tacoma International Airport (SEA). It'll give the carrier two nonstop Tokyo routes from SeaTac when the daily flights begin on March 27, 2027. But the route will have bigger symbolic meaning for the Atlanta-based carrier. The flight will mark Delta's return to Narita Airport (NRT) for the first time since the early days of the COVID-19 pandemic. Returning to Narita Rewind to the early 2010s and Narita was a linchpin in Delta's Pacific network. And its place in the company's heritage stretches back even further, thanks to the robust network previously operated there by Northwest Airlines — which Delta acquired in 2008. Delta had nonstop Narita service from the U.S. as well as a host of "fifth-freedom" flights from the airport to destinations in Asia and the South Pacific — including places like Manila to Singapore, Guam, Shanghai and Taipei. But over the course of the 2010s, Delta whittled down its Narita network in favor of Haneda Airport (HND), which is much closer to the city center. And over that same time, Delta also deepened its ties with Korean Air and Seoul's Incheon Airport (ICN) Tokyo Narita vs. Haneda: Which airport should I fly into? Delta's Seattle-Tokyo Narita route Now, Narita is coming back — and so is a route Delta previously operated from Seattle. The carrier plans to continue operating SEA-Haneda flights, noting this Narita route will "complement" the service to HND. "Japan continues to be one of the most important and beloved destinations in Delta's global network, and adding Seattle–Narita service gives our customers even more choice when planning their travel," Jeff Arinder, the carrier's vice president of international network planning, said in a statement announcing the news Thursday. Swimming with Mount Fuji in the distance: A tranquil stay at Tokyo's first JW Marriott hotel Delta will operate the daily SEA-NRT service with an Airbus A330-900neo, which sports the following seat layout by cabin: - 29 Delta One suites - 28 Delta Premium Select (premium economy) recliners - 56 Delta Comfort (extra legroom) seats - 168 economy seats Pacific expansion continues This is just the latest Pacific route Delta has announced from the West Coast. Earlier this summer, the airline revealed nonstop Manila service launching in 2027 from its hub at Los Angeles International Airport (LAX). In June, it launched Hong Kong flights from LAX. Specific to Tokyo, here's what Delta's route map will look like come next spring, as shown by Cirium. You can see the routes to Haneda on the first image. And then, swipe right to see the new (or - "returning," I suppose) Narita route from SEA. More Tokyo service Delta's newest Tokyo route likely won't quell any tension with its top SeaTac competitor — hometown carrier Alaska Airlines. As part of Alaska's global expansion, the airline now operates nonstop Seattle-Narita service itself with a beautiful new Boeing 787-9 Dreamliner obtained via its 2024 acquisition of Hawaiian Airlines. Narita Airport is located farther outside the Tokyo city center than Haneda, but has a wide array of international service. Beyond the proximity to the city, the biggest downside for Delta flyers at NRT? No Sky Club. Haneda is home to Delta's only lounge located outside the U.S. However, Delta passengers should have no problem using the Korean Air Lounge at NRT that belongs to its SkyTeam alliance partner. item.title: Book flights to Europe starting at 18,750 miles: Check out Flying Blue’s August Promo Rewards
item.description:
Source: The Points Guy Score: 4.06
Book flights to Europe starting at 18,750 miles: Check out Flying Blue’s August Promo Rewards Editor's Note You have plenty of options when it comes to booking award flights, but one of the most reliable ways to get good value is through the monthly Air France-KLM Flying Blue Promo Rewards offers. You can find these monthly discounts on this regularly updated page on the Flying Blue website. If you're planning a trip to or from Europe, this month's Flying Blue Promo Rewards deal is worth considering. What is Flying Blue's August award promotion? Airlines: Air France and KLM. Routes: Economy award fares are available on flights between select European cities and between Europe and select destinations in North America, the Caribbean, South America, Asia and Africa. Premium economy and business-class seats are also available on select routes. Cost: Short-haul economy awards start at 7,500 miles each way, and short-haul business-class awards start at 18,750 miles each way. Long-haul economy awards start at 18,750 miles each way, and long-haul premium economy awards start at 30,000 miles each way. Long-haul business-class awards start at 63,750 miles each way. Travel dates: Through Jan. 31, 2027. Book by: Aug. 31. August Promo Rewards between the US and Europe The August Flying Blue Promo Rewards promotion includes transatlantic routes between Europe and the following U.S. cities (in both directions): - Dallas (from 18,750 miles each way in economy) - Houston (from 30,000 miles each way in premium economy) - Las Vegas (from 30,000 miles each way in premium economy) - New York (from 30,000 miles each way in premium economy) - Phoenix (from 18,750 miles each way in economy) - San Diego (from 30,000 miles each way in premium economy) - San Francisco (from 30,000 miles each way in premium economy) - Seattle (from 18,750 miles each way in economy) - Washington, D.C. (from 30,000 miles each way in premium economy) - Los Angeles (from 18,750 miles each way in economy; available exclusively for Flying Blue Extra members) - Miami (from 18,750 miles each way in economy; available exclusively for Flying Blue Extra members) - Orlando (from 18,750 miles each way in economy; available exclusively for Flying Blue Extra members) If you'd like to plan a longer trip, additional routes are also on sale between Europe and other destinations. Promo Rewards are only available on flights operated by Air France and KLM. So, although you can fly to other destinations within Europe as part of a Promo Rewards ticket, you will need to connect through Paris or Amsterdam. You can book most Promo Rewards tickets online, but you must call the program at 800-375-8723 to use Flying Blue's free stopover option. Related: Travel to Europe using points and miles: How to redeem your rewards for flights How to book Flying Blue Promo Rewards flights Book Promo Rewards tickets on the Air France or KLM website. Log in to your account, then click the "Book with Miles" tab on the home screen. After, enter your desired itinerary before clicking "Search flights." If you don't see a Promo Rewards option on your desired travel date, look at surrounding dates for a price that matches the Promo Rewards rate. Once you find a flight you'd like to book, select it and follow the onscreen prompts to complete your reservation. If you plan to transfer credit card rewards to book a flight, make sure you find award space first; then, place your ticket on hold and transfer your points or miles. Also, be sure to check your transferable rewards accounts to see if any transfer bonuses are available. Related: How to find the cheapest redemption rates using Flying Blue miles How to earn Flying Blue miles Boosting your Flying Blue balance is easy because the program partners with major programs that have transferable points and miles. You can transfer rewards at a 1:1 ratio from American Express Membership Rewards, Bilt, Capital One, Chase Ultimate Rewards, Citi ThankYou Rewards, Rove and Wells Fargo Rewards. You can also transfer Marriott Bonvoy points at a 3:1 ratio, with a 5,000-mile bonus for every 60,000 points you transfer. Based on our tests, Amex, Bilt, Capital One, Chase, Citi and Wells Fargo transfers should post almost instantly. However, our test transfer from Marriott took three days to arrive in our Flying Blue account. TPG has not tested Rove transfer times. Because of this, points and miles from the other providers listed are your best bet if you hope to book right away. Best credit cards to book Flying Blue award flights We recommend using a card that earns bonus rewards on airfare purchases to pay the taxes and fees on your award ticket. Some of the best cards include: - American Express Platinum Card®: Earn 5 points per dollar spent on airfare booked directly with the airline or through American Express Travel® (on up to $500,000 on these purchases per calendar year, then 1 point per dollar). - Chase Sapphire Reserve® (see rates and fees): Earn 4 points per dollar spent on flights booked directly with the airline. - American Express® Gold Card: Earn 3 points per dollar spent on airfare when booked directly with the airline, through amextravel.com or the Amex Travel App. - Chase Sapphire Preferred® Card (see rates and fees): Earn 2 points per dollar spent on travel purchases (outside of the Chase Travel℠ portal). - Wells Fargo Autograph Journey℠ Card (see rates and fees): Earn 4 points per dollar spent on airline purchases. Bottom line Few sales are as reliable as the Promo Rewards we see each month from Air France-KLM Flying Blue. Best of all, boosting your Flying Blue balance is easy since the program partners with all major transferable rewards programs. If you're planning a trip to Europe, check whether this promotion works for you. Related reading:

item.title: American Express Gold checklist: 5 things to do when you get the card
item.description:
Source: The Points Guy Score: 4.06
American Express Gold checklist: 5 things to do when you get the card Editor's Note A few years ago, I applied for the American Express® Gold Card, which has since become one of my favorite rewards cards. It offers a high earning rate on dining at restaurants worldwide and U.S. supermarkets, as well as statement credits that more than cover its annual fee. Here are five things to do when you get your new card to make its $325 annual fee worth it (see rates and fees). Activate your dining and Uber benefits With the Amex Gold, you are eligible for up to $10 in monthly statement credits (up to $120 each calendar year) when you use your card at participating dining partners. These partners include Buffalo Wild Wings, The Cheesecake Factory, Five Guys, Grubhub and Wonder. You need to enroll your card for this perk on the Amex site or through the Amex mobile app under "Benefits," so do that as soon as you get your new card. The Amex Gold also offers up to $120 in annual Uber Cash each calendar year, distributed in up to $10 monthly increments. These credits can be used for Uber rides and Uber Eats orders in the U.S. Unlike the monthly up-to-$10 dining credit, which operates as a statement credit when used, this credit deposits up to $10 into your Uber account each month. If you don't use this Uber Cash by the end of the month, it will disappear. For this magic to happen, you must set up your Amex Gold card in your Uber account in the payment section and then pay with any Amex card. Here's a full guide walking you through how to set up and use your Amex Gold Uber credits; it's really easy once you get the card linked to your Uber account. Finally, in celebration of the Amex Gold's 60th anniversary, the card includes a one-time statement credit of up to $96 for an annual Uber One membership (enrollment required; enroll by Oct. 30). Related: A complete guide to the Amex Gold dining credit Maximize your Resy and Dunkin' statement credits Cardmembers can receive up to $100 in Resy credits per calendar year (split into two biannual statement credits of up to $50 each) to use at U.S. Resy restaurants. The Resy credit is generally easy to use, especially if you live in or near a major U.S. city. You just need to pay your bill with your enrolled Amex Gold card at any Resy-enrolled restaurant. No reservation is required. In addition to the Resy credit, cardmembers receive up to $84 in Dunkin' credits each calendar year to use at U.S. Dunkin' locations, issued in up to $7 monthly increments (enrollment required). You must pay for your Dunkin' order with your Amex Gold card to use this credit. As with the other benefits, you can't roll over any unused portion. If you don't live near a Dunkin' location, you can reload your Dunkin' account with $7 each month to use this statement credit. Related: Why Chase needs a competitor to the Amex Gold Make the Amex Gold your default Grubhub payment method If you use the food delivery service Grubhub, set your payment card as the Amex Gold to earn 4 points per dollar on dining at restaurants on the app (up to $50,000 per calendar year, then 1 point per dollar). This is an easy way to use the up to $10 monthly statement credit available to eligible dining partners (up to $120 each calendar year; enrollment required). Since a standard Grubhub+ membership costs $9.99 each month, you can use your Amex Gold's dining credit to pay for this charge. If you use Grubhub frequently, enrolling in Grubhub+ and paying for the membership with this statement credit may be worthwhile. This is how TPG credit cards editor Olivia Mittak uses her monthly dining credit. Related: A trick for using your $10 Amex dining credit Learn the card's bonus categories The Amex Gold sits at the top of the pack for spending on dining at restaurants worldwide and at U.S. supermarkets. The card earns 4 valuable Amex Membership Rewards points per dollar spent on dining at restaurants worldwide (up to $50,000 per calendar year, then 1 point per dollar) and at U.S. supermarkets (up to $25,000 per calendar year, then 1 point per dollar thereafter). Based on TPG's August 2026 valuations, these 4 points per dollar equal an 8% return on spending. This includes earning 4 bonus points for grocery delivery services like Instacart, in case you prefer to have your groceries delivered to your doorstep. The Amex Gold is also a great card when you need to split a dining bill with friends, as you can swipe your card and earn 4 points per dollar on the whole bill. Then, you can use the Amex Send & Split feature (enrollment required) to get reimbursed by your friends without anyone paying Venmo or PayPal fees. Related: 5 under-the-radar ways to maximize the Amex Gold's dining credits Claim your Hertz elite status The Amex Gold provides complimentary Hertz Gold+ Five Star status to cardmembers who enroll in the benefit and register with the program. Hertz Gold+ Five Star status includes: - Elevated points earning in the Hertz program on each rental - Eligibility for a one-class car upgrade (if the Hertz location you're renting from has cars in stock) - Access to a wider range of cars when renting from a Hertz location with an Ultimate Choice lot Bottom line There aren't as many tasks to complete when you get your Amex Gold as when you get an American Express Platinum Card®. However, there are still at least five things to do to reap the maximum rewards and perks from the powerful Amex Gold. To learn more, check out our full review of the American Express Gold. item.title: Complete guide to authorized users on the Amex Platinum Card
item.description:
Source: The Points Guy Score: 3.92
Complete guide to authorized users on the Amex Platinum Card Editor's Note You might want to add authorized users to your travel credit cards for many reasons. For example, your authorized users can help you hit a minimum spending requirement to earn a welcome offer, or you might want to build your child's credit history early on. But some cards also offer authorized users many of the same benefits as the primary cardmember. The American Express Platinum Card® is one of the most popular cards for authorized user benefits. In this guide, we'll consider the various perks that could still make adding authorized users to your Amex Platinum worthwhile. Overview of Amex Platinum authorized users The Amex Platinum comes with an $895 annual fee (see rates and fees) and has so many benefits that it's often referred to as a "membership card" (in some circles) — a card that you keep for its benefits rather than its earning potential. Right now, you can find out your offer and see if you're eligible for as high as 175,000 bonus points after spending $12,000 on purchases within the first six months of card membership. (Welcome offers vary, and you may not be eligible for an offer.) However, unlike some other premium travel cards, adding authorized users to the Amex Platinum incurs an additional cost. You can add children as authorized users, but American Express requires them to be at least 13 years old. American Express can report positive account history for additional cardmembers once they turn 18, which may help them build credit. Amex also offers additional non-Platinum cards, known as companion Platinum cards, that you can add to your account. These cards don't carry annual fees (see rates and fees) but feature very limited benefits. Adding authorized users to your Amex Platinum will incur an additional $195 annual fee per authorized user (see rates and fees). Let's explore the perks authorized users enjoy to determine whether this cost is worth it. Related: Authorized user on a company credit card: What to know Which Amex Platinum benefits apply to additional cardmembers? Here's a rundown of the key benefits that additional Amex Platinum cardmembers will enjoy. As noted above, these apply only to authorized user Amex Platinum cards, not to companion cards. Lounge access The first key benefit that extends to additional Amex Platinum cardmembers is lounge access, even when traveling without the primary cardmember. The American Express Global Lounge Collection includes several networks for eligible cardmembers, including American Express Centurion Lounges, Priority Pass lounges (enrollment required) Delta Sky Clubs on same-day Delta flights (limited to 10 annual visits) and Plaza Premium lounges. American Express doesn't allow most Amex Platinum cardmembers to bring in two complimentary guests when visiting Centurion Lounges. Instead, it'll cost you $50 per adult guest and $30 per child aged 2-17 (children under 2 are free). There are two ways to avoid this guest fee. First, you can charge $75,000 on your Platinum Card in a calendar year, unlocking the previous benefit of bringing in two guests. Alternatively, if you frequently travel with your spouse (or children over 12), you can add them as authorized users. Note that Centurion Lounges aren't the only ones that can be difficult or expensive to access for Platinum cardmembers. If you hold the Amex Platinum, you can enter the Sky Club if you're traveling on a same-day Delta-operated flight (limited to 10 annual visits; passengers traveling on Delta Main Basic fares are not eligible). The fee for bringing guests with you is $50 each time you visit. However, you can avoid these charges altogether when adding additional Platinum cardmembers to your account. If your authorized user would otherwise pay the $50 guest fee to access Centurion Lounges or Delta Sky Clubs, the $195 authorized user fee effectively pays for itself after four lounge visits per year. Of course, this won't help families with children under 12 (like mine). My daughter can't be added as an authorized user to my card. However, the $50 guest fee at Delta Sky Clubs should trigger my Platinum Card's up to $200 per calendar year airline fee statement credit since I've designated Delta as my eligible carrier (enrollment required). Finally, it's worth pointing out that you must enroll in Priority Pass to be eligible to access Priority Pass lounges (you can get into the other lounges in the American Express Global Lounge Collection by simply showing your Platinum Card). Additional cardmembers can't enroll online; they need to call the number on the back of their Amex Platinum to enroll. Related: The 10 best Priority Pass lounges around the world Global Entry/TSA PreCheck application fee credit Another great perk that extends to additional Amex Platinum cardmembers is the statement credit for Global Entry ($120) or TSA PreCheck (up to $85) application fees. Just like the benefit provided to primary cardmembers, each authorized user can use this benefit once every four years for Global Entry or TSA PreCheck. Also, you don't even need to use the credit for your own membership — any qualifying charge for a friend or family member will trigger the credit. If you add an authorized user who applies for Global Entry in the first year, you'll receive $120 worth of benefits right off the bat, which covers almost all of the $195 authorized user annual fee. Related: Top credit cards for Global Entry and TSA PreCheck Hotel elite status Amex Platinum authorized users can also take advantage of complimentary Gold status with Marriott Bonvoy and Hilton Honors, plus Leaders Club Sterling status from The Leading Hotels of the World. Both the primary cardmember and authorized users should be able to enroll for these statuses online. If you frequent Marriott, Hilton or Leading Hotels of the World properties, this can bring you room upgrades (when available), bonus points and additional on-property perks. Access to Fine Hotels + Resorts and The Hotel Collection As an additional Amex Platinum cardmember, you can also use Fine Hotels + Resorts and The Hotel Collection benefits on the card (minimum two-night stay required for The Hotel Collection). When you book a prepaid stay through the Fine Hotels + Resorts program, you'll earn 5 points per dollar spent and get access to the program's elitelike benefits. These benefits include a room upgrade upon arrival (when available), daily breakfast for two, guaranteed 4 p.m. late checkout, noon check-in (when available), complimentary Wi-Fi and a $100 experience credit. Car rental elite status Additional Platinum cardmembers receive complimentary Hertz Gold Plus Rewards President's Circle, Avis Preferred Plus and National Emerald Club Executive status. You can enroll in each of these memberships on Amex's website. Related: How you can redeem points and miles for car rentals Other benefits Amex Platinum authorized users can also access the following benefits: - Amex Offers - Cruise Privileges - International Airline Program Which Amex Platinum benefits are shared among cardmembers? Beyond the above perks, primary and additional cardmembers share several Amex Platinum benefits. In other words, these perks are granted once per account — but purchases by any card on the account will trigger them (enrollment required for select benefits). - Up to $600 statement credit each calendar year (up to $300 semiannually) on prepaid bookings at Fine Hotels + Resorts or The Hotel Collection properties made through American Express Travel® (minimum two-night stay requirement for The Hotel Collection) - Up to $300 per calendar year (up to $25 monthly) in digital entertainment statement credits for select merchants - Up to $300 Equinox statement credit each calendar year to eligible Equinox memberships or access to the Equinox+ app (subject to auto-renewal) - Up to $300 Lululemon statement credit each calendar year (up to $75 each quarter; U.S. stores and online only; outlets excluded) - Up to $219 Clear+ statement credit per calendar year for a Clear+ membership (subject to auto-renewal) - Airline fee statement credit of up to $200 per calendar year (provided as statement credits for incidental fees charged by the airline you select) - Up to $155 in Walmart+ statement credits per calendar year, where you can receive a statement credit each month that covers the full cost of one $12.95 (plus tax) Walmart+ membership (subject to auto-renewal; Plus Up Benefits not eligible) - Up to $120 in Uber One statement credits each calendar year when an eligible card is used to pay for an auto-renewing monthly or annual Uber One membership (subject to auto-renewal; one benefit per account) This is a great way to ensure you maximize these statement credits. For example, you may not want to use the Equinox credit if you use a different gym or fitness provider. However, if your authorized user charges an Equinox membership to the card, those purchases will trigger the statement credit until the $300 per calendar year maximum is reached. What benefits are not included? Note that a few benefits aren't granted to authorized users. Most importantly, there's no additional welcome offer. While all purchases count toward the spending requirement for the primary card's welcome bonus, the account receives only one welcome offer. The primary cardmember can receive up to $200 in Uber Cash each calendar year (provided as $15 each month, plus an additional $20 in December; for eligible U.S. rides and Uber Eats orders). Additional Platinum cardmembers do not receive their own Uber Cash. The benefit can be linked to only one Uber account. If the eligible Platinum Card is added to multiple Uber accounts, only the first account it was added to will receive Uber Cash. Related: The best premium credit cards: A side-by-side comparison Is it worth adding authorized users to your Amex Platinum? The annual fee structure for additional Amex Platinum cardmembers can have existing customers questioning whether it's worth it. More casual travelers may not benefit enough to warrant the $195 annual fee for each additional Amex Platinum cardmember. If you're thinking about adding new authorized users (or looking ahead to your next renewal and considering removing existing authorized users), here are some questions to ask: - Will your authorized users sign up for Global Entry or TSA PreCheck? If so, that can be up to $120 in immediate value, depending on which service your authorized user enrolls in. However, this isn't an annual perk. - How frequently will your authorized users use the card's hotel perks? Semifrequent travelers who won't earn Gold status with Marriott or Hilton or Sterling status from The Leading Hotels of the World in their own right could still get hundreds of dollars in value from these benefits each year. The same holds true for stays at Fine Hotels + Resorts or The Hotel Collection properties. A single FHR stay for your additional Platinum cardmember (with complimentary breakfast and an on-property credit) could cover the $195 annual fee on its own. - How valuable is lounge access for your authorized users? As noted earlier, it'll cost you $50 per visit to bring guests into Centurion Lounges and Sky Clubs as a Platinum cardmember unless you meet certain spending requirements. At face value, you'd need at least four visits per year to cover this added cost. However, this may be less valuable if you rarely visit these locations (or can offset Sky Club guest fees with the Platinum's up to $200 per calendar year airline fee credit). Use these questions to estimate the yearly value your additional Platinum cardmember will get. If that's significantly higher than the new $195 annual fee, it's worth it. Otherwise, you may want to reconsider. Other key considerations Of course, adding an authorized user is not as simple as gaining access to additional benefits. As the primary cardmember, you are responsible for all charges on your account, including those charged by others. For this reason, you should only add other cardmembers you trust to avoid running up your balance. Remember, too, that you must pay your Amex Platinum's balance in full each month (though you should really do this with all credit cards). If done right, adding an authorized user to your card can be a great way to build someone's credit history. This can go a long way toward helping a friend or family member with poor credit, since American Express reports the on-time payment history for every cardmember on your account to the credit bureaus. Again, make sure the authorized user is someone you can trust. Related: Quick Points: The benefits of adding a relative as an authorized user How to add additional cardmembers If you've decided to add additional cardmembers to your Amex Platinum account, the process is relatively simple: - Log in to the dashboard for your Amex Platinum account. - Click on the "Account Services" link at the top. - Click "Manage Other Users" on the left-hand side. - Click "Add Someone to Your Account." - Ensure the Amex Platinum is selected, then click "Continue." - Choose the type of card you want to add (Platinum or companion), enter the user's information, then click "Agree & Submit." Note that you don't have to immediately enter the new authorized user's Social Security number or date of birth, but Amex requires that information within 60 days of the card being issued. Otherwise, the card will be canceled. Related: How to maximize benefits with the Amex Platinum Card Bottom line Having additional cardmembers can expand your earning potential, and on certain cards, it can also unlock a variety of perks for your authorized users. On the Amex Platinum, it costs $195 for each new authorized user, but given the array of benefits they'll enjoy, this can be a solid option under the right circumstances. Just be sure that this additional cost is worth it. To learn more, read our full review of the Amex Platinum. Apply here: American Express Platinum Card For rates and fees of the Amex Platinum, click here.

item.title: United is getting the terminal of its dreams at Washington Dulles. How will it change?
item.description:
Source: The Points Guy Score: 3.92
United is getting the terminal of its dreams at Washington Dulles. How will it change? United Airlines' hub at Dulles International Airport (IAD) has long been on the cusp of something big. In 2018, Scott Kirby, then-president and now CEO of United, said growth at IAD was doing "really well" and hinted at more to come. A year later, the airline added gates at the airport to support more flights. Then, the COVID-19 pandemic erased much of those gains. Fast forward to 2026, and things are looking up again for United at the Washington, D.C.-area airport. United's hub at the airport is bigger — a lot bigger — than it was during its previous peak in 2019. Seats are set to jump 24% this year compared to seven years ago, according to schedule data from aviation analytics firm Cirium. The growth at IAD is second only to United's strategic mid-continent hub at Denver International Airport (DEN). And its growth at IAD is about to be super-charged, thanks to the July 29 agreement to build out the airport's master plan over the next decade. This means travelers will finally be able to say goodbye to the dated and cramped "temporary" Concourse C-D and jet-age mobile lounges in the next few years. It also means a lot more space for United to play with. The Dulles plan Unveiled July 29 at the White House, the estimated $22.5 billion redevelopment of IAD will completely revamp the airport into what Kirby said will be a "world-class airport experience." The program is not actually new but rather a greatly accelerated buildout of the airport's 2025 master plan. The work is split into five key pieces: - Main Terminal and Concourse A: Known as Package A, the highlight of this phase is the expansion of IAD's iconic main terminal, designed by Eero Saarinen. It's also a reconfiguration of the space, so ticket counters and bag drop are perpendicular to the drop-off curb rather than parallel. It includes a new above-ground connector to Concourse A (currently known as Concourse A-B) as well as an expanded international arrivals facility, an expanded Concourse Z, a renovation of Concourse A and a 14-16 gate extension of Concourse A on the site of the current ground-level United Express gates. - AeroTrain and pedestrian tunnel: This piece includes an extension of the AeroTrain to two new stations and all concourses, and a new pedestrian tunnel linking the main terminal with all of the concourses. - Concourse E: This is the full build-out of Concourse E, the first phase of which is set to open this fall. It will be renamed Concourse C. - Concourse D: This is a new Concourse D south of the current Concourse E for domestic airlines. - Concourse B: This is a new regional concourse situated on the site of the current-day Concourse C-D. The redevelopment will add an estimated 5 million square feet of additional terminal and concourse space for travelers. It's unclear how many additional gates the project will add. United's dream terminal "We designed it by and large," Kirby said of the IAD plan in June. "We're excited about it." And United has good reason to be excited. The master plan includes both more and better terminal facilities for the airline, enabling significant growth. It is expected to move all international flights to the renovated Concourse A and expanded Concourse Z; meanwhile, the under-construction Concourse E and future Concourse B will be the backbone of its domestic operations. Executives have already hinted at some of its plans. A new luxe Polaris lounge is planned for the above-ground connector between the terminal and Concourse A, United chief commercial officer Andrew Nocella let slip in March. That is on top of the 40,000-square-foot, Washington, D.C.-themed United Club that is under construction in the new Concourse E. View this post on Instagram The number of gates United will gain is uncertain. In 2024, the airline had 89 "narrowbody-equivalent" gates, a standardized measure based on the space needed for Airbus A320- or Boeing 737-sized aircraft. The actual number of physical gates is lower because some are large enough to accommodate wide-body aircraft, such as the Boeing 787, as shown in the airport's master plan. The number includes both gates on Concourse C-D and the 31 ground-level regional gates on Concourse A. United's count would rise by a quarter to 111 narrowbody-equivalent gates by 2045 under the master plan. More gates would mean room for new international and domestic flights at IAD. United added nine new routes from IAD in 2026, according to Cirium schedules. While routes range from John Wayne Airport (SNA) in Southern California to Keflavik International Airport (KEF) in Iceland, one of the more significant additions comes in December when flights to Rafael Nunez International Airport (CTG) in Cartagena, Colombia, begin. Cartagena is notable as one of United's newest Latin American destinations, with the airline choosing Dulles International Airport (IAD) for its new nonstop service rather than Newark Liberty International Airport (EWR), its New York-area hub. Historically, the carrier has connected destinations in Latin America to either its George Bush Intercontinental Airport (IAH) or EWR hubs before IAD. That may be changing as IAD has space to grow, and EWR suffers from severe space constraints and airspace congestion. "We can connect all kinds of cities to the nation's capital because there's more demand than we ever appreciated," Kirby said in December 2024, adding that the airline saw an opportunity to "double the size" of its international footprint at IAD. United also plans to base an undisclosed number of its new long-haul Airbus A321XLRs at IAD for new flights to Europe, Kirby has said. Obstacles to Dulles' expansion As beneficial as IAD's expansion could be to United, neither the redevelopment nor the airline's growth is a sure thing. The project's price tag, an estimated $22.5 billion, is extremely steep for an airport that last year handled just 29 million passengers. In comparison, Los Angeles International Airport (LAX) is building out a $30 billion capital program for the 2028 Olympics, yet the airport served 73.7 million passengers in 2025. The IAD redevelopment is an order of magnitude more expensive per passenger than the LAX capital program. Without federal grants or other outside funding, airlines and travelers could ultimately bear the cost of the IAD project through higher airport fees — and potentially higher airfares. Still, United CEO Scott Kirby pushed back against projections that the project could result in costs of $90 per passenger. "The $90 CPE is not correct because there's going to be more Es," Kirby said in June. CPE, or "cost per enplanement," is the average amount an airline pays an airport for each passenger it boards. By "more Es," Kirby was referring to United's expected growth at IAD: As more passengers travel through the airport, the project's costs would be spread across a larger number of enplanements, potentially reducing the cost per passenger. Another obstacle is how challenges to the plan could affect Saarinen's landmark terminal. Renderings released by the Trump administration show the building dwarfed and almost subsumed by a new expansion. "The Dulles Main Terminal is one of the most significant works of modern architecture in the United States and a globally recognized masterpiece by Eero Saarinen," modern architecture preservation organization Docomomo DC wrote in a comment to the U.S. Department of Transportation in January. The organization "strongly opposes any revitalization approach that would compromise the essential form, structure, materials, or spatial qualities of Saarinen's design," it added. The Metropolitan Washington Airports Authority, which operates Dulles, appears ready to thread the needle between the need to redevelop IAD and the need to preserve the main terminal. "The Authority intends to maintain the iconic architectural design while undertaking a comprehensive transformation of the interior spaces," MWAA wrote in its June solicitation for a design-builder of the terminal expansion. Related reading:

item.title: American tightens business-class upgrade policy: Now, you'll get premium economy
item.description:
Source: The Points Guy Score: 3.81
American tightens business-class upgrade policy: Now, you'll get premium economy - American will limit complimentary business-class upgrades. - The change affects domestic flights that offer premium economy. - Passengers who get upgraded will get a premium economy seat, instead. American Airlines is offering premium economy on a growing number of domestic flights. As a result, the carrier is changing its complimentary upgrade policy. On certain domestic routes, the airline will limit business-class upgrades for AAdvantage elite status members Beginning Aug. 25, if you're booked in economy, you'll be eligible for an upgrade to premium economy — but not a lie-flat business-class seat, like the carrier currently allows. This move will affect a relatively small number of routes: The changes will apply to domestic flights that have a premium economy cabin. What's that mean on a practical level? If you regularly fly American on top coast-to-coast or Hawaii routes, you'll likely find it harder to get into business class once the new policy takes effect. Plus, AAdvantage elite members flying on the carrier's new Airbus A321XLRs won't get into AA's new Flagship Suites quite as easily on domestic flights. Review: American Airlines A321XLR Flagship Suites business class from JFK-LAX Here's how American framed the changes: "As American Airlines expands its offering of Premium Economy on more domestic routes, we are streamlining our complimentary upgrade process to deliver a more consistent customer experience," the carrier said in a statement. How American is changing its upgrade policy AAdvantage elite status members are entitled to complimentary upgrades when premium seats are available on domestic flights (and certain short-haul international ones). Most of the time, this involves an upgrade to a domestic first-class seat. But if you happen to be flying on one of American's few domestic routes with lie-flat seats, you're eligible to be upgraded to that business-class cabin, free of charge. Soon, that's going to get a little trickier. Premium economy, not business-class Beginning Aug. 25, you economy passengers on will only be eligible for upgrades to premium economy — not business-class. A key exception: If your original seat is in premium economy, you'll still be eligible for an upgrade to business. The upgrade queue for premium economy will work the same as it does now, with AAdvantage members cleared based on factors such as status and their rolling 12-month Loyalty Points tally. Who will this change affect? This move will likely sting for AAdvantage elite members who like to take advantage of business-class upgrades on long flights to and from Hawaii. Ditto for flyers who regularly take advantage of the flatbed upgrades on prime transcontinental routes. What's not changing? American's domestic first-class upgrades are unchanged. If you're an elite flying economy on a standard-configuration domestic aircraft, you'll still be placed in the first-class upgrade queue. The carrier's Systemwide Upgrades will remain the same, too. Which AA domestic flights have premium economy? American currently offers premium economy on certain flights across three domestic routes within the U.S. mainland, including - John F. Kennedy International Airport (JFK) in New York City to Los Angeles International Airport (LAX) - JFK to San Francisco International Airport (SFO) - Boston Logan International Airport (BOS) to LAX Plus, depending on the flight, you'll also find premium economy on six routes to and from Hawaii: - Dallas Fort Worth International Airport (DFW) to Daniel K. Inouye International Airport (HNL) in Honolulu - DFW to Kona International Airport (KOA) on the Big Island - DFW to Kahului International Airport (OGG) on Maui - Phoenix Sky Harbor International Airport (PHX) to HNL - O'Hare International Airport (ORD) in Chicago to HNL - ORD to OGG How to still upgrade into American's business class for free There's still a way to score a complimentary coach-to-business upgrade on certain transcontinental AA routes — at least for now. A handful of the airline's older Airbus A321Ts are still flying. These are the planes that have Flagship First, business class and economy cabins (but not premium economy). Because there's no premium economy cabin, complimentary status upgrades will still get you a business-class seat. The bad news? American is in the process of phasing this configuration out. Related reading:

We don't cover all available credit cards, but our analysis, reviews, and opinions are entirely from our editorial team. Terms apply to the offers listed on this page. Please view our advertising policy and product review methodology for more information. Editorial note: This is a recurring post, regularly updated with new information and offers. Editorial disclaimer: Opinions expressed here are the author's alone, not those of any bank, credit card issuer, airline or hotel chain, and have not been reviewed, approved or otherwise endorsed by any of these entities. 5% cash back on hotels and rental cars booked through Capital One Business Travel Intro offer Earn a $750 bonus Annual fee $0 Regular APR 16.74% - 22.74% (Variable) Recommended credit 740-850 Excellent Quick summary A straightforward business card with no annual fee offers unlimited flat-rate cash back on all purchases, making it appealing for new or cost-conscious businesses. The card features simple rewards, basic travel and purchase protections, and practical business tools such as free employee cards and year-end spending summaries. No foreign transaction fees add value for businesses with occasional international expenses. While the card's benefits are modest, its simplicity may suit those not seeking premium perks or complex earning structures. What to consider The card is best for businesses prioritizing low costs over maximizing rewards, as its earning rate and benefits are less competitive than some alternatives. Rewards can be redeemed for any amount and do not expire as long as the account remains open. Businesses with high spending or significant expenses in bonus categories may benefit more from a card with a higher earning rate, even if it charges an annual fee. What you'll miss from the article A detailed comparison of similar business cards, including trade-offs between higher earning rates and annual fees, plus guidance on choosing the best fit for your business needs. Generated by AI with support from our editorial team. There's a time and a place for choosing a business credit card with an annual fee. However, if you're just getting your business off the ground and still figuring out your finances, keeping your overhead low is likely your bigger priority. That's where the Capital One Spark Cash Select can make a lot of sense. It earns an unlimited 1.5% cash back on every purchase without adding another annual expense, since it has no annual fee (see rates and fees). Card rating*: ⭐⭐⭐ *Card rating is based on the opinion of TPG’s editors and is not influenced by the card issuer. Capital One Spark Cash Select: The basics One thing I've learned from reviewing business credit cards is that more isn't always better. Sometimes a straightforward card with no annual fee is exactly what a business needs — especially if you're trying to keep costs low while still earning rewards. If you want to earn your cash back without paying an annual fee, the Spark Cash Select is a sensible option for your business . Just keep in mind that its simplicity can also be its biggest drawback, and some businesses may find its rewards and benefits just a little too basic. TPG recommends applicants have a credit score of 740 or higher to increase their chances of approval. Let's dive deeper into what this card can offer you and your business. Capital One Spark Cash Select pros and cons Pros Cons No annual fee keeps costs low Unlimited 1.5% back Cash back can become Capital One miles with the right companion card Limited benefits Lower rewards rate than some competitors Simple earning structure may not maximize rewards for high-spending businesses Capital One Spark Cash Select benefits The Spark Cash Select doesn't offer many premium perks, but the benefits it does include complement its straightforward, no-annual-fee approach. Overall, the Spark Cash Select's perks are considerably light compared to what other top business credit cards have to offer. Business management tools The Spark Cash Select includes several features designed to make running your business a little easier. You can add employee cards at no additional cost (see rates and fees) and receive year-end spending summaries that can help simplify bookkeeping and tax season. No foreign transaction fees A standout benefit of the Spark Cash Select is that it doesn't charge foreign transaction fees (see rates and fees). If your business occasionally takes you overseas, you can use the card without paying extra on purchases made outside the U.S. Travel and purchase protections The Spark Cash Select includes a couple of basic protections that can come in handy from time to time. Eligible purchases receive an extended warranty, which can add additional time to the original manufacturer's warranty on eligible items when you pay with your card. Terms apply. You'll also have access to roadside assistance if you run into trouble on the road. This pay-per-use dispatch service can arrange help with services like towing, fuel delivery and more, though you'll pay a pre-negotiated fee for any service you use. These aren't industry-leading protections, but they provide a little extra peace of mind without increasing the card's annual cost. (see rates and fees) One of the best things about the Spark Cash Select is its simple earning structure. If you don't want to keep track of bonus categories or adjust your spending habits to maximize rewards, this card makes earning cash back almost effortless. Earning rewards The Spark Cash Select earns 5% cash back on hotels and rental cars booked through Capital One's travel booking site and an unlimited 1.5% cash back on all other purchases. I especially like this earning structure for businesses with expenses that don't fit neatly into common bonus categories. Instead of worrying about whether a purchase qualifies for extra rewards, you'll earn the same flat rate on everything you buy. That said, businesses with high spending in bonus categories like advertising, shipping or office supplies may be able to earn more with a different business credit card. Just like earning rewards, redeeming your Spark Cash Select rewards is simple and straightforward. You can redeem your cash-back rewards for any amount, and the rewards won't expire as long as your account is open. Where the Capital One Spark Cash Select falls short The biggest drawback of the Spark Cash Select is that its simplicity can become limiting as your business grows. While an unlimited 1.5% cash back on everyday purchases is easy to understand, it's not among the most competitive flat-rate cash-back cards. If your business spends heavily or has significant expenses in bonus categories, you may earn substantially more with another card — even one that charges an annual fee. The card's benefits are also fairly modest. The lack of foreign transaction fees and practical business features like free employee cards are convenient, but you won't find premium travel perks, statement credits or robust travel protections here (see rates and fees). For many small businesses, that won't matter. But if you're looking for a card you'll grow into, there are stronger long-term options. Capital One Spark Cash Select vs. Capital One Spark Cash The Spark Cash Select and Capital One Spark Cash are very similar cards. Both earn unlimited cash back, offer no foreign transaction fees and include useful business features like free employee cards (see rates and fees for the Spark Cash Select) and (see rates and fees for the Spark Cash). The biggest difference is that the Spark Cash charges an annual fee but earns a higher flat-rate cash-back rate on every purchase (see rates and fees). I'd choose the Spark Cash Select if your priority is keeping business expenses low while still earning straightforward cash back. It's an especially good fit for newer businesses or anyone who isn't sure they'll earn enough rewards to justify paying an annual fee. I'd choose the Spark Cash if your business has significant monthly spending. The higher earning rate can quickly outweigh the annual fee, making it a better long-term value for many established businesses. Is the Capital One Spark Cash Select worth it? The Spark Cash Select delivers exactly what it promises. It won't earn the most rewards or come with luxury benefits, but it keeps costs low while providing a reliable return on every purchase. For many small businesses, that's more valuable than chasing a higher earning rate that may never offset an annual fee. When to apply for the Capital One Spark Cash Select Currently, new cardholders earn a one-time $750 cash bonus after spending $6,000 on purchases within the first three months of opening an account with this card. I believe this is a compelling time to apply if you've already been considering the card. A $750 welcome bonus is generous for a no-annual-fee business card, and because there's no annual fee to offset, you can put the full value of that bonus right back into your business (see rates and fees). Other cards to consider if you don’t want the Capital One Spark Cash Select If you want to earn a higher return on your business expenses or have more options for redeeming your rewards, one of the following cards will likely be a better fit. If you spend enough to justify paying an annual fee: The Capital One Spark Cash Plus earns a higher 2% back on all purchases but has a $150 annual fee (see rates and fees). You'll get your annual fee refunded after you spend $150,000 each year, so this is a better option if you spend enough to reap this card's additional benefits. To learn more, check out our full review of the Spark Cash Plus. If you want more reward redemption options: The Capital One Venture Business earns unlimited rewards as miles, allowing you to transfer your rewards to any of Capital One's 15-plus airline and hotel partners. To learn more, check out our full review of the Venture Business card. If you want to earn Chase Ultimate Rewards: The (see rates and fees) also earns an unlimited 1.5% cash back on all purchases. But if you also have a card that allows you to transfer your rewards to travel partners, like the (see rates and fees) or the (see rates and fees), you can transfer the rewards you earn with the Ink Business Unlimited as well. To learn more, check out our full review of the Ink Business Unlimited. If you want a business card that earns cash-back rewards at a flat rate and doesn't have an annual fee, the Spark Cash Select checks the box (see rates and fees). But if you have significant business expenses, you'll want to opt for a card with higher earning potential and more substantial benefits. item.title: OpenAI is giving ChatGPT free users unlimited text chats
item.description:
Source: The Verge Score: 5.39
OpenAI is making a big change for ChatGPT users on its free and Go tiers: Starting next week, users on those tiers will be able to have unlimited text chats with the chatbot, according to OpenAI. Right now, you may run into rate limits if you do too many text chats on those tiers, but those limits, just for text, will be going away soon. Messages that include things like file uploads and images will continue to have limits. OpenAI is giving ChatGPT free users unlimited text chats ChatGPT’s GPT-5.6 Sol model will also be ‘more reliable with facts’ for Plus and Pro users. Next week, OpenAI is also adding a “Think” button for free and Go users that they can use to “access higher reasoning for harder questions.” This week, for those users, the company is additionally upgrading ChatGPT’s default AI model to the recently released GPT-5.6 Luna. For Plus and Pro subscribers, GPT-5.6 Sol in ChatGPT is being updated to be “more reliable with facts,” OpenAI says. “The new GPT‑5.6 Sol is designed to make fewer mistakes — especially when answers depend on dates, numbers, sources, rules, or assumptions — by better using the sources it finds to answer your question.” The updated GPT-5.6 Sol will also give you “more direct responses” with “tighter formatting,” and OpenAI says ChatGPT will “avoid extra detail when it does not help.” Plus and Pro subscribers can also use a new slider to decide “how much thought ChatGPT puts into an answer.” Both the updated GPT-5.6 Sol and the slider will be available starting Thursday.

Apple bumped up its trade-in offers for iPhones, iPads, Macs, Apple Watches, and certain Android phones, with some devices now worth over $100 more, 9to5Mac reports. Best Buy kicked off a sale on Apple products with discounts on its latest smartwatches to phones.
