The value proposition of the WiiM Sound Lite is interesting. As best we can tell, it’s exactly the same speaker as the WiiM Sound, just without the touchscreen and physical remote control. And it usually costs about $70 less. That makes the Lite version a great single-speaker option if you’re uninterested in the added features. Or, since both models also support stereo pairing, the Lite version makes a great second speaker to get the sound quality of a traditional stereo system without paying for the redundancy of two touchscreens and two remotes. The WiiM Home app is pretty easy and intuitive to use. The app has a clean layout that makes it easy to browse streaming services, set up favorite channels, add new devices, and launch playback to multiple Linkplay devices on your network. It even works well with turntable integration, which isn’t a given for these types of systems. It’s not as intuitive as AirPlay or a closed system when it comes to setting up audio zones and moving music around the house, but since many Linkplay-compatible devices also support AirPlay or Google Cast, you can move seamlessly between wireless protocols depending on your needs. The openness of the Linkplay ecosystem doesn’t always go in both directions. In previous tests, we really liked Audio Pro’s A10 MKII WiiM Edition speaker, both for its flexibility and its sound quality. So we made a point of testing the newer A10 MkII W — which, despite the “W,” has no WiiM affiliation. We were curious how the dropping of the WiiM partnership might affect the speaker’s compatibility within the Linkplay ecosystem. The Audio Pro app looks like a reskinned version of the WiiM Home app; however, whereas the WiiM Home app found the A10 MkII W and added it to the list of available speakers, we couldn’t get the Audio Pro app to add any of the WiiM products we tested. So just be aware that, with this approach, two-way compatibility between different Linkplay components is not guaranteed. This article was edited by Adrienne Maxwell and Grant Clauser. Further reading - by Brent Butterworth Great sound doesn’t have to come in a boring, boxy speaker design. We tested an array of lifestyle speakers that score high in both looks and performance. - by Brent Butterworth A great pair of bookshelf speakers should last for years and deliver better performance than you can get from a tabletop speaker. - by Dennis Burger and Adrienne Maxwell The Denon AVR-X1800H is an easy-to-use AV receiver that sounds great and has the necessary features to meet most people’s movie, music, and video-gaming needs.

item.title: The Best Packable Daypack for Travel
item.description:
Source: Wirecutter Score: 5.66
Packable daypacks are a perfect option if you need a lightweight spare bag to stash inside your luggage when you travel. They’re also great if you need an extra bag while running an unexpected errand during your daily commute. After testing 18 packable daypacks, we chose three lightweight, portable, well-constructed bags to fit a variety of situations, including traveling, hiking, and commuting. Although every trip has its specific considerations, the bags we recommend share a few similar qualities. All of them are water resistant to some degree, pack down small enough to fit easily into a carry-on bag, and hold at least 20 liters comfortably. We picked a pack good enough for daily use and a lightweight bag that stays dry in stormy weather. For space-conscious travelers, we have a pick that fits in the palm of your hand. Why you should trust us I’ve covered travel luggage and bag design for Wirecutter for nine years and have personally researched, tested, and compared hundreds of bags in that time. - For this guide, I built on previous years of experience and research by a writer and two editors who have, among them, worked remotely from every continent except Antarctica. - We developed our earliest criteria for this piece after doing an interview with Sara Morrow, an archaeologist who spends summers working expeditions on a small island off the coast of Ireland. She uses a packable daypack to transport her tools, notebooks, and personal items between the base camp and dig sites, and she considers it a necessity in the field. - Personally, I try to pack lightly and almost always travel with at least one packable bag to use on small day journeys once I’ve reached my destination. - Like all Wirecutter journalists, I review and test products with complete editorial independence. I’m never made aware of any business implications of my editorial recommendations. Read more about our editorial standards. Good for daily carry: WaterField Packable Backpack Top pick Slightly heavier weight and more-advanced materials give this backpack a reassuring heft and impressive water resistance — and a high price tag. It’s comfortable enough to use as your daily backpack. Who this is for: Anyone who values a slightly mature look with extra durability and protection from the rain will appreciate this pack. However, it is our most expensive pick. The WaterField Packable Backpack is a well-built travel backpack that marries the heft of a regular backpack with the compactness of an easy-to-pack tote. It looks and feels like a regular backpack. In addition to being the most traditional-looking backpack of our picks, it feels the most like a traditional backpack. The shoulder straps, which are ergonomically shaped and lined with breathable mesh fabric, make the bag easier to carry over long distances. It has more organization. WaterField’s Packable Backpack has a front zippered pocket and two open side pockets that could hold a water bottle and an umbrella. When you’re not using the bag, you can fold it down into a built-in packing pocket, which doubles as an interior zippered pocket when the bag is on your back. Its high performance matches its high price. However, it’s WaterField’s attention to materials that sets this bag apart from our other picks (and increases the overall price). A layer of Taslan nylon — a very thin, but sturdy, fabric — is layered with a structural tricot mesh and a robust water-resistant coating. Water practically bounced away from this bag during testing — even more so than with our pick from Matador — so it’s a good option for wet climates. Flaws but not dealbreakers It’s our bulkiest pick. The WaterField Packable Backpack weighs about 12 ounces; it’s heavier than our other picks but not by much. The bag holds 16 liters of stuff, which is on the smaller side compared with our other picks but still plenty big for a single traveler on a walk. It doesn’t pack down as small as our other picks. It’s a little tricky to pack into its self-contained pocket. It’s not as simple as just inverting it and stuffing away to your heart’s content. You have to do a series of particular folds to pack the bag properly, which WaterField shared in a video. There’s a fine line between portability and irritability, and this bag cuts that line very close. Specs - Expanded dimensions: 15 by 11 by 6 inches (height by width by depth) - Packed dimensions: 9 by 9 by 3 inches - Weight: 12 ounces - Capacity: 16 liters - Warranty: lifetime repair or replacement A lightweight bag to carry in the rain: Matador Freerain22 Waterproof Packable Backpack Top pick This bag will keep your things dry during adventures in wet climates or unpredictable weather. It packs down to about the size of a potato, but its lack of overall structure isn’t ideal for long hikes or days of carrying. Matador recently replaced the Freerain22 with the new 18L Waterproof Packable Backpack. (The Freerain22 remains available at some retailers.) We’re testing the updated pack and will report back soon. Who this is for: If you need a spare lightweight bag that can stand up to the elements while taking up very little space, the Freerain22 backpack is for you. The Matador Freerain22 Waterproof Packable Backpack is excellent in wet climates or anywhere where you might realistically expect to get caught in the rain — think hiking around Seattle or touring London in the fall. It’s mini but mighty. The Freerain22 backpack folds down so small — to about the size of a pocket camera — that it feels like a magic trick. Made from 30-denier abrasion-resistant Cordura nylon (denier is a measure of the fiber thickness in a fabric), it kept our things dry even in a rainstorm, although a small amount of humidity and moisture did get in on occasion while we were hiking around Hawaii. The main compartment opens and closes with a roll top that buckles down on the sides like a dry bag. It’s the best possible design if you’re serious about keeping out water. It’s versatile — to a point. During our testing, it worked well for travel and on the trail, as long as we didn’t try to carry too much, too far. This pack’s mesh shoulder straps, though very breathable and wide enough to distribute the weight, are like two pieces of hosiery: barely there. And though they are wide enough to resist pinching, a thin strip of fabric can only do so much to protect your clavicles. In addition to using this pack for travel and hikes, we also liked to throw the Freerain22 pack into a jacket pocket in case it rained during commutes around town. It has some nice extras. Along with a sternum strap, removable hip strap, and loops to hold trekking poles or ice axes, it has two side pockets for water bottles, with side buckles for securing the containers in place, and a zippered front pocket. Other than that, it doesn’t have much organization. But that’s not why you buy a bag like this. The Freerain22 backpack is best as a just-in-case bag. It’s so small that you can bring it with you everywhere, and when you need it, you’ll be glad you have it. Flaws but not dealbreakers The compromises needed to shrink a bag this small also become its flaws. The shoulder straps are so thin and insubstantial that it’s impossible for the Freerain22 backpack to be comfortable over long distances, especially when you’re carrying more than 10 pounds. The straps may be too long. Some of our testers found that the shoulder straps, though adjustable, were so long that they couldn’t get the straps short enough to fit their shoulders and frame. It’s not as structured as our other picks. It feels like a reusable shopping bag on your back. If you want a stiffer, more traditional backpack feel, consider the WaterField Packable Backpack. Specs - Expanded dimensions: 19.5 by 11 by 9.5 inches (height by width by depth) - Packed dimensions: 5 by 3 inches (length by diameter) - Weight: 6.6 ounces - Capacity: 22 liters - Warranty: one-year repair or replacement A pack that fits in your palm: Sea to Summit Ultra-Sil Day Pack Top pick Toss this lightweight, phone-size packable bag into your luggage or coat pocket, and you’ll never get caught without a spare bag again. If you need something to carry more often, though, you might prefer one of our more structured picks. Who this is for: It’s fantastic for anyone who needs a light, spare bag that they can take with them anywhere, anytime. The Sea to Summit Ultra-Sil Day Pack is perfect to keep in your pocket or in the glove compartment of your car — it’s handy for when, say, you need a spare bag at the market. It’s our most packable pick. The Ultra-Sil pack is the smallest and lightest packable backpack we recommend. Packed up, it’s very discreet: nearly the size of a keychain accessory. It’s tougher than it looks. The bag itself is a no-frills sack made from a paper-thin siliconized Cordura nylon, which means it’s very light and water resistant. It has reinforced stitching at stress points, so it can carry more weight than you would expect. That said, since this pack is made of such thin, light material, carrying large or awkwardly shaped loads is somewhat uncomfortable, especially when compared with our more-structured picks. Flaws but not dealbreakers Any flaw is an aspect of its narrowly engineered use. Are the shoulder straps thin? Of course! Would it be nice if this bag — which deploys from a small sack that fits in the palm of your hand — had more back padding? Yes. But that would also make it larger and heavier. If you’re not willing to trade some comfort to get the smallest possible carry, this isn’t the bag for you. It’s not waterproof. The bag won’t keep your things dry in the rain like our other picks, the WaterField Packable Backpack and the Matador Freerain22 Waterproof Packable Backpack, will. Specs - Expanded dimensions: 19 by 11 by 8 inches (height by width by depth) - Packed dimensions: 3.5 by 2 by 1.5 inches - Weight: 2.5 ounces - Capacity: 20 liters - Warranty: lifetime repair or replacement How we picked and tested Depending on whether you plan to scale cliffs or tour museums, certain features become more or less important when you’re choosing a day bag. To help make sense of what to prioritize among the dozens of available options, we pored over articles across many outdoor publications and consulted other comparative reviews and advice from sources such as REI and GearLab. We also considered our own experiences to determine what makes a great packable daypack. Here’s what we look for: - Weight and size: The whole point of a packable daypack is that it packs well, so weight and compressed size are important factors. Carrying capacity generally correlates to the weight and size of a bag, except in more explicitly technical packs, which may cut down on weight by using lighter, but more expensive, materials. - Ergonomic features: Stowable daypacks can look and feel like stuff sacks with straps, or they can be full, ergonomically shaped backpacks. The wearability of a bag usually comes down to its load distribution and support system (such as the sternum strap on the Matador Freerain22 Waterproof Packable Backpack). - Organization: Most packable daypacks come with at least two compartments — the largest, or main, compartment and the (often attached) pouch into which the whole pack stows away. Beyond those, an external pocket that can hold small, frequent-use items (such as keys) or sleeves for water bottles are useful. The drawback of adding more organization is that it decreases the packability of a bag and often contributes to weight. - High-quality materials: Because a packable daypack needs to be able to carry at least some weight when in use but still fold up for storage, materials make the difference between a lightweight pack that feels cheap and flimsy versus one that you feel confident filling to the max and carrying into a rainstorm. The fabrics and composite materials used in higher-quality bags are light and durable but remain nearly invulnerable to water. - 15- to 25-liter capacity: This seems to be the ideal range for a pack that can hold a full day’s worth of stuff while remaining reasonably lightweight and portable. It’s enough to accommodate a 13-inch laptop, along with some rain protection, a camera, an extra layer of clothing, and whatever else you might need for a day about town. - Weather resistance and durability: Although a few bags we liked, such as the Matador Freerain22 pack and the WaterField Packable Backpack, come extremely close, total waterproofing is a lot to ask of any lightweight bag. At a minimum, a pack should provide enough protection to keep you and your gear dry through at least a few minutes of wet weather. The better packs often feature more-careful construction, which is visible in details such as sealed and tighter stitching (our pick from Matador) and reinforced bottoms (our pick from WaterField). Other packable bags worth considering If you’re planning some heavy excursions and looking for the absolute best equipment: You might consider the Hyperlite Summit 30. It’s a remarkable piece of equipment, a full-size 30-liter backpack weighing only 0.8 pounds. Made of Dyneema composite fabric, Hyperlite backpacks are highly water resistant and long-lasting. And each one folds up to take the same space as a couple of T-shirts. Most people looking for a spare travel bag don’t need a $210 ultralight backpack designed for hiking. But for a rare type of traveler, the Summit 30 might be the best choice. If you need a heavy-duty bag for hiking: The Matador Beast28 Ultralight Technical Backpack is a capable hiking daypack that’s hydration-bladder compatible, but not everyone needs a packable bag this hefty. Alone, it’s 1.25 pounds, which is heavier than any of our picks. For the price, we prefer the simplicity of our other picks. But the Beast28 is a good bag, albeit with a large footprint even when it’s packed up. If none of our picks are available: Consider the REI Co-op Flash 18 Pack, another decent choice in the sub-$50 cinch-top-bag category. It’s a fine alternative, but for a little more money you get a lot more value with our other choices. The competition Aer Go Pack 2: The previous version was a pick, but the current model is too bulky to be packable; it takes up more space in your suitcase than would ever be worth it on a trip. Cotopaxi Luzon 18L Backpack: This is a decent small backpack, but the drawstring closure top kept this out of consideration. Not only are drawstrings a hazard if they slip out, but they are prone to breaking, and the cinch closure is useless against bad weather. Fjällräven High Coast Foldsack 24: This is a good bag at a slightly high price, but it didn’t make the cut for us because of its weight and large size even when rolled up. Gonex 20L Lightweight Packable Backpack: Although it has rave reviews online, we found the stitching was more fragile than we like to recommend. L.L.Bean Stowaway Pack: The Stowaway Pack was organized and comfortable enough that we liked carrying it on the hiking trail, but we preferred our pick from Matador for its better weatherproofing. REI Co-op Stuff Travel Pack - 20L: This is a competitor of the Matador Freerain22 pack that falls short. It mimics our Matador pick in its design, but not in the quality of its materials. Its flimsier fabric and zipper will fail sooner. (REI has since released a new version with no intentionally added PFAS; the design otherwise remains the same.) We also tested and dismissed packable bags from Away, Dakine, Eddie Bauer, Mystery Ranch, and Patagonia that have since been discontinued. This article was edited by Ria Misra and Christine Ryan. Further reading - by India Edwards Whether you’re packing for a long weekend or an overnight stay, these travel bags get the job done without weighing you down. - by Maria Adelmann The New York Times’s Frugal Traveler columnist Elaine Glusac has been on almost every trip you can imagine. She’s learned a thing or two about what to pack. - by Wirecutter Staff We put in another year and tens of thousands more miles of travel to test the best travel gear — and we stand by last year’s choices alongside a few new picks.

item.title: The Best Cooling Pet Beds, Mats, Bottles, and Other Accessories to Get Your Dogs and Cats Through Summer
item.description:
Source: Wirecutter Score: 5.57
Plenty of pets love to sunbathe. My dog Dave spends hours working on his tan, no matter that he’s covered with a thin layer of black fur. Most animals regulate their heat on a warm day by moving to the shade, drinking water, or splaying out on the cool tiles of the bathroom floor. But sometimes animal friends need a little extra help to avoid overheating and risking heatstroke. “The general rule of thumb is, if it’s too hot for people, it’s too hot for animals to be outside for any extended period of time as well,” said Jerry Klein, chief veterinarian for the American Kennel Club. The best thing you can do is tune in to your pet’s behavior and try to prevent heatstroke altogether. Give them access to water and a space to cool off, and fan them or wet them down to help them regulate their temperature. You can also immerse them in water, said Emily Hall, a veterinarian and lecturer at the Royal Veterinary College UK, whose research has focused on heatstroke in pets. If you have taken those steps and still see signs that your pet might be overheating — panting excessively, acting lethargic, vomiting, or just seeming off — they might need medical care. A good rule of thumb is “wet, then vet,” said Hall. “You want to start cooling them before you start transporting them,” she said. Klein seconded that. He added, “If a dog overheats and it looks like heatstroke, and you think you’ve got it under control, always get them seen by a vet. Because sometimes there can be internal changes that can occur hours later.” That said, some dogs and cats are better acclimated to heat than others — owing to variables such as size, age, breed, and type of fur — and a daily walk or afternoon outing on a summer day doesn’t usually require a follow-up emergency visit. You can even use some products to help ensure that your pet stays cool and comfortable. We tried several to see how well they worked, and we found beds, mats, water bottles, harnesses, and cots that can help a pet stay a little cooler in the heat. Chilling at home In addition to the fans and ACs that you may already be running to keep yourself cool, a variety of beds, cots, and mats might help your dog or cat stay less hot while they snooze the day away. Cooling beds and elevated cots You can find loads of pet beds that are made with “cooling-gel foam,” but they don’t actually reduce your pet’s body temperature — they simply don’t get quite as hot as some beds lacking the gel might. “Synthetic foam (memory foam, polyfoam) retains more heat than more breathable materials (latex, cotton, etc.) do. So the ‘cooling gel’ is typically added to offset the extra heat retention of the foam, rather than being objectively cooler than a material with better breathability,” said Wirecutter deputy director Courtney Schley, who has overseen our coverage of sleep products. Of the beds we tested, a couple did the job as advertised — they warmed up less than our control bed made from regular, non-gel foam. The FurHaven Velvet Waves Perfect Comfort Cooling Gel Bolster Cat & Dog Bed, the “cooling” version of our main dog bed pick, performed the best. The surface temperature of the bed rose an average of 9 Fahrenheit degrees after our pet lay on it for five minutes, versus an 11-degree increase on the standard bed. That result is in line with FurHaven’s claims that the foam “reduces sleeping surface temperature by 1-2 degrees.” While that isn’t the most dramatic difference, if you want to take the edge off the heat in your pet’s bed, this model is a good option. This bed is soft and supportive, and with the cooling gel layer, it can help keep a pet a few degrees cooler than a regular bed might. If your dog prefers a breathable, elevated bed, the K&H Original Pet Cot and the Kuranda Chew Proof Aluminum Dog Bed are great options for both indoors and out. The Kuranda bed is more expensive, but its thick aluminum frame makes it more durable and resistant to chewing. This cot keeps your dog elevated and promotes airflow to help regulate their temperature. Cooling mats and blankets “I have a part of my house which has a stone floor. And when it’s hot, that’s where the cats lie. They starfish out on the stone floor and cool themselves down,” said Hall. If you don’t have stone or tile flooring, a cooling mat might be your next best option; in our testing, these flat, thin pads got less hot than the cooling beds. Instead of foam, they’re made with a pressure-activated gel that absorbs some of the heat from your pet’s body. All the mats we tested cooled better than any of the beds we tried. The Green Pet Shop Cool Pet Pad and Arf Pets Self-Cooling Solid Gel Pad both got only about 4 degrees warmer after five minutes of our using them indoors, versus the FurHaven cooling bed’s 9-degree increase under the same conditions. These mats are more portable than many beds, but since they’re filled with gel, they can get heavy depending on the size. And their cooling effects can fade quickly in direct sunlight or on extremely hot days. Both manufacturers claim that their mats are nontoxic, but you still shouldn’t let your pet chew on the materials, and always make sure to monitor your animal when using one of these. While both of these mats felt chilly and refreshing on my back after we came home all sweaty from a walk, my dog Dave, their intended customer, wasn’t so into them. He’s generally not fond of slick or slippery surfaces, and he rarely lies on an uncarpeted floor if a softer option is available. So Dave often parked himself nearby on the Pelsbarn Cooling Mat or the similar Bedsure ArcticMax Cooling Mat. Even though these models have “mat” in their names, they both feel more like a blanket. Their cooling effects were similar to one another, but the Bedsure is currently roughly half the price of the Pelsbarn. Despite being called a mat, this fabric model feels more like a blanket, but it cools just as well as the gel-filled versions. It’s also light enough to carry on outings with your pet. Considering those differences, I was genuinely surprised that the Pelsbarn and Bedsure mats performed just as well as the gel-filled mats at keeping heat in check, increasing by only about 4 degrees after five minutes of use. These two are both lighter than the gel mats, so you can easily pack them for a picnic, and they’re machine-washable. Keeping cool on the go Keep an eye on the weather report. If it’s going to be very hot out, “exercise your dogs in the early morning or late in the evening,” said Klein. Tyra Davis, a veterinarian based in Hammond, Louisiana, has a handy rule she always tells her clients: No play in the heat of the day. If your pup needs a bathroom break during the warmest part of a hot day, keep it short and try to stay in shady, grassy areas. If it’s not excessively hot, and it’s safe to go outside, a harness, vest, or gaiter that provides evaporative cooling can help extend the time your pup can spend with you outdoors. Evaporation in general “is your best help in trying to cool a dog down,” said Klein. It’s similar to how people sweat: As moisture evaporates from skin, it makes one feel cooler. (You can also pour or spray water directly onto your pet or get them into a pool, lake, or other body of water, said Hall.) Evaporative-cooling garments can be helpful, but they don’t work as well in high humidity, since the moisture is less likely to evaporate in those conditions. You also need to keep tabs on the garments and make sure that they stay wet; otherwise they can become just another insulation layer, making your pet even hotter. If you’re using any of these garments, Klein emphasized, “you should use common sense and take breaks, offer the dog plenty of water, and periodically check to see if there’s no chafing or rubbing,” especially on the elbows or groin. Also, consider your dog’s health, sensitivities, and coat to confirm that the garment is right for them. “Some of the cooling vests might be too cold for dogs that are older or have arthritic joints. A breed like a whippet has very thin skin versus a dog like a golden retriever, which is double-coated. It might be more beneficial for that golden, and it might be uncomfortable for that whippet,” said Klein. “I think we have to treat each dog very individually and assess the dog, the climate, and the product,” he added. If you’re ever in doubt, check with your vet. Cooling harnesses The Swamp Cooler Dog Harness from Ruffwear, which has been making a version of this harness since 2008, employs three layers that work together to pull moisture and heat away from the dog. This durable, well-built harness uses evaporative cooling to pull moisture and heat away from your dog. It has six adjustment points and a thick padded handle on the back for emergency lifts. This harness uses a specialized fabric to help with wicking, transporting, and evaporating moisture and heat. It has six points of adjustment and a handle strap on the back. The inner and outermost layers are made from a Bluesign-approved polyester mesh, while the middle layer is kind of like a felt, according to Peter Kearns, head of product at Ruffwear. This middle layer “holds a significant amount of water,” said Kearns, so it acts as a sort of a sponge or reservoir. “And that action of having the water pulled away from that reservoir through that outer layer, that’s what’s cooling the dog down, lowering the total surface temperature,” Kearns explained. The Canada Pooch Max Chill Cooling Harness works similarly to the Ruffwear model. It uses three layers of fabric from Coolcore, which makes performance apparel for humans. These layers work together to wick, transport, and, finally, evaporate moisture (and with it, heat) away from the surface of a dog’s body, according to Tara Hoth, director of product and innovation at Canada Pooch. These harnesses performed equally well in my testing, both remaining wet and cooler than the air even after two hours in direct sunlight on a 76-degree day. Only the Ruffwear harness is machine-washable. (Canada Pooch says the Max Chill harness should be spot-cleaned only, but I ran it through the machine a few times, along with the Ruffwear model, and it came out fine.) Neither harness can be tumble-dried. And the Ruffwear model required a little extra cleaning, as it trapped a few bits of dirt and debris in between the top two layers. Kearns suggested using a brush to dislodge the bits and then flushing them out with water. The buckles on the Canada Pooch harness are bulkier than those on the Ruffwear model, so they may be easier to grasp, but we found them slightly more difficult to snap in place. Cooling vests If you think your dog might benefit from something with more coverage, a cooling vest may be a better option. These vests look like little capes. Since they touch more surface area of the dog’s body, they might help to cool the dog down a bit more. But they might take some getting used to — unlike with the harnesses, Dave seemed a little confused when he tried on the vests for the first time. The Ruffwear Swamp Cooler Dog Vest and Canada Pooch Max Chill Cooling Vest are both made with the same evaporative cooling layers as their harness counterparts — the vests just have more material. This cooling vest covers more of a dog’s body than a harness, so it has more surface area to work with. The Canada Pooch vest is made from a more flexible material than the Ruffwear vest, so it drapes a bit better over a dog’s body, and it features rear-leg straps that can help keep it in place. Because the Ruffwear vest is slightly stiffer, it can stick up a bit near a dog’s rear when they bend down to sniff something. Cooling gaiters and snoods If you want something that’s simple to pop onto your dog, a gaiter or snood is lower-profile, lower-cost, and lower-effort to use than a vest or a harness, but it’s likely not to cool as much. The Ruffwear Swamp Cooler Neck Gaiter and the Canada Pooch Max Chill Cooling Snood performed the best of those we tested. They each stayed wet and cool for about two hours in direct sunlight on a warm day. The Frisco Summer Cooling Pullover Dog Gaitor is about a third of the price of the Ruffwear and Canada Pooch options, but it dried up the fastest. The Canada Pooch snood comes in fewer sizes than the Ruffwear gaiter, but it has a cinch toggle around the neck so you can adjust the fit. The Ruffwear gaiter comes in six sizes, but they’re not adjustable. No matter which one you choose, be prepared for your dog to look like a scarf-wearing hipster in the summer. Boots Since the ground can often be hotter than the air above it, a breathable set of boots may help protect your dog’s paw pads from getting scalded (good luck getting shoes on a cat’s feet). “Artificial grass, black tarmac, all those things are going to absorb the radiant heat from the sun,” said Hall. These surfaces can reach up to 140 °F in the sun, Hall warned. And even with outside temperatures as low as 77 °F, the pavement can reach 125 °F, according to the Washington State University College of Veterinary Medicine. You can test the ground by touching the back of your hand to it, said Hall, not your palm, which is likely to be slightly more calloused and less sensitive. “If you can’t keep your hand in contact with the ground, it’s not safe to be walking your dog without protective booties on,” she said. Natural grass, shady areas, and paler surfaces are cooler, so try to stick to those. Hot-weather boots should be breathable but also protect your dog’s paw pads from getting scalded. We like the Wagwear WagWellies Mojave boots, which look like Crocs. They’re dotted with holes that make them breathable and also allow water to drain out if you get caught in a summer storm. These boots, which protect paws from burns and scrapes, are ideal for summertime and hot climates, but they can’t stand up to lots of abuse. The Ruffwear Grip Trex boots have a thick, durable sole and a breathable woven mesh upper that make them great for longer hikes over rough terrain. They don’t have big holes like the Wagwear boots, so if you’re on a hike, these shoes can help keep dirt and large debris from getting inside. These boots have great ventilation and sturdy soles to protect paws from rough or hot ground, but they take some getting used to. The Mountain Ridge Tough Boots with Grip are less expensive than the Wagwear and Ruffwear boots, and they’re easy to put on. They’re sold in singles, so you can buy spares, but they’re not as breathable, and they provide a thinner barrier between your dog’s paws and the ground. Whether your dog is wearing boots or not, check their paws frequently to make sure they’re in good shape. Kiddie pools If you have the space for it and your dog enjoys getting wet, a kiddie pool can be a fun way to help cool them off. The Bilibara Foldable Dog Pet Bath Pool is a good option. We haven’t tested it yet for pets, mostly because Dave thinks water is the enemy, but our emergency prep writer Colleen Hagerty put it through its paces when testing utility pumps. Colleen was impressed by the pool’s durability and said it was “also pretty painless to empty and fold back down.” It comes in seven sizes, so it can accommodate dogs, kids, and adults. The Frisco Outdoor Dog Swimming Pool is a similar option that also looks good and is well-reviewed. Steer clear of inflatable pools — it takes only one sharp dog claw to leave you with a flat piece of wet plastic. And always use caution: Since brachycephalic dogs can drown easily, Hall warned against dunking these flat-faced breeds in water where that might be a possibility. Always supervise your dog when they’re in the water, whatever their breed. Float coats If your dog likes to swim in deeper waters, they may benefit from a float coat, which is kind of like a doggie life vest. We tested several models for fit and quality, and found the Vivaglory Ripstop Dog Life Vest to be one of our favorites, and at a reasonable price. It comes in over a dozen colors and patterns, has reflective strips, elastic strap keepers, and a rescue handle on top. It also was the only one we tested that had an extra piece of hook-and-loop material that you could place over the excess on the front adjustment panel, to prevent your dog’s fur from getting caught. If you want your dog to look like a mermaid, the Top Paw Flotation Aid is a decent option, at roughly half the price of the Vivaglory (at this writing). It’s less bulky than the Vivaglory, and doesn’t have some of the thoughtful details either. It’s eye-catchingly adorable but the mermaid tail doesn’t serve any practical purpose and our tester found that it “flops forward onto [the dog’s] back half the time, ruining the mermaid effect.” Staying hydrated It’s critical to keep a dog or cat hydrated in the hot weather, so no matter where you are, make sure your pet has easy access to fresh water. Dogs and cats both pant when they’re hot because it helps them cool down, but dogs rely on it more than cats. “Panting uses up a heck of a lot of moisture,” said Hall, because it’s evaporating the water in their respiratory tract. “So if you’re a dehydrated dog, you’re not able to cool as effectively through panting. You will get hotter quicker, and it will take longer for you to cool down after,” she said. Bowls and fountains at home Your pet’s regular water bowl or fountain should be clean and full, so they can drink whenever they want. Unfortunately not all pets are big drinkers. Some will even happily eat a rotting animal carcass only to then turn around and act as if a bowl of fresh water offended their refined palates. For these stubborn beasts, you might need to resort to a little trickery: Try mixing water into their regular kibble, feeding them more canned wet food, or adding some flavoring to their water bowl. Bottles for on-the-go refreshment You may already have a water bottle that you love, but if you don’t relish the idea of sharing your Stanley Tumbler or Owala FreeSip with your dog, there’s no shortage of pet-specific options. The 20.3-ounce OllyDog OllyBottle is a light and compact BPA-free plastic bottle with a detachable, trough-like bowl. It’s dishwasher-safe, but the cap is connected, so it might get in the way when you’re taking a sip. This bottle also comes in a 33.8-ounce version, which might be better for bigger dogs or thirstier humans. The Springer Flip Portable Dog Water Bottle has, as the name implies, a flip-up food-grade silicone bowl integrated into the top that you squeeze water into from the bottle beneath. It holds 20 ounces of liquid and comes in a bunch of pleasing colors. The Säker Slurpy Sack 2.0 is unique in that the entire thing can collapse to a small, lightweight bundle that packs away easily when it’s empty. It comes in three sizes, 350 ml (about 12 ounces), 550 ml (about 18 ounces), and 750 (about 25 ounces). It works similar to the Springer Flip bottle, but here you unfold the leaf-shaped cup, unlock the opening, and squeeze water out. When your dog is done drinking, you squeeze again to suck the remaining water back in. If you want to carry only one bottle for both yourself and your dog, the Springer Dog and Me Insulated Water Bottle has a detachable bowl integrated into the bottom. It holds 24 ounces and has a flexible silicone cup that slides over the bottle. None of these four bottles leaked in our testing, even when we shook them vigorously, which is more than we can say for some of the others we tried. And they were all fairly easy to clean. Portable water bowls You might also consider collapsible water bowls that are lightweight and can be stored nearly flat so they don’t take a ton of space in a bag. We like the Comsun Collapsible Dog Bowl, which is made of BPA-free food-grade silicone. It flattens in an accordion-like way into a thin disc. These staff-favorite silicone, BPA-free bowls flatten into portable discs, so they’re easy to use on the go. We also like the Ruffwear Quencher Packable Bowl, which is made of flexible polyester ripstop and nylon taffeta. The Quencher’s mouth is wide enough to accommodate large dog snouts, but it can still fold down to about the size of a thick handkerchief and fit into a back pocket. Additional reporting by Haley Sprankle. This article was edited by Harry Sawyers.

item.title: The Best Dish Soap
item.description:
Source: Wirecutter Score: 4.63
Whether you’re tackling a sink full of dishes or simply washing your chef’s knife, squirting dish soap is likely part of your daily routine. Your chosen soap should make washing dishes a little easier, and it gets bonus points if it smells good (or at least doesn’t smell awful). After we tested 35 dish soaps, Palmolive Ultra Pure + Clear Dish Liquid bubbled up to the top as the best choice for hand-washing dishes. For those who prefer sprays designed for spritzing directly on dirty dishes, Dawn Platinum Plus Powerwash Free & Clear is the best all-around option. For beyond-the-sink cleaning, like spot-treating makeup stains on fabrics or scrubbing hard surfaces (like floors, walls, and tables), we recommend Dawn Ultra Dishwashing Liquid. And if your top priority is reducing plastic waste, Cleancult Dish Soap Lemon Verbena does a great job cleaning and comes in a refillable, recyclable aluminum bottle. Everything we recommend Top pick Top pick Best for... Best for... This plant-based, pleasant-smelling dish soap cleans well, and it comes in a refillable and recyclable aluminum bottle. It is dye-free, but it contains allergens that some may find irritating. How we tested - Cleaning performanceWe assessed each dish soap’s ability to remove oils and other common soils. - Scrubbing effortWe considered how much effort it took to scrub stubborn soils off dishes and professionally greased stainless steel tiles. - VersatilityTo test each dish soap’s versatility, we not only hand-washed dishes but also cleaned hard surfaces and attempted to remove stains from textiles. - FormulaWe favored dish soaps that are fragrance-free or mildly scented and hypoallergenic. Top pick Of the 35 dish soaps we tested, Palmolive Ultra Pure + Clear Dish Liquid was the best of the bunch overall. It handily lifted oil from plates, and scrubbing through a variety of soils took minimal effort. In our testing, this dish soap cut grease with ease, even on industrially greased stainless steel tiles. Ultra Pure + Clear is fragrance- and dye-free, as well as hypoallergenic. This soap dispenses easily from the bottle, and it rinses clean from a sponge. In our informal sniff test, we found that sponges used with this soap didn’t smell bad over time. This dish soap typically costs about 12 cents per ounce. Top pick If you prefer a spray-on dish cleaner, Dawn Platinum Plus Powerwash Free & Clear is the best all-around dish spray. It’s easy-to-use and highly effective, powering through grease stains in record time in my tests. This formula is potent, and using too much can lead to an overload of suds (one spritz usually does the trick). Platinum Plus Powerwash Free & Clear has a light, pleasant pear scent that is not overpowering, but you may not like it if you’re sensitive to fragrance. This dish spray typically costs about 32 cents per ounce. Best for... Dawn Ultra Dishwashing Liquid does a fine job of washing dishes. But it truly shines when it’s applied to cleaning projects that remove oils, like wiping down grease-splattered kitchen backsplashes, polishing eye glasses, or spot-treating oily fabric stains. Dawn Ultra has a new scent, which launched in 2024 and is milder than that of the brand’s other dishwashing liquids (including our previous pick, Dawn Platinum Dishwashing Liquid). Dawn Ultra contains synthetic dyes and the preservative methylisothiazolinone (often referred to as MI or MIT), which some people are allergic to. This dish soap typically costs about 18 cents per ounce. Best for... This plant-based, pleasant-smelling dish soap cleans well, and it comes in a refillable and recyclable aluminum bottle. It is dye-free, but it contains allergens that some may find irritating. Cleancult Dish Soap Lemon Verbena was the best plant-based, dye-free dish soap not packaged in plastic that we tested. It cleaned well, though not quite to the level of our other picks. It comes in a refillable and recyclable aluminum bottle (but it has a plastic pump), and the refill liquid is packaged in a recyclable paper carton. The pleasant-smelling formula doesn’t contain synthetic dyes, but the fragrance is naturally derived and potentially allergenic. (There is no fragrance-free version at this time.) This dish soap is the most expensive of our picks, and it typically costs about 37 cents per ounce. Why you should trust us I’m a writer at Wirecutter covering large cleaning appliances and the detergents used in them. I have tested dozens of dishwashers and even more dishwasher detergents. I am also adept at dirtying plates in the name of research. We’ve been recommending dish soap since 2016. For this guide: - I researched dozens of dish soaps and have tested over 40 as of 2026. - I polled almost everyone I know about their dishwashing habits, and I practically drove my closest friends and family to tears with my nonstop questions. - I interviewed an array of experts, including two chemical engineers who are experts in surfactants, representatives from multiple dish soap brands, and a spokesperson from the Environmental Working Group (EWG). - I read several academic papers on the science of surfactants and dish soap. - Paid testers of diverse backgrounds and mobility levels tried a handful of dish soaps at our office in Long Island City, New York. - I visited Procter & Gamble’s research and development facilities in Cincinnati, where I toured the company’s hand-dish lab and interviewed several detergent formulators about the differences between dish soap and dishwasher detergent. - Like all Wirecutter journalists, I review and test products with complete editorial independence. I’m never made aware of any business implications of my editorial recommendations. Read more about our editorial standards. How we picked and tested Dirty dishes are covered with plenty of difficult soils, like blobs of dried yogurt, crusts of baked egg, and glue-like streaks of oatmeal. Water, wiping, and scrubbing can tackle many of these, but oil and grease require dish soap, explained Brian Grady, a chemical engineering professor and the director of the Institute for Applied Surfactant Research at the University of Oklahoma. “With dish soap, the goal is to make fats, which naturally resist water, soluble,” he said. Dish soap is powered by surfactants (short for surface-active agents), which are soap-like molecules that bind oil and water together so they can be washed away. Surfactants are a major component in all kinds of cleaning products, but they are especially important in dish soap. Most of the dish soaps we tested were either traditional liquid formulations or foaming dish sprays, but we also tested concentrated options and solid bars that are marketed as more sustainable (most of these did not clean particularly well). Here’s how we assessed traditional dish soaps: pH level: Common household cleaners are usually either acidic or alkaline, and both types easily bust through grit and grime. But since traditional dish soap comes into contact with skin (which is slightly acidic), it should have a pH ranging from neutral to slightly alkaline to prevent irritation, explained chemical engineer and surfactant expert Steven Abbott. Achieving this ideal pH in a high-performing cleaner is a difficult feat of chemical engineering, he emphasized. We tested the pH of every traditional dish soap, both diluted and straight. Most of them fell within an acceptable, skin-safe range. We disqualified a few moderately alkaline dish soaps (including several bar-style soaps) from further testing, reasoning that if they failed the first basic requirement of a dish-soap formula, there was no need to evaluate them further. Because dish sprays are not meant to come into prolonged contact with skin, we did not include them in this qualifying criteria. Grease-cutting and cleaning power: We ran multiple series of cleaning tests. First, we combined a blue oil-based food dye with canola oil and spread 4 mL of the mixture onto a plate. After leaving the plates to dry for about five minutes (for two rounds of tests) and overnight (for one round), we soaked the dishes for two minutes in 75 °F water that had been mixed with 1 teaspoon of dish soap for 20 seconds. This method measures how the dish soap alone works to clean away oil, and it doesn’t involve scrubbing, which is a hard variable to consistently control. We eyeballed the amount of remaining oil in comparison with our control, which had about 40% of the oil left. And we gave each dish soap a score: excellent (5% to 10% oil remaining); very, very good (10% to 15% oil left); very good (15%); good (20%); okay (25%); and poor (35% or more). Then we ran the highest-performing dish soaps through a modified version of our dishwasher test. We soaked dishes, which were coated in several types of soils, in each formula to see how they fared. We also soaked and scrubbed porcelain and stainless steel tiles; these tiles had been professionally treated with a baked-on grease that is incredibly hard to remove. We recorded how many swipes it took to clean the tiles and how much effort it took to do so. (Two Wirecutter staffers helped us with this test; they didn’t know which dish soaps they were using, and their conclusions were the same.) Additionally, a group of paid testers scrubbed sets of dishes with the highest-performing dye-free dish soaps (with brands concealed). From there, we were able to easily identify two dye-free front-runners. Unlike traditional dish soaps, dish sprays are not designed to be used in a sinkful of water. To test them, I modified our scrubbing test and applied dish sprays to greasy casserole dishes, plates with four types of soils (again, similar to our dishwasher tests), starchy and oily plates, and industrial tiles of grime and grease. I then rinsed them and evaluated the results. Scent, as well as smell over time: We took into account each dish soap’s fragrance (or lack thereof), and we favored fragrance-free options. We also used each dish soap with its own designated sponge for the duration of testing in order to evaluate how the product affects the sponge’s smell over time. Some soaps left sponges smelling terribly, even after repeated hot-water rinses. And other dish soaps began to smell a bit foul themselves after a few weeks. Still others came in bottles that broke easily or collected drippy gunk that was hard to clean. Cleaning versatility: Dish soap is commonly used as a laundry-stain remover and as a cleaner for everything from stainless steel appliances to yoga mats. We tested our top contenders’ ability to clean textiles of oil-based stains like mascara, foundation makeup, lipstick, and dyed cooking oil. We also informally cleaned stainless steel surfaces. Suds: In the cleaning industry, dish soap manufacturers tend to measure the power of a dish soap by the volume and longevity of its suds. The surfactant scientists I spoke with had a similar take: Suds indicate, on some level, that there is dish soap in the water. But suds alone are not a requirement for a good dish soap. As Grady explained, a basin of water mixed with dish soap might be even more powerful once the suds die down because the dishwashing solution is more concentrated. Still, we paid attention to suds, though they were not an official data point in our testing. Top pick: Palmolive Ultra Pure + Clear Dish Liquid Top pick A strong cleaner, fragrance-free Palmolive Ultra Pure + Clear Dish Liquid is the most well-rounded dish soap we tested. It’s a powerful cleaner and degreaser. In our testing, this dish soap consistently removed oil and grease quickly and easily from plates. We used the Ultra Pure + Clear soap in the most challenging stress test, which involved cleaning a stainless steel tile that was professionally coated with grease. Multiple testers found that the tile cleaned with this soap needed the fewest swipes. The formula is free of fragrances and dyes. It is Safer Choice–certified by the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA), and the EWG gives it an A in its cleaning database. Ultra Pure + Clear Dish Liquid is also hypoallergenic, and it does not contain the synthetic preservative methylisothiazolinone, which can cause skin irritation. Its smell didn’t change over time. Some fragrance- and dye-free dish soaps we tested began to develop an acrid odor after a few weeks and left sponges smelling foul. Ultra Pure + Clear Dish Liquid did not; sponges and dishes smelled consistently neutral. It’s affordable and widely available. At about 12 cents per ounce, Ultra Pure + Clear Dish Liquid is one of the most affordable fragrance- and dye-free dish soaps we tested. And we’ve come across this soap fairly often in stores. Flaws but not dealbreakers It’s available only in a plastic bottle. Although the bottle is made of recyclable polyethylene terephthalate (PET) plastic, those looking to cut back on single-use plastics may want to try Cleancult Dish Soap Lemon Verbena, our pick with nearly plastic-free packaging. It’s not as powerful for odd jobs. Ultra Pure + Clear Dish Liquid wasn’t quite as effective at removing oil stains from textiles or hard surfaces. It worked, but not as effortlessly as Dawn Ultra Dishwashing Liquid, our pick for household cleaning projects. (We needed to use more of the Ultra Pure + Clear Dish Liquid to get the same effect.) Best dish spray: Dawn Platinum Plus Powerwash Free & Clear Top pick Dish sprays are designed to be sprayed onto stubborn crud, left for a few minutes, and then wiped or rinsed off. Of the eight dish sprays that I tested, Dawn Platinum Plus Powerwash Free & Clear was the best all around. It eradicated the widest variety of stains — especially grease. Platinum Plus Powerwash Free & Clear easily cut through baked-on oil, grease, and brownie batter, as well as cheesy pasta and sticky jam. Technically, dish sprays like Platinum Plus Powerwash Free & Clear are solvents, not dish soap, explained Grady. Rather than lift away grease like a traditional dish soap, this dish spray “literally softens the grease,” he said, which allows you to remove it without scrubbing or soaking. It’s easy to use. Platinum Plus Powerwash Free & Clear sprays evenly, and the nozzle simply screws onto refill bottles. And as the product begins to work on soils, the suds dissipate, providing a visual cue for when a dish is ready to be wiped down. You can choose from multiple fragrances. While I suggest starting with the lightly pear-scented Free & Clear, Platinum Plus Powerwash also comes in a variety of scents, including apple and lemon. (The Heavy Duty version geared toward cleaning grills, tools, and cars smelled unpleasant.) It can double as a stain remover. Over the years, I have found Platinum Plus Powerwash Free & Clear to be exceptional at spot-treating and pretreating non-biological stains, like kids paint, mascara, some magic marker, and even glue. Just one spritz should be sufficient for pretreating most stains, otherwise you risk overfilling your washing machine with suds. Flaws but not dealbreakers It could irritate your skin. Unlike most dish soaps, which are gentle enough for washing your hands, Platinum Plus Powerwash Free & Clear is alkaline and not formulated to come in direct contact with skin, said Morgan Eberhard, principal scientist at Procter & Gamble. One spritz goes a long way. While it’s tempting to spray Platinum Plus Powerwash Free & Clear onto crusty bakeware or oily saucepans before loading them into the dishwasher, this can cause sudsing at the bottom of your machine (and, if done often enough, damage). Save this dish spray for hand-washing dishes, and always start with one spray. The scent may be too much for those who are sensitive to fragrance. It’s subtle (I actually didn’t notice it until weeks into testing), but it might be too much if fragrance isn’t your thing. It’s expensive. At about 32 cents per ounce, Platinum Plus Powerwash Free & Clear costs almost as much as our most expensive dish soap recommendation. Best for household cleaning projects: Dawn Ultra Dishwashing Liquid Best for... Dawn is a classic for a reason. Dawn Ultra Dishwashing Liquid shines at household cleaning tasks like washing hard surfaces and removing stains from fabric. Just a drop or two can combat greasy, oily messes without leaving soapy residue. It works well on dishes, of course, but its effectiveness and versatility outside the sink were the things that really impressed us. It’s notably good at removing makeup and other oily stains. Dawn Ultra removes oil-based stains (especially lipstick and foundation makeup) from fabrics more efficiently than any of the contenders we tested. (For really tough oil stains, however, you’ll probably still need the enzymatic boost found in a good liquid laundry detergent.) We recommend using Dawn Ultra for spot-cleaning rather than pretreating (too much dish soap can leave behind a sudsy mess in your washing machine). It’s powerful. Dawn Ultra is a strong degreaser that’s excellent for cleaning a variety of surfaces, like stainless steel, kitchen cabinets, and countertops. Its new scent is milder than the classic Dawn fragrance. The current fresh scent of Dawn Ultra launched in late 2024. (If you prefer the previous version, it is available in some areas in bottles labeled “Classic Scent.”) It does a terrific job on dishes, too. Scoring an overall “excellent” rating in our testing, Dawn Ultra was great at cleaning dishes full of gunk and grime. Our paid testers had an easy time scrubbing through plates of gritty marinara sauce. The suds last a long time — but not too long. Suds aren’t a measure of a good dish soap, but many people prefer voluminous froth when washing dishes. Dawn Ultra delivers the suds in the sink, but for other cleaning tasks, a smaller amount creates very little soapy residue to wipe down. Flaws but not dealbreakers It can leave some sponges smelling funky. Dawn dish soaps have polarizing scents, and I often hear from people that the formulas make sponges smell. In our informal sniff test, the sponges designated for Dawn Ultra smelled a touch mustier than those used with other dish soaps. (Though this was easily combatted with a hot water rinse.) It comes in a plastic bottle. Dawn Ultra comes in a pretty standard, albeit recyclable, PET plastic bottle. If you’re eager to cut back on single-use plastics, you might consider our Cleancult pick, which comes in a refillable and recyclable aluminum bottle. The formula contains ingredients that some people want to avoid. Dawn Ultra is not hypoallergenic, and it’s formulated with synthetic dyes and fragrances. Tools and other non-dish items can be washed with — though not soaked in — Dawn Ultra. The company recommends foregoing a soak and applying diluted soap directly instead. (Prolonged soaking can cause etching on the tools.) It’s pricier than our top pick. At about 18 cents an ounce, Dawn Ultra costs a bit more than our top pick. Best for (nearly) non-plastic packaging: Cleancult Dish Soap Lemon Verbena Best for... This plant-based, pleasant-smelling dish soap cleans well, and it comes in a refillable and recyclable aluminum bottle. It is dye-free, but it contains allergens that some may find irritating. Among the many plant-based, dye-free dish soaps not packaged in plastic that we tested, Cleancult Dish Soap Lemon Verbena is our favorite. It’s mild yet effective, and it comes in a refillable, recyclable aluminum bottle. But it’s not without its quirks. It’s the best dish soap of its type. Of the dish soaps we tested that purport to be sustainable, Cleancult Dish Soap consistently lifted the most oil off dishes, earning scores that ranged from “good” to “very good.” The bottle is refillable aluminum. Cleancult Dish Soap comes in a refillable and recyclable aluminum bottle. The bottle’s pump is plastic, but it’s easier to use than a screw top, which are often found on aluminum bottles and can lead to messy pours. Cleancult refills come in recyclable paper cartons. Its surfactants are plant-based. Most widely available dish soaps, including our other three picks, contain some surfactants that are derived from petroleum. Cleancult’s are derived from plants. It’s certified cruelty-free. Our pick from Cleancult is the only dish soap we recommend that is approved by Leaping Bunny. You can find it at brick-and-mortar stores. This is one of the only alternative dish soaps that’s widely available at stores like Walmart, Harris Teeter, CVS, and Walgreens. The scent is mild and pleasant. Every tester who tried this dish soap, including those who generally don’t like fragrance, loved its smell. We preferred the Lemon Verbena scent, but it also comes in nice Fresh Rain and Wild Lavender options. Bonus: The sponge we used with Cleancult Dish Soap smelled pleasantly neutral by the end of testing. Flaws but not dealbreakers Stubborn messes required scrubbing. Don’t expect miracles here: Our paid testers noted that Cleancult required more elbow grease when they were using it to clean tougher soils. And you’ll probably need a stronger option, like one of our picks, for non-dish cleaning projects. It is not hypoallergenic, and there is no fragrance-free version. Both the preservatives and fragrances used in this dish soap’s formula are potentially allergenic. It’s pricey. At 37 cents per ounce, Cleancult Dish Soap is by far the most expensive one we recommend. Other dish soaps worth considering If you want to stick with Dawn but dislike fragrance: Dawn Free & Clear scored high marks too, but it ultimately lost points due to its limited availability. If you need an extra-sudsy dishwashing liquid for grimy messes: Dawn Platinum Dishwashing Liquid, which was a pick in previous versions of this guide, delivers rich suds and powerful cleaning. But the viscous liquid creates an incredibly potent cleaning solution that can leave a stubborn residue. In contrast, a solution of our Dawn Ultra pick and water requires fewer wipe-downs. If you want a dish spray with an enzymatic formula: Method Super Shine Foaming Dish Spray is a solid choice and works well on organic soils, like starch and protein. If you want a plant-based dish soap that has a natural fragrance and is widely available: A former top pick, Seventh Generation Dish Liquid has essential-oil-based scents, which we found to be milder than those of other popular dish soaps. (We tested both the Free & Clear and Yuzu Basil versions.) Seventh Generation dish soap didn’t perform as well as our picks in testing, and it’s not hypoallergenic (even the Free & Clear version), but it’s still worth buying. If you want a heavy-hitting dish soap and you don’t mind scent or dyes: Palmolive Ultra Strength Dish Liquid is the scented and dyed counterpart of our fragrance- and dye-free pick, and it was a very good performer. If you want an inexpensive, widely available throwback. Joy, a matriarch of the dish soap pantheon, is available in multiple pleasant scents, and it earned a “very good” score in testing. If you want a different free-and-clear dish soap that works well: We almost made Puracy Dish Soap a top pick, but it lost out due to its spotty availability and an ever-so-slight difference in performance compared with that of our Palmolive top pick. If you want suds from across the pond: We tested Fairy Dishwashing Liquid, a bright-green dish soap that has a pleasant, fresh scent and is popular in Ireland and the UK. It generated a nice amount of bubbles, and it performed on a par with our Dawn Ultra pick (both are made by Procter & Gamble), but ounce for ounce, it’s expensive to purchase in the US. What about biodegradability? All four of our dish soap picks are biodegradable. In fact, the surfactants in dish soaps need to be biodegradable in order to be processed in wastewater treatment plants, Grady said. Otherwise, the suds would cause buildup and create major issues for municipal water systems. A note on potential ingredients of concern There are typically two main surfactants in dish liquid: sodium lauryl sulfate (SLS) and sodium lauryl ether sulfate (SLES). As Grady explained, SLES is a modified version of SLS, and it has the benefit of creating less soap scum. When SLES is made, the reaction creates a small amount of a compound called 1,4-dioxane, which can be hazardous in high doses. A risk evaluation completed by the EPA in 2020 found “no unreasonable risks” to consumers from dish soaps that contain 1,4-dioxane as a by-product. If you’re still worried about it, dish gloves create a barrier between your skin and the soap. (We like the Evriholder Glam-Gloves and the latex-free Clorox Ultra Comfort Premium Gloves.) None of our picks contains phthalates, a class of chemicals known as plasticizers used in some fragrances. The competition Liquid dish soaps Ajax Ultra Citrus Scent + Salt, Dermassage Dishwashing Liquid, and Ivory Ultra Concentrated Liquid Dish Soap are all quintessential grocery-aisle soaps. And they were all good cleaners, but they didn’t stand out in comparison with our picks. Amazon Basics Liquid Dish Soap, Target’s Everspring Free & Clear Dish Soap, Walmart’s Great Value Ultra Dish Liquid, and Costco’s Kirkland Signature Ultra Shine Platinum Performance Dishwashing Liquid all performed decently for their prices. But in scrubbing tests, they lost marks in comparison with similar formulas. And we had to use more soap for them to be effective. The mildly scented Lemon Essence version of Dawn Free & Clear began to smell strange over time, and the inverted bottle was sometimes tricky to handle. Dawn Platinum Plus PowerSuds failed to impress us for the price (it costs more than twice as much per ounce as our top-pick dish liquid). It was still good overall, however. Method Dish Soap, Mrs. Meyer’s Clean Day, and Rebel Green Super Deluxe Dish Soap are all popular and widely available plant-based dish soaps. They all performed adequately in our testing, and they come in a variety of scents. But none of them had an edge over our picks in cleaning power, packaging, or formula. Attitude Dishwashing Liquid and Molly’s Suds Dish Soap were among the worst-performing liquid dish soaps we tested. Only TrulyFree Natural Dish Soap — a hyperconcentrated gel that comes in a pouch and has to be watered down before use — performed worse. It barely budged oil, even compared with a simple soak in water. Dr. Bronner’s Pure-Castile Magic Soap was terrible at lifting oils and breaking down starches. It was also one of the most alkaline soaps we tested. We had high hopes for Ecover Dish Soap, but it struggled to lift oil from plates and seriously disappointed us. Ecos Dish Soap fared slightly better, but the cloying scent was too much for us. The free-and-clear version was an olfactory improvement, but it did not match the cleaning efficacy of our top pick. Palmolive Ultra Oxy Power Degreaser showed no real performance boost for the price (which is typically more than $8 for a 32.5-ounce bottle). Public Goods Dish Soap was decent for a basic, dye-free dish soap, but it didn’t have any major advantages over our top pick. Solid dish soaps Blueland Dish Soap is a powder (made mostly of baking soda), and it’s a great concept. But we disqualified it because it performs less like a dish soap and more like an Ajax or Bar Keepers Friend powder cleanser. (The bottle collected a large amount of dust and crud throughout testing, too.) It’s better suited for cleaning pots and pans: It did a great job on stubborn soils like baked-on grease, likely due to its abrasive formula. We tested Meliora’s Dish Soap Bar out of curiosity, but its performance was mediocre. Nellie’s Dish Butter is adorable, but you have to dig into it and scoop it out, and we found it hard to control how much soap we used. Also, the ceramic container was slippery, and for tough soils, we had to scrub more than we did with other soaps. The container eventually fell off a table and cracked into pieces. Vove Dish Soap Bar melted down so quickly that we barely had time to test it, and what we managed to try didn’t impress us. Dish Sprays Seventh Generation Power+ Foaming Dish Spray wasn’t easy to neatly apply, and it struggled with crusty starch stains. J.R. Watkins Foaming Dish Soap smelled good but lacked the oomph of our Dawn spray pick. You may still find it online, but it seems to have been discontinued. Ecos Foaming Dish Spray required more sprays and more wipe-downs than other dish sprays. Leigh Krietsch Boerner contributed reporting. This article was edited by Rory Evans, Ingrid Skjong, and Marguerite Preston. Sources - Brian Grady, PhD, professor of chemical engineering at the University of Oklahoma, video interview, May 2025 - Tre Wright, chemical engineer, phone interview, May 2024 - Morgan Eberhard, principal scientist and scientific communications director, NA Home Care at Procter & Gamble, in-person interview, February 2025 - Steven Abbott, chemist and consultant on surfactants, video interview, March 2025 Meet your guide Andrea Barnes I research and report on dishwashers, washing machines, dryers, and laundry. This involves touring factories, visiting showrooms, attending trade shows, speaking with appliance-brand representatives, interviewing experts, studying patents and schematics, and reading manuals. I am based in New York City, and I test appliances in our Long Island City office. Further reading - by Wirecutter Staff Dish soap is cheap, safe to use, and one of the best all-purpose cleaners. Here are the surprising places you can use it around your home.

item.title: How to Shop for a Used Laptop or Desktop PC
item.description:
Source: Wirecutter Score: 3.71
As tech prices soar, it can be nearly impossible to find an affordable computer with a screen that’s nice to look at, a keyboard and trackpad that are comfortable to use — or just not terrible — and fast-enough performance that won’t leave you waiting for apps and tabs to open. One solution? A used PC. Buying a good used PC entails a little more work than getting something new, but a laptop or desktop from a few years ago should still be good enough for you to browse the internet, hop on video calls, edit documents and other school projects, and chat with friends. Manufacturers like Apple and Dell and stores like Best Buy, Newegg, and others all sell refurbished PCs, saving you from riskier sites like Craigslist and eBay. Why you might want to buy used In getting a used PC, you can save a few hundred dollars on a computer that can do most of the same stuff a new one can. For the things most people do on their computers — browsing the web, editing documents and spreadsheets, or looking at and editing pictures and videos from your phone — a new computer and one from a few years ago don’t perform that differently from one another. If you’re on a strict budget, buying used may allow you to buy something that’s nicer than a modern budget laptop for the same money. A high-end Lenovo ThinkPad that sold for $1,400 two or three years ago, for example, will have an as-fast-or-faster processor, more memory, and a better screen than a new laptop that’s selling for $700. Plus, buying a used PC cuts down on electronic waste. You rescue an old but functional computer from getting thrown in the trash, and you avoid buying a cheap PC that will wear out and be disposed of in a few years. Reasons not to buy used If you’re looking to play high-end games or do professional 3D drafting work, a used PC might not be the best choice. Graphics processors still advance faster than other computer components, and newer PC games have higher system requirements. Many used laptops have limited to no customer service or warranty support. The best support comes with manufacturer-refurbished PCs, which carry a like-new warranty from the company that made the computer. It’s more common to find limited 30- to 90-day warranties from retailers that will cover if the computer is dead on arrival, but not much else. Third-party extended warranties from companies like Asurion, Geek Squad, or SquareTrade are almost never worth it. You also have fewer choices when shopping for a used PC. You might not be able to find a particular model, but you can find something good from a reliable manufacturer with a decent warranty and fast enough specs, if you know where to look and what to look for. Where to buy a used computer When it comes to buying used PCs, avoid sites like Craigslist, eBay, or Reddit. Although it’s possible to find good deals, if you don’t know exactly what you’re looking for, it’s easy to get tripped up by fake or misleading listings or even a PC preloaded with malware. You can avoid scams and heartbreak by buying directly from manufacturers or sticking to major retailers with good warranties. Computers from these sellers are also more likely to be professionally cleaned and restored. Since you’re limited to a smaller pool of available devices, we recommend that you pick a manufacturer first and then look for a computer with our recommended specs on its website. Manufacturer-refurbished computers Manufacturer-refurbished computers have been returned to the company that made them, repaired with new parts, and resold in like-new condition, often (but not always) with the same warranty you get with new devices. They’re a great option to save some money and avoid many of the risks that come with buying used. Apple and Dell typically have the best stock of refurbished PCs, with frequently updated inventories of near-new desktops and laptops. Both companies offer the same warranties that they provide with their new products, including the ability to extend those warranties for years. They also make it easy to sort computers by specs. If you’re buying a refurbished Mac, stick to models released after 2020 that have Apple’s faster M-series chips; these MacBooks also have longer battery life and more reliable keyboards than older models. We also recommend 16 GB of memory, if you can find it. Business desktops and laptops make great refurbs — they’re chunkier than sleek ultrabooks, but they’re more durable and easier to upgrade and repair. For a refurbished Dell computer, look at the Dell Latitude and Pro series. And check Dell’s coupon codes to see if there are any models with particularly good discounts; these codes refresh every week or so. Lenovo and HP also offer refurbs with a one-year warranty — we recommend the Lenovo ThinkCentre and ThinkPad family, and the HP Pro and Elite lineup — though you have to call to order from HP. We don’t recommend any manufacturer refurb with a warranty shorter than one year. Retailer-refurbished and used computers Another option is shopping the refurbished and used sections from a trustworthy retailer like Best Buy, Newegg, or OWC. But there’s a difference between a manufacturer-refurbished PC and one listed as “refurbished” on retailer sites like Best Buy and Newegg — at many online stores, “refurbished” is usually just a fancy word for “used.” When you’re shopping retailer refurbs, Wirecutter Deals senior editor Nathan Burrow recommends looking for the longest warranty possible and then sticking to items in “excellent,” “like new,” or “very good” condition. If you’re looking for a Mac, OWC has a great reputation for used and refurbished products, and it offers a range of models. These computers have 90-day warranties out of the box, but you can add up to two years of additional warranty coverage. Best Buy has a wide selection of preowned, refurbished, and open-box laptops and desktops. The site’s filters help narrow down your search by specs, and the desktops in particular are good deals if you can upgrade the memory or install an SSD yourself. But Best Buy’s standard 90-day warranty is shorter than we’d like to see. For Best Buy’s open-box items, Nathan recommends finding what you’re looking for in a nearby store and then checking it out in person for issues before purchasing. Newegg also has a lot of used laptop and desktop listings, though its search function isn’t as nice, and you have to be extra vigilant about checking for our recommended specs. Use the “sold/shipped by Newegg” search filters to avoid anything sold by a sketchy third party. And since you can’t inspect the device, look for a manufacturer warranty or a 180-day warranty. Avoid Newegg’s open-box section — the 30-day return window is too short. Local computer stores may also be a good place to check for used hardware. Micro Center has a decent selection of refurbished desktops and laptops; some are available online, but many are available only in a physical store. You might have other options local to you — in the San Francisco Bay Area, for example, Central Computers is a well-regarded local chain. A little research and checking Yelp and the BBB might reveal good, reasonably priced options near you, and calling ahead with our recommended specs can help you figure out if any of the store’s in-stock systems fit your needs. We don’t recommend Amazon Renewed computers because the 90-day warranty is short, and you have no way to examine things before you buy them. Amazon claims its Renewed products have been “professionally inspected and tested to meet quality standards by an Amazon qualified and performance-managed supplier,” but the company also says “If that supplier is a third-party seller, the third-party seller tests and inspects the product.” If you take your chances on a site like eBay, it’s especially important to make sure the pictures in the listing are of the actual computer you’ll be buying — not one laptop among several, or pictures that claim to be “representative” of what you’re buying. Avoid buying computers from outside the US, since they can take several weeks to ship, such listings are more likely to be scams, and you may be on the hook for unexpected customs fees. Check the listings for laptops to make sure that the charger is included. And don’t buy from sellers with little feedback or negative feedback. What to look for The three most important things to look for in a used PC are its physical condition (especially for laptops, which take more physical punishment), the warranty, and its specifications. The only way to guarantee you’ll get something close to new is to buy a manufacturer-refurbished system. For retailer-refurbished PCs, stick to those in “excellent,” “like new,” or “very good” condition; other sellers may assign letter grades — look for an A or a B rating. Look for the longest warranty you can find — at least one year for manufacturer-refurbished systems, and at least 180 days (six months) for a used PC from an online retailer. Wirecutter Deals senior editor Nathan Burrow recommends manufacturer warranties over retailer ones, where they’re available. If you can check out the computer in person before buying it, you can get away with a shorter, 90-day warranty, but longer is always better. Generally, we suggest sticking to PCs made by Dell, HP, or Lenovo (or Apple, if you’re buying a Mac). It’s okay to buy used computers made by Acer or Asus, but it’s usually easier to find parts and support for older computers made by the bigger companies. Recommended specs Most people will be well served by a computer that meets our recommended specs for basic tasks like web browsing, document editing, and video chatting. Here’s what to look for: - Processor: Look for a 12th-generation or newer Intel Core i5 or i7 U–series processor; they have model numbers that start with i5 or i7 and end with 12xxxU or 13xxxU. (Avoid models with P at the end, which had heat and battery life issues in our testing.) We also recommend newer 100–series, 200–series, and 300–series Core 5 or Core 7 processors from Intel — they have a similar naming scheme, with model numbers that look like 1xxU, 2xxU or 2xxV, or 3xx. On the AMD side, look for 7000–series or newer AMD Ryzen 3, 5, or 7 processors, which start with the Ryzen 3, Ryzen 5, or Ryzen 7 name and end with 7xxxU. Like Intel, AMD also rebooted its naming scheme in recent years, and we also recommend newer 100–series, 200–series, AI 300–series, and AI 400–series Ryzen 3, 5, and 7 processors. - Memory: Aim for 16 GB of memory if you can find it, which will help your computer feel fast and responsive for everyday tasks for years to come.
