You can get by with 8 GB on macOS and Windows, but on Windows you’ll need to be especially careful not to run too many programs or open too many browser tabs at once. If you do buy a computer with 8 GB or less, check to see if you can upgrade the memory yourself — you can almost always upgrade a desktop, but lots of laptops don’t allow it. - Storage: An SSD that’s 128 GB or larger is enough for your operating system, apps, and important documents. If you need more space for photos, large files, or games, look for a larger drive or plan to supplement with a cloud storage service or an external drive. - Screen resolution: A resolution of 1920×1080 (also called 1080p or Full HD) provides the best combination of sharpness and battery life for a laptop. You may be able to find laptops with 4K displays, but this higher resolution adds to the laptop’s cost and reduces battery life. In Macs, look for a Retina Display. - Screen type: For laptops, look for IPS or OLED displays, which provide better color reproduction and viewing angles than cheap TN displays. Used-computer listings don’t always specify the display technology, but 1080p screens are more likely (albeit not guaranteed) to be IPS. - USB-C or Thunderbolt ports: These aren’t a necessity, but a USB-C port that can charge a laptop and connect to newer monitors is especially convenient (these ports are not as big a deal for desktops). Replacement USB-C chargers are also easier to find and cheaper to buy. Things to avoid with used PCs - Old or slow processors: This list includes Intel Celerons and Pentiums, tenth-generation and earlier Intel Core processors, as well as AMD A–series and 3000–series and 5000–series processors. These are older or slower processors that will all feel their age as you use them. Some may even have trouble supporting basic features of Windows. - 4 GB of RAM: This isn’t sufficient for even the most basic of tasks on Windows, and feels frustrating to use with only a single app open. - 1366×768 screens: These low-resolution screens, sometimes called HD or WXGA displays, can’t fit as much information and don’t look as sharp as higher-resolution screens. They’re also more likely to use cheap, washed-out TN display panels. - Spinning hard drives (HDD): A traditional hard drive is the slowest part of any older or cheaper computer. If you buy a computer with an HDD, consider replacing that storage with an SSD. - Less than 64 GB of storage: That isn’t enough space to install Windows and important apps while leaving enough room for Windows Update to work properly. - 802.11n Wi-Fi (aka Wi-Fi 4): A computer with an older Wi-Fi adapter can still connect to newer networks, but Wi-Fi 5 (or 802.11ac) has been standard in most computers for more than a decade. (Wi-Fi 6 was introduced in 2021, and the newer, faster Wi-Fi 7 launched in 2024.) So you should avoid Wi-Fi 4. What to look for and things to avoid with used Macs - Look for Apple Silicon processors: Even for used models, we recommend sticking to Apple’s M-series processors, since they offer far better speed and battery life. M1 and M2 MacBook Airs, especially those with 8 GB of memory, are fine for basic web browsing and checking emails, but will start to lag when working across many tabs and applications. - Look for 16 GB of memory: Starting in late 2024, all Apple computers (except for the MacBook Neo) come with 16 GB of memory to help power the company’s AI features. The 16 GB models will be much more capable at juggling tons of Chrome tabs, working across multiple apps, and handling media work like recording music or editing video. - Avoid MacBooks released between 2016 and 2019: 13- and 15-inch MacBook Pros released between 2016 and 2019, 13-inch MacBook Airs released in 2018 and 2019, and all models of the 12-inch MacBook all employ a shallow, unsatisfying “butterfly” keyboard with well-documented reliability problems. Upgrades and repairs When you buy a used PC, you might find that it needs maintenance more quickly or more regularly than a brand-new computer. Or it might need some extra memory or faster storage to help it cope better with modern websites and apps. You can upgrade nearly all desktops and many laptops with a bit of time, research, and a few tools. We can’t advise you on every possible repair to every possible system — iFixit has some PC repair guides, though not for all models — but we can cover the basics. And we have some more advice for repairing and resuscitating an old laptop. - SSD: If you buy a used PC with a spinning hard drive, that component will be by far the slowest thing in the entire computer. Upgrading to a solid-state drive will dramatically speed things up. We have SSD recommendations for older and newer computers — Crucial’s System Advisor page can give you some information on the kind of drive you need. - Memory: A Windows PC with 4 GB of memory will struggle once you’ve opened more than an app and a few browser tabs, and even 8 GB feels limiting nowadays. If you’re upgrading, we recommend 16 GB to keep things running smoothly for the next few years. Again, the Crucial System Advisor page can tell you what kind of memory to buy for your system — though many laptops, including all MacBooks made after 2012, don’t allow memory upgrades at all. - Chargers: Some used laptops are sold without chargers, and older MacBook power supplies in particular are prone to fraying. It’s safest to buy a replacement directly from your computer’s manufacturer, and Acer, Apple, Asus, Dell, HP, and Lenovo all have stores you can try. Avoid cheap knock-off chargers, which don’t last as long and can be fire hazards, and don’t buy Apple chargers from eBay, where counterfeits are almost unavoidable. OWC sells genuine Apple chargers for older MacBooks for less than Apple’s prices. For newer USB-C laptops, any certified USB-C charger should work fine. - Wi-Fi: Wi-Fi adapters might not be included in your used PC, especially in older desktops. That’s fine if you can connect the computer to your router with a wire, but if you can’t, reliable USB Wi-Fi adapters are available for as little as $20. Software updates - Windows 10 and 11: If your used PC came with Windows 10 installed, you should upgrade to Windows 11 — Microsoft stopped providing security updates for Windows 10 in October 2025, unless you enroll in the Extended Security Updates program to receive security updates through October 2027. Typically, PCs produced after 2016 or 2017 will have a new enough processor and the required security chip to run this latest version of Windows. But if it came with Windows 7 or 8 (which are no longer receiving security updates), you should upgrade. See our instructions on how to upgrade or install Windows from scratch. - macOS: Apple makes it pretty easy to upgrade to the latest version of macOS that your particular Mac is capable of running — this page can help you determine whether you can install the latest version and what you need to do. Meet your guides I’ve been Wirecutter’s resident laptop expert for more than a decade. In that time, I’ve tested hundreds of laptops—including ultrabooks, gaming laptops, Chromebooks, and budget Windows laptops—as well as thousands of keyboards, mice, and other peripherals. Dave Gershgorn I am based in Seattle and responsible for Wirecutter’s computer monitor coverage, as well as all our guides to Apple laptops and desktops. I also review higher-powered laptops, such as business laptops and laptops for photo and video editing. Plus, I write our reviews for all-in-one computers, ergonomic keyboards, and home 3D printers. If it has a screen, sits on a desk, and isn’t a basic Windows ultrabook, I’m usually the person to try it out.

item.title: The Best Compact Washer and Dryer
item.description:
Source: Wirecutter Score: 3.17
If you can’t quite fit a full-size washer and dryer into your home, a 24-inch compact washer and dryer pair will usually work instead. After months of testing compact washing machines and dryers, we think the Miele WXD160 washer and its companion ventless dryer, the Miele TXD160, are the first models you should consider. Everything we recommend Top pick This compact washer is effective at lifting stains but still gentle on fabrics. Miele is well known for manufacturing durable appliances. This ventless heat-pump dryer matches our favorite compact washer and can plug into a standard 120-volt outlet. It is more energy efficient than a traditional dryer, but it takes longer to dry a typical laundry load. Runner-up This compact washer has a shorter wash time and a fast spin cycle that thoroughly wrings out excess water. This ventless condenser dryer can piggyback off the power supply of its matching washing machine, so you’ll need only one 240-volt outlet. But dry times are long. Best for... This compact washer excels at cleaning, accommodates slightly larger loads, and can be plugged into a regular outlet. It’s more affordable than our other two picks, but Electrolux isn’t as well known for reliability. This ventless condenser dryer fits more laundry than our other picks. But it runs hot and dries slowly. How we tested - Stain removalWe ran industrial stain removal tests to evaluate how well each washing machine cleaned laundry. - Fabric careWe looked for machines that washed and dried with minimal wear and tear on fabrics. - Ease of useWe prioritized easy-to-see control panels, doors that opened and closed smoothly, and models that are stackable. - ReliabilityWe spoke with brand experts and repair techs and read owner reviews to get a sense of a machine’s dependability. I wrote our guide to full-size washing machines and their matching dryers and conducted multiple rounds of testing for it. We’ve been evaluating compact washing machines and dryers since 2017. This guide builds on previous testing and extensive research. For this guide: - I spoke with product managers at various appliance manufacturers, toured showrooms around New York City, interviewed a number of appliance repair experts, and spoke with several independent washing machine and dryer experts, including the author of a dissertation on washing machine design. - I chatted with customer service representatives for each appliance brand we tested. - Like all Wirecutter journalists, I review and test products with complete editorial independence. I’m never made aware of any business implications of my editorial recommendations. Read more about our editorial standards. Who this is for If you’re short on space and can’t fit a traditional, full-size washer-dryer pair, a compact washing machine and dryer might be the solution. Unlike full-size washing machines and dryers, which are generally wider than 27 inches, most compact washing machines and dryers are 24 inches wide (or less), about 24 inches deep, and around 33 inches tall. They generally take up about the same amount of space as a dishwasher. You often find compact washers and dryers in spaces with narrower dimensions, like older homes with slimmer entryways, small apartments, or condos. Compact laundry machines still need most of the same plumbing and electrical requirements as a standard washer and dryer, including hot- and cold-water hookups, a 240-volt outlet (though one of our picks can be plugged into a 120-volt outlet), and a drain nearby. But even the best compact washing machines and dryers have downsides: They usually have around half the capacity of today’s full-size machines. Washing large items like comforters or hefty, family-size loads in one go is out of the question. They’re also more expensive than their full-size counterparts. Compact dryers are often (though not always) ventless, meaning they don’t require a vent to blow exhaust through a window, wall, or duct. Some compact dryers will need to be hooked up to a drain. Others collect water in a reservoir instead (this style of compact dryer is easier and more flexible to install). Although many compact dryers require a 240-volt outlet, our pick requires a 120-volt outlet, offering even more flexibility. But the condenser technology used in compact dryers tends to dry items more slowly than traditional dryers would, due to both the drying design and the smaller capacity. Even if you consistently wash smaller loads, we recommend going with a full-size washer and dryer if you have the space. Full-size machines are nearly always less expensive, and you’ll spend a lot less time waiting for your laundry to dry. How we picked and tested For our most recent round of testing, we assessed six pairs of 24-inch (or European-style) front-loading compact washers and their matching ventless dryers. We limited our recommendations to matching pairs, since these machines are easier to stack and often work better as a set. Based on our testing of full-size washers and dryers, we’re able to draw some conclusions regarding the washing and drying performance of compact machines. Compacts present a few more limitations, particularly if the dryers are ventless, which will extend drying time. However, overall we expect a brand's compact washers and dryers will perform similarly to their full-size counterparts. Here’s how we evaluated them: Cleaning performance: We paid attention to stain and odor removal, how gently the machines handled fabric, and how loud they were while running. We also washed a variety of load sizes (from 4 pounds to 16 pounds) with a range of laundry, including duvets, sheets, towels, and a mixture of clothing that a typical household might go through to get a sense of the machines’ usability and capacity. Spin speed: The washer’s spin speed impacts how quickly and fully your clothes will dry. A faster spin wrings out more water, leaving less work for the dryer to do. This is especially important with ventless dryers, since they dry items more slowly and less efficiently than traditional vented models. We looked for compact washers with a minimum spin speed of 1,200 rpm. (The higher the number, the drier the clothes.) We weighed loads before and after each test wash to gauge the power of each machine’s spin cycle. Capacity: The models we recommend easily held 16-pound loads in our tests, but they operated best with loads of about 10 pounds. This is fairly small (family-size loads are typically in the 12- to 16-pound range), but a larger load will take much longer to dry. One of our washing-machine picks can handle loads as heavy as 20 pounds, but expect a long dry time. An accelerated wash cycle: That is, an option to run a “normal” cleaning cycle in about 40 minutes or less. (This type of cycle is typically less water and energy efficient.) The “normal” cycle of a compact front-loader can take up to 120 minutes, so we prioritized washers that also offered a shorter cycle (40 minutes or less) that still washed effectively. Drying time: No ventless dryer that uses condenser technology will dry clothing as fast as a traditional, vented dryer. But we paid close attention to exactly how long each dry cycle took, and some machines were far faster than others. We also evaluated sensor accuracy and temperature controls. Moisture removal: Ventless dryers usually need to be hooked up to a drain, but some models store evaporated water in a reservoir, which needs to be emptied regularly for the dryer to work properly. (Our top and best-for picks operate this way.) Convenience and quietness: We checked that filters were easily accessible for routine maintenance. We paid attention to how much noise and vibration the machines produced, especially during the fastest spin cycles. Reliability and customer service: Compact laundry machines, especially in the US, are much less popular than full-size washers and dryers, so user feedback is scarce. To assess reliability and customer service, we called and chatted with customer service reps, perused Reddit and asked for feedback on specific models, studied warranties, and talked to various service techs about parts and service availability nationwide. We also drew on our research into and experience with brands that make full-size washing machines and dryers we have tested. Price: Perhaps unintuitively, compact washers and dryers cost more than full-size machines; even less expensive models tend to have a list price of $1,000 or higher. This is partly due to their lower demand. While we considered price, we focused on reliability and performance in making our recommendations. What to know about ventless dryers Most compact dryers are ventless (they don’t require a vent to blow exhaust to the outside), which makes them more flexible to install (in a closet, for example). There are, however, a few things to keep in mind about ventless dryers: They are always electric. Ventless models are always electric and never gas-powered. They often need to plug into a 240-volt outlet, just like a standard dryer (though some models, like one of our picks, require only a 120-volt outlet). If you’re setting up a new laundry space, you might need to call an electrician to rig a new connection. They have to connect to a drain, or collect moisture in a reservoir. Unlike traditional vented dryers that release moisture from clothing via steam, ventless dryers often rely on a condenser, which converts evaporated moisture from the laundry into water. Some machines snake excess moisture out via a drain, and others collect water in a reservoir that needs to be emptied regularly. These dryers can also release some humidity into the air. Their filter systems require regular attention. You should clean out your lint trap regularly regardless of the type of dryer you own, but it is essential to do so in order to keep a condenser dryer running smoothly. Condenser dryers (whether or not they use a heat pump) require multiple layers of filtration to operate optimally. Cycles are longer. Ventless dryers take longer to dry clothing — depending on the model, sometimes twice as long. The dry time might be shorter if laundry is washed in a washer with a very fast spin cycle. (You could also consider using a good drying rack along with your dryer to lighten the load.) Dry times can also be lengthened by high humidity. Conversely, a condenser dryer will radiate some heat and moisture into a living space, which is worth noting if you live somewhere with a humid climate. Ventless condenser dryers can be a little rough on fabrics. Though condenser dryers often run at cooler temperatures than vented dryers, their longer cycles can cause more mechanical damage to fabrics — similar to the wear that a full-size traditional washing machine will dole out over time. Ventless heat pump dryers are an upgrade. Heat pump dryers remove moisture via a refrigeration system that works similarly to a dehumidifier, extracting moisture rather than heating it until it evaporates. (Our top pick is a heat pump ventless dryer.) Because heat pump dryers have a closed-loop system, they use about half as much energy as both vented dryers and traditional condenser dryers. They also dry clothes at much lower temperatures, which is easier on clothes. And unlike traditional condenser dryers, they will not introduce humidity into your home. The WXD160, which is the base model of Miele’s W1 washer series, ranks consistently high in our tests, even when compared with full-size washing machines. Though the set is expensive, we think its high performance and reputation for longevity make it well worth the investment. Stain and odor removal is outstanding. The WXD160 washer scored some of the highest marks for cleaning and stain removal in our tests, including when compared with full-size machines. It accomplished this with the same size load as full-size machines, despite the smaller drum with less room for water and detergent to circulate. The washer has an excellent accelerated cycle and treats fabrics with care. The WXD160’s accelerated wash cycle can run in less than 35 minutes. (But the spin speed is slower than in the normal wash cycle, which means clothes may require a longer dry time.) This machine also scored the highest marks possible on our gentleness test. The WXD160 has a very fast spin cycle. This washer spins at 1,600 rpm, which is the fastest of our picks. In our tests, the WXD160 extracted more water per load — at least 2 cups — than all of the full-size models we tested. This helps to reduce drying time. The TXD160 is a ventless heat-pump dryer. Heat-pump dryers are more expensive, but they dry laundry at lower temperatures (which is gentler on fabrics) and are more energy efficient than ventless condenser models. The dryer doesn’t require a drain hookup. The TXD160 collects moisture in a reservoir that must be emptied and cleaned periodically (one to two times per week in our experience). Because this model doesn’t need a drain, its installation options are a bit more flexible. The pair is Wi-Fi–enabled. Both machines can be connected to the Miele app so you can utilize features like alerts that tell you when cycles are finished. This can be convenient, but you don’t need the app to run the machines. Installation is particularly flexible. Both the WXD160 and the TXD160 can be plugged into a regular 120-volt outlet. And the TXD160’s drainless system means you can put the dryer almost anywhere. This situates this set among the most convenient compact laundry duos available. These machines are also stackable. Both machines have above-average warranties. The WXD160 and the TXD160 each come with a two-year warranty, which is longer than we’ve found for most compacts. You can extend that to either five or 10 years. And Miele is known for making long-lasting appliances. Flaws but not dealbreakers This pair is pricey. Despite being entry-level machines, the WXD160 and the TXD160 together typically cost over $3,000. After testing many compact washers and dryers, we believe this set is worth the price and should be the first compact pair you consider. Miele service techs can be harder to find. If your Miele washer or dryer breaks, finding a qualified technician can be tricky if you don’t live near a major metropolitan area. Check that there are qualified technicians in your vicinity before you buy. You’ll need to clean the plinth filter and lint trap regularly. In condenser dryers, even the smallest amount of lint can damage the drying system. To combat this, Miele has designed the TXD160 to alert users whenever the plinth filter needs to be cleaned (usually once every 10 or so dry cycles). The dryer will stop its cycle until you do so, which can be annoying, but ultimately protects the lifespan of the dryer. The lengthy warm-water cycles can fade clothing. The WXD160’s excellent cleaning technology and longer warm-water cycles can lead to fabric fading over time. The machine also defaults to a warm wash, making it easy to accidentally select (even if you typically wash in cold). This is a somewhat common complaint about the WXD160 and something to keep in mind if you wash a lot of darker, colorful items.
